places.n: Bistro Beppinsha (カリー＆ワイン ビストロべっぴん舎 お茶の水本店)
places.hood: 千代田区神田小川町 (Kanda-Ogawamachi / Ochanomizu–Jimbocho), Tokyo
places.cu: Medicinal (薬膳) Japanese-style spice curry & wine bistro
places.notes: [GF] Beppinsha actively markets its spice curries as wheat-free (グルテンフリーカリー) and the thin, roux-free 薬膳 broth is thickened by spices, not flour — a genuinely low-risk base. But it is a shared curry-and-wine bistro with no formal celiac handling, so ask the staff to confirm no wheat-based soy/Worcestershire sauce touches your plate, order the curry over plain rice, and skip any bread. Cash only; lunch-only at present with irregular closing days (Mon & Wed).
places.chef: owner-manager · Tokyo, Japan · Beppinsha opened in 2016 in the Kanda-Jimbocho/Ochanomizu district, originally conceived as a curry-and-wine bistro serving curry only at lunch. The owner-manager brought experience from a long-established curry shop and a wine bistro; the curry lineage traces back through Kashiwa's 「ボンベイ」 (Bombay) to Ueno's 「デリー」 (Delhi), often cited as Japan's first authentic Indian restaurant. After winning the 神田カレーグランプリ (Kanda Curry Grand Prix) two years running, the shop pivoted to focus on curry. It was selected as a Michelin Guide Tokyo 2021 Bib Gourmand and repeatedly listed in Tabelog's Curry TOKYO 100 (2019, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2026). · Curry as wellness — an oil-light, wheat-flour-free 薬膳 (medicinal) broth built from 20+ spices that the manager calls 「元気になれるカレー」 ("curry that restores vitality"), easy on the stomach with a clean, refreshing finish. · 赤のべっぴん薬膳カリー — the "red" medicinal curry with eight wine-simmered vegetables and 20+ medicinal spices in a thin, roux-free broth.
places.gfd: Beppinsha's signature medicinal (薬膳) spice curries are made without wheat flour by design — the shop states plainly 「小麦粉を使わないグルテンフリーカリー」 ("The spice curry without wheat flour") and describes 「小麦粉を使わないさらさらの薬膳カレー」, a thin, roux-free broth built from 20+ spices rather than a flour thickener. This makes the core curries structurally wheat-free, but it is a shared bistro kitchen (14 seats, curry + wine) with no celiac allergy protocol, so cross-contact and wheat-containing seasonings (soy sauce, Wor…
places.vgd: The core curries contain animal protein (chicken drumstick, beef tendon, shrimp) and the lunch set includes potato salad (typically mayonnaise-based). There is no advertised vegan curry; a mostly-vegetable version might be negotiable but is not documented. Vegan diners should ask directly.
places.hours: Tue–Sun & holidays 11:00–15:30 (lunch only at present); closed Mon & Wed. (Formerly also dinner 18:00–20:00.)

places.n: BIOSSA (ビオッサ)
places.hood: 文京区春日 (Kasuga, Bunkyo-ku) — ~1.2km NW of Suidobashi, ~9 min walk from Myogadani Station
places.cu: Gluten-free rice-flour bakery (米粉パン)
places.notes: [GF-dedicated] A completely wheat-free, 100% rice-flour bakery — the strongest celiac option in the wider Suidobashi/Bunkyo area and safe for a 13-year-old celiac to eat freely, since no wheat is handled on-site. It is a takeout bakery (no seating/reservations), so grab loaves, rolls and buns to go. Note it sits ~1.2km NW of Suidobashi, just OUTSIDE the strict 1km circle — flagged for Greg. Closed Tuesdays; cards and QR payment (PayPay, d払い, Rakuten Pay, au PAY) accepted.
places.chef: 宮城伸夫 (Miyagi Nobuo) · Founder, 代表取締役 (Representative Director) · Tokyo, Japan · 宮城伸夫 (Miyagi Nobuo) founded 株式会社biossa in August 2019 and opened the Kasuga bakery on 18 December 2019 in Bunkyo-ku. He himself has a wheat allergy (代表の宮城氏自身も小麦アレルギーを持つ), which became the personal driving force behind the business. The company built a completely gluten-free manufacturing facility that brings no wheat in — 「小麦を持ち込まない完全グルテンフリー製造工場」 — using reliable technique and quality ingredients to make health-conscious, original breads. In 2023 they added a new factory in Kawaguchi, Saitama (operations from December 2023, full production from January 2024) to mass-produce five staple lines: BIO食パン, BIOバゲット, BIOプチブール and BIOバンズ among them. · 「パンとしておいしくなくては、食べ続けることはできません。開発にあたっては、味や食感にこだわった製品を目指しました」 — bread has to taste good or you can't keep eating it. Rather than the typical dense 'mochi-mochi' rice-bread texture, BIOSSA deliberately engineers a light, fluffy crumb like wheat bread by finely tuning the amylose content of the rice flour and the ratio of thickener to water. · Completely gluten-free 100% 国産米粉 (domestic rice flour) breads made with rice oil and beet sugar, including a signature rice-flo…
places.gfd: [Owner review 2026-10-14: GF dedicated. Band 1 (the disproven claim was not about gluten; GF basis verified and intact) — restored per recommendation.] BIOSSA is a 100% rice-flour, completely wheat-free dedicated bakery — the gold standard for a celiac. Their own site states 「『完全』グルテンフリーのベーカリー…グルテンを含む原材料を生産現場に持ち込まない」 (a 'completely' gluten-free bakery that does NOT bring gluten-containing ingredients into the production site) and 「小麦を持ち込まない完全グルテンフリー製造工場」 (a completely gluten-free manufacturing …
places.vgd: Not a vegan bakery, but many items are plant-based: they build on 国産米粉100% with 米油 (rice oil) and てんさい糖 (beet sugar) rather than butter. Baguettes, bean/red-bean breads and the soy (SOI) bread are typically dairy- and egg-free, while items like the 塩バターロール (salt butter roll), 豆乳クリームパン (soy-milk cream bun) and some sweet breads may contain butter, egg or dairy. Confirm the specific loaf's ingredie…
places.hours: 10:00-18:00 daily; closed Tuesdays

places.n: Cafe de Forte (カフェ・ド・フォルテ)
places.hood: 文京区春日 (Kasuga, Bunkyo-ku) — 小石川Jフラッツ 1F, ~0.9km WNW of Suidobashi; ~11 min walk from Myog…
places.cu: Rice-flour (米粉) cafe — Japanese home-style light meals, pancakes & sweets
places.notes: [GF] — A 米粉 (rice-flour) cafe run by an Iwate-born owner and her daughter; it caters to celiac/gluten-intolerant guests but openly states 「全てのメニューがグルテンフリーではありません」and 「アレルギー完全対応ではありません」, so wheat is present in a shared kitchen. For a celiac 13-year-old: stick to the clearly rice-flour items (米粉パン, 米粉パンケーキ/ワッフル, 盛岡米粉冷めん, acai bowl with GF granola), avoid the hamburg/loco-moco/hayashi/beef-stew and 醤油麹 soy-koji dishes, and confirm soy sauce is tamari on any savory order. Tell staff in advance (they ask allergy guests to notify them). Seasonal pancakes are reservation-only.
places.chef: owner, cook · Iwate Prefecture, Japan · Cafe de Forte is a small home-style cafe run by an Iwate-born (岩手県出身) owner together with her daughter, which opened in Kasuga, Bunkyo-ku in spring 2024 (around March; early blog posts date to April–May 2024). The owner describes the shop's food as growing out of dishes she used to make for her own children, centered on domestic rice flour (国産米粉) and body-friendly, low-sugar, additive-free cooking. She leans on ingredients from her home region of Iwate — Iwaizumi yogurt (岩泉ヨーグルト), a Morioka-style rice-flour cold noodle (盛岡米粉冷めん), and additive-free (無添加) seasonings. The cafe explicitly welcomes guests with gluten intolerance and celiac disease, while stating it is not a fully allergy-compliant kitchen. It is a hidden-gem (隠れ家) style cafe emphasizing a warm, 'friend's house' atmosphere. · 体に優しい — health-first, low-sugar, additive-free home cooking built around domestic rice flour, welcoming gluten-intolerant and celiac guests while being honest that not every dish is gluten-free. · 米粉 (rice-flour) pancakes and rice-flour bread; seasonal reservation-only pancake specials
places.gfd: A rice-flour (米粉) focused home-style cafe that markets itself as celiac-aware — its own materials say it caters to 「グルテン不耐症やセリアック病を含む様々なお客様」(guests with gluten intolerance and celiac disease). BUT the venue explicitly disclaims full safety: its own site states 「全てのメニューがグルテンフリーではありません」(not all menu items are gluten-free) and 「アレルギー完全対応ではありません」(we are not fully allergy-compliant), asking allergy guests to notify staff in advance. The JP celiac guide jp.japan-glutenfree.com corroborates that wheat…
places.vgd: The menu leans on dairy and meat — Iwate Iwaizumi yogurt on the acai bowl, butter and vanilla ice cream on the pancakes, plus roast beef, hamburg, beef stew and chicken dishes. A vegetable salad and the rice-flour breads/noodles may be adaptable, but no explicitly vegan dishes were confirmed, so vegans should ask and expect few options.
places.hours: Tue/Wed/Fri 9:30–15:00; Sat (biweekly) ~12:00–17:00; closed Sun/Mon/Thu. Hours are irregular — seasonal pancakes are reservation-only.

places.n: Be green by KIELO COFFEE (ビー グリーン バイ キエロ コーヒー)
places.hood: 文京区本郷 (Hongo, Bunkyo-ku) — ~3 min from Hongo-sanchome Stn, ~0.9km NE of Suidobashi
places.cu: Vegan & gluten-free café, specialty coffee roastery and gluten-free bakery
places.notes: [GF] — The entire sweets/bakery menu is gluten-free and vegan (rice-flour cakes, cashew cream), and no wheat products were found on the menu, so this is a rare fully-GF stop for a celiac teen. Coffee is naturally GF; all milks are plant-based. There is no formal celiac cross-contamination protocol published, so it is worth a quick spoken check (「小麦は使っていますか？」) but the risk profile is much better than a mixed bakery. Small counter (~5 seats + 2 outside); takeout available.
places.chef: Hiroki Yoshiike (吉池浩紀) · founder, roaster, owner · Tokyo, Japan · KIELO COFFEE was founded by roaster 吉池浩紀 (Hiroki Yoshiike), who became interested in coffee through a student part-time job and fell for Nordic-style light-roast coffee on a trip to Northern Europe (「kielo」 references a Finnish/Nordic sensibility). The original KIELO COFFEE stands near Akihabara; 「Be green by KIELO COFFEE」 in Hongo is the brand's second location and roastery, opened as a sustainability-focused café. The Hongo shop is run day-to-day by a store manager (reported as Shimizu / 清水) who emphasises face-to-face conversation with customers over one-way messaging. Roasting is done on-site (notably Tuesdays) using specialty beans said to be in the top ~5% of the market, prepared as light roasts to highlight origin character. · 「All for green すべては自然のために」 — minimise environmental load and body burden: plant-based only, gluten-free baking, traceable specialty coffee, renewable-energy extraction, and food-waste reduction (the carrot cake reuses pulp from a neighbouring juice/smoothie shop). · Light-roast single-origin specialty coffee plus vegan & gluten-free rice-flour baked goods (signature carrot cake with cas…
places.gfd: [Held at "ask" 2026-08-20] The description below was not traceable to any source, so the GF label is held down until it is. Every sweet and baked good on the menu is gluten-free and made without wheat: the shop describes its offering as 「ヴィーガン＆グルテンフリーの焼き菓子」 (vegan & gluten-free baked goods, ~6 seasonal varieties) and reviewers report 「ドリンクやデザートはすべて植物性の材料で作られており ヴィーガンかつグルテンフリー」 (all drinks and desserts are plant-based, vegan and gluten-free). Cakes such as the signature carrot cake are 米粉 (rice-…
places.vgd: A fully plant-based café: all milk is oat, almond, soy or pistachio (no dairy upcharge) and every dessert and baked good is vegan. Vegewel lists it as vegan-certified. Concept is 「All for green すべては自然のために」 (everything for nature).

places.n: Sumatra Curry Kyoeido (スマトラカレー 共栄堂)
places.hood: 神田神保町 (Jimbocho), Chiyoda — ~0.8 km SW of Suidobashi, 2 min from Jimbocho Stn A5 exit
places.cu: Sumatra-style Japanese curry rice
places.notes: [GF] A rare Japanese-curry option for celiacs because the shop deliberately builds its Sumatra sauce 「小麦粉を一切使わず」 (with no wheat flour), unlike standard flour-roux curry. Order any curry over plain Koshihikari rice, but tell them no fukujinzuke pickle and skip the complimentary potage soup, and understand there is no allergen handling in this century-old counter kitchen. Cash only, no reservations, one curry per person required.
places.chef: Owner, Curry maker · Jimbocho, Tokyo · Kyoeido opened in Taishō 13 (1924) in Kanda-Jimbocho and has served the same Sumatra-style curry for a full century. The recipe traces to Itō Yūjirō, a friend of the founder who traveled widely through Southeast Asia in the late Meiji/Taishō era and taught the shop how to cook a Sumatra-island curry, which was then adapted to the Japanese palate. The shop is now run by later generations of the family and remains a single-purpose curry counter in the basement of the Jimbocho Sun Building. It is a fixture of the Kanda curry scene and a recurring Michelin Bib/guide mention. · Depth through spice and time rather than flour: roast 20-odd spices for an hour, simmer meat and vegetables until the vegetables dissolve completely, and let the curry stay 'sarari' (light-bodied) yet concentrated — no thickening roux. · Jet-black, bitter-edged Sumatra spice curry, each protein simmered in its own pot so pork, chicken, beef, shrimp and tongue each taste distinct.
places.gfd: The signature dark Sumatra curry sauce is genuinely wheat-free by design — the shop states 「濃褐色のソースは小麦粉を一切使わず、20数種類の香辛料を1時間かけて炒めて作ります」 (the dark-brown sauce uses no wheat flour at all; 20-odd spices are toasted for an hour), which removes the roux/flour that thickens ordinary Japanese curry. That makes the curry-over-rice naturally low-gluten, BUT this is a 1924 old-school single-item curry counter with NO allergy protocol and a shared kitchen, so it caps at 'options,' not 'high.' Skip the free…
places.vgd: Every curry is built on separately simmered meat, seafood or beef tongue (pork, chicken, beef, shrimp, tongue) plus a meat-and-vegetable base; there is no vegetable-only curry on the menu. Not a vegan destination.
places.hours: 11:00–20:00 (L.O. 19:45); closed Sundays and some public holidays (irregular)

places.n: LA VORO Iidabashi (LA VORO 飯田橋店 / ラ ボーロ)
places.hood: 千代田区飯田橋 (Iidabashi, Chiyoda-ku) — ~0.4km W of Suidobashi Stn / 5 min from JR Iidabashi
places.cu: Gluten-free rice-flour baumkuchen & yogashi (Western confectionery, takeout)
places.notes: [GF] Takeout-only baumkuchen/confectionery shop — not a sit-down meal, but a genuinely safe sweet stop for a celiac 13-year-old. The whole line is 100% rice flour (no wheat products made here), and the signature エテルノ and モンコーネ are marketed as gluten-free 米粉100%. All items contain egg and dairy. Closed weekends, so plan a weekday visit; cut-baum singles (~¥540) are in-store only.
places.chef: 小久保凌 (Kokubo Ryo) · owner / founder, rice farmer · Tsukuba, Ibaraki, Japan · LA VORO is run by 小久保凌, who also operates 筑波農場 (Tsukuba Farm) in Tsukuba City, Ibaraki, growing and selling rice under the proprietary brand 常陸小田米 (Hitachi Oda-mai). His company is オーパス (Opus), Tsukuba. He founded LA VORO to achieve 「生産から加工、販売まで一貫して取り組む『6次産業化』」 — value-added, farm-to-shop processing of his own rice. The farm mills its own fresh 生米粉 (raw rice flour) from unprocessed grain, a moisture-rich flour said to be possible only for a working farm. The Iidabashi shop opened 3 April 2024 as the second location after the original Tsukuba store, and its first in Tokyo. · Six-industry (6次産業化) farm-to-confectionery integration — turning his own freshly milled rice into gluten-free baumkuchen so people with wheat allergy can eat with peace of mind; his site calls the pieces 『作品』 (works of art) made with こだわり. · 100% 生米粉 (raw rice flour) gluten-free baumkuchen using own-brand 常陸小田米
places.gfd: Rice-flour baumkuchen specialist whose entire product line is 100% 生米粉 (raw rice flour from their own 常陸小田米) with no wheat used at all. The shop states 「自家製の生米粉を使用したこだわりの品はグルテンフリーのため安心してお召し上がりいただけます」 and press describes it as 「米粉100％のグルテンフリーバウムクーヘン」. Because there is no verified explicit dedicated/no-wheat-facility statement (some sources phrase only the products, not the workshop, as gluten-free), rated high rather than dedicated; for a celiac, the all-rice-flour lineup is reassuring but confi…
places.vgd: Every product carries the allergen listing 卵・米粉・乳 (egg, rice flour, milk) — the baumkuchen is built on eggs, cream and butter (モンコーネ also uses 発酵バター and アーモンドパウダー). Nothing on the menu is vegan.
places.hours: Mon-Fri 10:00-19:00; closed Sat & Sun

places.n: PAMOJA (コーヒーとおにぎり PAMOJA 神保町本店)
places.hood: 神田猿楽町 (Kanda-Sarugakucho), Jimbocho, Chiyoda — ~4 min from Jimbocho Stn, ~7 min from Ocha…
places.cu: Onigiri (rice balls), vegetable deli plates, specialty coffee & sweets
places.notes: [GF] — Naturally rice-based but NOT a gluten-free shop: no GF protocol, shared soy sauce, and many fillings are soy-simmered or miso-based (wheat risk). A celiac should ask filling-by-filling and stick to plain-salt fish (塩サバ, 旨味サケ) or simple items, confirming tamari vs wheat shoyu. Vegans have good choice but this is a mixed (meat/fish/vegan) shop — do not assume any item is vegan without asking.
places.chef: 江藤智幸 (Toshiyuki Etoh) · Founder, CEO · Tokyo, Japan · PAMOJA was founded by Toshiyuki Etoh (江藤智幸), representative of 株式会社PAMOJA, which was established in April 2023. The Jimbocho flagship (本店) sits in Kanda-Sarugakucho, a quiet block just off the bookshop district, and centers on freshly hand-pressed onigiri (握りたて) made with organic ingredients. The shop name PAMOJA is Swahili for "together": Etoh's stated concept is a table where vegans and non-vegans can enjoy food side by side, which is why the lineup deliberately spans vegan, fish, and meat fillings. The café pairs its rice with specialty coffee and rotating seasonal sweets, and runs irregular morning/evening pop-up service announced via Instagram. · 「みんなで食を楽しむ」 — everyone enjoying food together, regardless of diet; organic, seasonal ingredients and an inclusive table where vegan and non-vegan guests share the same menu. · Freshly pressed organic onigiri (10+ seasonal fillings, both vegan and non-vegan) with specialty coffee.
places.gfd: PAMOJA is a rice-based onigiri & coffee café, so the plain rice base is naturally gluten-free — but the shop makes NO gluten-free claim of its own. The only GF signal is an aggregator tag on Vegewel (「グルテンフリーメニューあり」), which cannot establish celiac safety. Many fillings are wheat risks: soy-sauce-simmered tsukudani/nimono (生姜昆布, まぐろ昆布, アサリの佃煮, いわしの生姜煮), teriyaki tofu, miso-based fillings (barley), and okaka (soy sauce). There is no allergen protocol and the kitchen shares soy sauce; a celiac mus…
places.vgd: Despite the seed describing it as all-vegan, PAMOJA is a MIXED shop — its concept (PAMOJA = Swahili for "together") is vegans and non-vegans eating at the same table, so the menu includes fish and meat onigiri (塩サバ, 旨味サケ, 生たらこ, いわしの生姜煮, 肉味噌) alongside a strong vegan lineup. Clearly vegan items include 豆＆TOFUチーズ and 黒ゴマきなこ onigiri, the 野菜DELI/ヴィーガンプレート, 厚揚げのTERIYAKI, and vegan sweets (ヴィーガンスノーボール)…

places.n: Sagatani Jūwari Soba, Jimbocho (十割蕎麦 嵯峨谷 神保町店)
places.hood: 神田神保町 (Kanda-Jimbocho), Chiyoda, Tokyo
places.cu: Standing jūwari (100% buckwheat) soba — low-price rō-men shop
places.notes: [GF] Genuine 100% buckwheat noodle, stone-milled and made in-house, in an all-soba shop (no shared wheat-udon water) — but the tsuyu uses wheat soy sauce and tempura is fried on the premises. For a celiac this is negotiate-only: ask for plain noodles with no tsuyu (bring tamari), and understand airborne flour + shared fryer are unavoidable in a fast standing shop with no allergy training. A cautious lunch, not a guaranteed-safe meal.
places.chef: Chain / operator: 株式会社フォーユー (For You Co., Ltd.) · Tokyo (chain) · 嵯峨谷 (Sagatani) is a low-price standing-soba (立ち食いそば) chain operated by 株式会社フォーユー (For You Co., Ltd.), which grew into central Tokyo — Shibuya, Shinjuku and the Jimbocho branch here — and is frequently cited (e.g. Nikkei xtrend) as part of a 'new force' shaking up the standing-soba world. Its distinguishing move is doing on-site stone-milling and noodle-making in a cheap standing shop, which is unusual for the format. The Jimbocho branch sits in the 三光堂ビル 1F at 神田神保町1-7, about a 2-minute walk from Jimbocho Station. · 「毎日食べても飽きがこない体にも財布にも優しい食事」— food you can eat every day that is gentle on both body and wallet: cheap prices with real 100% buckwheat quality, achieved by 「挽きたて・打ちたて・茹でたて・揚げたて」 (freshly ground, rolled, boiled, fried). · 100% buckwheat (十割) mori/kake soba from a few hundred yen; signature 'aji-gohan' (あじ御飯) rice side and cheap don sets.
places.gfd: The noodle itself is a genuine plus: this is a 100% buckwheat (十割) shop that stone-mills and makes its own noodles in-house — the operator states 「石臼での店内製粉」 and 「挽きたて・打ちたて・茹でたて・揚げたて」, and because the whole shop is jūwari soba, the boiling water is not shared with wheat udon. HOWEVER the standard tsuyu (soup/dipping broth, described 「甘辛濃いめ」) is made with ordinary wheat-containing soy sauce, and tempura/kakiage is deep-fried on-site — so shared frying oil and airborne wheat flour are present. Thi…
places.vgd: The buckwheat noodles themselves are plant-based (soba flour, water), but the standard tsuyu is a katsuo (bonito) dashi broth, so ordered as served the soba is not vegan. No dedicated vegan option is advertised; a plain no-tsuyu bowl would be needed and there is no allergy/vegan handling.

places.cu: Tororo kaiseki
places.notes: Founded on June 10, 1929 (Shōwa 4) beside the Sumida River near the Kaminarimon/Komagata-bashi area of Asakusa. According to the company's own history, founder Tazō Nakajima had worked for a produce (vegetable/fruit) wholesaler and wanted to start a food business of his own; he i
places.chef: Founder: Tazō Nakajima (中島太蔵) · Founded on June 10, 1929 (Shōwa 4) beside the Sumida River near the Kaminarimon/Komagata-bashi area of Asakusa. According to the company's own history, founder Tazō Nakajima had worked for a produce (vegetable/fruit) wholesaler and wanted to start a food business of his own; he is said to have traveled the country searching for the best mountain yam before settling on a strain and opening a shop built entirely around tororo (grated yam). The restaurant has been run by the same family and stayed on essentially the same stretch of riverbank for nearly a century, expanding over the decades into a multi-floor kaiseki restaurant while keeping the original tororo recipe at its core. · The shop's founding wish was simply 'we want everyone to be able to eat one bowl of mugitoro' — a focus on making a single humble, health-associated dish available to ordinary diners, which still shapes the menu today. · Mugitoro (麦とろ) — barley-mixed rice topped with tororo (grated Japanese mountain yam, made from a strong, low-astringency yamato-imo), seasoned with a secret bonito-and-kelp dashi recipe passed down since the 1929 founding. The restaurant also serves broader …
places.gfd: No gluten-free menu, wheat-free soy sauce, or dedicated fryer was found in any available source. This is a traditional Japanese restaurant relying on conventional soy sauce and dashi seasonings and offering tempura-style dishes on some menus, so wheat exposure and cross-contamination should be assumed likely. Diners with celiac disease or severe wheat allergy should not treat this as a safe option without direct, in-person confirmation from staff.
places.vgd: The restaurant's signature seasoning is a secret dashi (broth) based on bonito flakes (katsuobushi) and kelp, used since the 1929 founding, so the core mugitoro dish and much of the kaiseki menu are not vegan. No vegan-specific menu, substitutions, or plant-based dashi option were found in available sources.

places.chef: neighborhood chicken specialist, yakitori & oyako-don restaurant · Asakusa, Taito-ku, Tokyo — a few minutes' walk from Sensō-ji, near Tawaramachi Station and the Tsukuba Express Asakusa Station · Toriyoshi traces its roots to the postwar years, when the shop began as a traditional Japanese kappo (割烹) restaurant. places.chef: owner · Asakusa, Tokyo · Kikuya is a long-running sweets stall on Asakusa's Nakamise-dori, the covered shopping street that runs from Kaminarimon Gate to Sensoji Temple. It sits about nine shops in from Kaminarimon, on the right-hand side as you walk toward the temple, and specializes in grilled dango and daifuku made in-house. · The shop describes sourcing carefully selected domestic ingredients — Tokachi red beans, Shiga-grown mochi rice — and avoiding additives so the natural flavor of the rice and beans comes through. · Freshly grilled mitarashi dango — skewered dango made from jōshinko (non-glutinous rice flour), grilled to order and finished with warm mitarashi sauce for a just-made, chewy texture — and mame daifuku, mochi (made with Shiga-grown rice) wrapped around whole Tokachi azuki beans for a lightly salted, textured tsubu-an filling.
places.gfd: No shop-specific gluten-free statement was found. The mame daifuku (mochi + azuki + sugar) uses ingredients that are naturally free of wheat, but the mitarashi dango's base is made from jōshinko (rice flour, gluten-free grain) while the mitarashi sauce itself is typically soy-sauce-based — and soy sauce (shoyu) sold in Japan is usually brewed with wheat — so the finished dango is not confirmed gluten-free. Ask staff about the sauce's ingredients and about shared prep surfaces before ordering if…

places.chef: founding chef-owner (Kanda Yabusoba-trained) · Founded in 1984 (Showa 59) by a founding chef-owner who spent 20 years training at the famed Kanda Yabusoba before striking out on his own — a direct lineage from one of Tokyo's most storied soba houses. · Despite the name 'Azumabashi' (Azuma Bridge), the shop today actually stands at the Sumida-ku foot of Komagata-bashi, one bridge south of Azuma-bashi itself, along the Sumida River a few minutes from Asakusa Station. It's a small, old-school Edo-mae soba-ya that keeps a lunch-only rhythm true to the genre — the room fills at midday with regulars sharing a quiet 'hiru-zake' (daytime drinking) ritual of a small carafe of sake alongside their soba before the kitchen closes for the day. · Thin, fragrant, firm-textured Edo-mae buckwheat noodles paired with a rich, salty dipping sauce in the classic Yabu-soba style handed down from Kanda Yabusoba. · Duck (kamo) soba dishes — cold kamo-jiru zaru, hot kamo nanban — and a sesame-broth (goma-jiru) soba are the standout, most-loved items alongside the classic mori-soba.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Edo-mae "Yabu" style soba shop, which by convention uses nihachi (2:8) noodles — roughly 20% wheat flour blended with buckwheat — not 100%-buckwheat (juwari) noodles, so the noodles themselves are not gluten-free. The Kanda-Yabusoba-lineage dipping sauce (tsuyu) is a soy-sauce-based warishita, and tempura dishes on the menu use wheat batter. No gluten-free noodle substitute, dedicated fryer, or allergy accommodation was found in any available source. Not recommended for di…

No vegan menu, substitution, or dashi disclosure was found in any available source. A plain mori-soba mi…

places.chef: 4th-generation owner (current), Iida Tadayuki — presumptive 5th-generation successor · Founded in 1902 (Meiji 35) as a dedicated dojō (loach) specialty shop in Nishi-Asakusa, with the family's food-service roots in the same neighborhood reaching back to the Keiō era (1865-68). · Idaya has stayed in the same Nishi-Asakusa spot for over a century, passing the kitchen and the sauce recipe down through five generations of the Iida family. The current fourth-generation owner is training his son, Tadayuki, to take over as the fifth. · The recipe for the sweet-savory warishita sauce is a closely guarded family secret handed to only one successor at a time, and the kitchen still follows the same cooking method used since the shop's founding. The house precept — 'Father's job is to make the sauce and mind the shoe check' — is taken as a reminder that hospitality should extend all the way down to a guest's feet. · Dojō nabe — live loach hot pot, cooked to order in a shallow iron pot with the house's own soy-based warishita sauce and a heavy mound of chopped scallion; the bones are gently pre-softened so a little pleasant resistance remains in the bite. The menu also runs to hone-nuki nabe (…
places.gfd: No gluten-free menu, labeling, or accommodation was found. The signature warishita sauce and the various soup bases (dojō-jiru, tofu-jiru, etc.) are built on standard Japanese soy sauce and miso, both of which normally contain wheat, and there is a fried dish (dojō karaage) on the menu with no information on a dedicated fryer. Not recommended for celiac or strict gluten-free diners without direct, detailed confirmation from the restaurant.
places.vgd: The entire menu is built around dojō (loach), unagi (eel), and seasonal namazu (catfish); even the soups and side dishes (e.g., tofu-jiru) come out of the same kitchen and most likely share fish-based dashi. No plant-based main dish or confirmed vegan option was found. Not a suitable choice for vegan diners.

places.chef: Koyama Konomi (小山このみ) · Owner · Tokyo · Koyama Konomi became vegetarian in spring/summer 2017 and vegan later that same summer. The turning point traces back to 2016, when a scene in Osamu Tezuka's manga "Buddha" — in which a rabbit sacrifices its own life for a human — planted the first seed of doubt that eventually led her toward vegetarianism. Her shift progressed in stages: first for health reasons, then out of concern for animals, and finally for the environment. · Koyama believes that how veganism is communicated matters most — rather than lecturing, she wants guests to first have a delicious, enjoyable meal, and let that experience become a gentle entry point for thinking about animals and the planet. Because she and her entire staff are vegan themselves, she says the restaurant can attentively serve both committed vegans and the vegan-curious. · 100% plant-based, gluten-free lunch plates, salad lunches, curry rice, and gluten-free sweets, all made without the "five pungent" vegetables (garlic, onion, scallion, Chinese chives, rakkyo), alcohol, added sugar, or additives.

places.chef: independent kanmidokoro (traditional sweets shop) · Opened July 4, 2012, tucked in a small alley just off Nakamise-dori, about a two-minute walk from Tokyo Metro Ginza Line Asakusa Station Exit 6. · Kanmidokoro Saika is an independent traditional Japanese sweets (kanmi) shop near Sensō-ji and Nakamise-dori, serving classic kanmi alongside its well-known shaved ice. · Close attention to ice quality and shaving technique, paired with housemade matcha jelly and syrups made from carefully sourced Japanese ingredients, across a menu of 80+ sweets. · Fluffy, 'powder-snow' style shaved ice (kakigori) — the shop shaves unusually hard ice blocks with a very sharp blade to get an ultra-fine, light texture said to feel barely cold on the first bite. places.chef: family-run Showa-era teishoku-ya (set-meal diner) and neighborhood eatery/izakaya · Opened in 1950 (Shōwa 25) in Asakusa Rokku, Asakusa's old entertainment district, and has stayed in the same neighborhood ever since — marking roughly 75 years in business as of the mid-2020s. · Mizuguchi began as a plain teishoku-ya serving the workers and performers of Asakusa Rokku in the postwar years. It has grown into a sprawling two-floor shokudō-and-izakaya known for its huge, old-fashioned menu spanning Japanese, Western and Chinese-style home cooking — everything from fried horse mackerel and pork sauté to omurice, ginger pork, mapo tofu and hand-mixed hamburg steak — served in a boisterous, nostalgic Shōwa-retro dining room. · A no-frills, high-volume local shokudō where regulars — from neighborhood workers to solo diners stopping in for a drink — are as much a part of the atmosphere as the food. · Iri-buta — pork and onion stir-fried in Mizuguchi's own curry-tinged, sweet-savory sauce, reportedly created together with one of the shop's cooks around the time of the Tokyo air raids of 1945 and still the table everyone orders.

places.chef: Chiba Kenta (千葉健太) · owner, founder · Grew up locally in Asakusa · Chiba began an apprenticeship as an itamae (traditional Japanese chef) at age 18 and trained for five years. At 24 he struck out on his own, opening a dining bar, and went on to run other food-and-drink businesses. In August of a recent year he founded a company called Asakusa-cho ("Asakusa Town"), deliberately registering it on the 8th of the month for its association with sue-hirogari, a fan-shaped character read as a symbol of ever-widening prosperity. Asakusa Udon, opened near the Hanayashiki amusement park in October 2025, is the company's flagship shop. · "The town raises the people, and the people raise the town" (街が人を育み、人が街を育む) — the stated motto behind Chiba's company and this shop. · Kake udon and bukkake udon (served hot, either in broth or dipping-style), to which diners add freshly fried tempura (such as kara-age chicken or shrimp) and toppings like a seasoned egg yolk or beef and shiitake mushroom.

places.chef: Hiranuma Takayuki · owner/soba craftsman: Hiranuma Takayuki (name spelling per secondary sources; not independently confirmed via primary site) · Opened in 1989 as "Asakusa Issa-an," the shop was renamed "Komagata Sobashonin" in October 1997. The owner, Hiranuma Takayuki, trained under Katakura Yasuo, a noted postwar soba craftsman credited with establishing hand-cut, thin-sliced specialty soba as a standard of the trade. Buckwheat is sourced from high-elevation (700m+) fields in the Aizu region of Fukushima Prefecture and stone-milled in-house on five large mills, ground slowly to preserve aroma and flavor. · Five-color soba (五色そば) — a tasting set of five hand-cut noodle varieties (plain/seiro, rustic/inaka, poppy-seed/keshi-kiri, lemon/lemon-kiri, and tea/cha-kiri) — and duck nanban soba (鴨南そば) served in a yuzu-scented duck broth.

places.chef: 荒井昇 (Arai Noboru) · Owner-chef · Born and raised in Asakusa, Tokyo (b. 1974) · After training in Japan and then at Michelin-starred restaurants in France — including under chef Régis Marcon in Paris and at a one-star house in southern France — Arai returned to Japan and spent a year working as a fish broker at the Tsukiji market to save the capital he needed. In 2000, at age 26, he opened HOMMAGE in his home neighborhood of Asakusa; the restaurant was promoted to two Michelin stars in the 2018 Tokyo guide and has held that rating since. · The restaurant's name, French for "tribute" or "respect," reflects Arai's guiding idea: gratitude toward nature's ingredients, the producers who grow them, his mentors, his staff, his family, and the guests who return to the restaurant. He emphasizes personal relationships with producers over simply sourcing by region or prestige. · An omakase-only tasting menu that fuses classical French technique with Japanese ingredients and umami-building elements — Arai is known for working fermented soy products such as soy-sauce moromi and miso into French-style dishes rather than a single fixed signature plate.

Founded in 1945 in the postwar years, it is now run by the third generation of the same family and has kept the same style of cooking for more than 80 years. · The kitchen's stated aim is a cutlet that feels crisp and satisfying without sitting heavy afterward: loin from Gunma-raised Yamato pork, panko that the shop bakes and grinds in-house from domestic-wheat bread for a sweeter, crunchier crust, and frying in cottonseed oil rather than lard so the dish is lighter on the stomach than a typical tonkatsu. · Rosu-katsu (pork loin cutlet) set meal — a cutlet prized for its thin, crackling crust and pink, juicy meat that diners describe as unusually light and easy on the stomach for fried pork.

places.chef: owner-operator, dim sum cook (originally brought from China), occasional second cook, a former washoku chef, on some weekday evenings · A closet-sized dim sum counter that opened in 2010 in a Nishi-Asakusa backstreet near the Kappabashi kitchenware district, a few minutes' walk from Tsukuba Express Asakusa Station. It's run out of a single storefront window with steam baskets fogging the glass, mostly by one owner at a five-stool counter, with a dim sum cook originally brought over from China making the dumplings. · There's no fixed script here — write-ups describe an 'omakase' course that changes visit to visit depending on who's cooking and what's fresh, rather than a set menu recited the same way every time. · Thick-skinned pan-fried gyoza packed with cabbage, chives and pork, alongside shrimp and crab shumai, xiaolongbao and other bamboo-steamer dim sum, most of it priced around a flat 500 yen a plate.

Treat this as not viable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners; there is no indication staff are set up to prevent cross-contact even if you tried to order around the wrappers.
places.vgd: The menu centers entirely on pork, shrimp and crab dim sum and gyoza; no vegetarian or plant-based dish is mentioned in any review, blog, or listing found. Not a realistic option for vegan or vegetarian diners.

places.chef: shaved ice specialty shop · Asakusa Himurodo's Asakusa main branch opened in May 2023 in the Crest Asakusa building, a short walk from Asakusa Station. It is a dedicated kakigori (shaved ice) shop built around ice quality: the shop uses carefully selected, high-purity ice that is prized for melting almost instantly, giving the dessert what fans describe as a roughly "three-minute" window of peak texture before it's meant to be eaten. · A focus on the purity of the ice itself and on natural, additive-free syrups made in-house, with menus that shift with the seasons to showcase fruit at its best. · Shaved ice topped with handmade syrups made without artificial colors, flavors, or sweeteners, built around seasonal fruit. Standouts include the fresh-strawberry kakigori and an Asakusa-location-exclusive ripe sweet potato (mitsuimo) kakigori, plus a version topped with real mitarashi dango.
places.gfd: No source discusses gluten-free preparation directly. The base shaved ice and homemade fruit syrups are plausibly wheat-free, but no source confirms whether any syrup or topping contains wheat-derived ingredients, and toppings like the mitarashi-dango version use a soy-sauce-based glaze — soy sauce in Japan is very often wheat-based unless specified otherwise, and this was not confirmed either way here. No information on shared equipment or cross-contamination practices was found. Ask staff dir…
places.vgd: No source specifically addresses vegan suitability. Fruit-based shaved ice syrups are often plant-based, but no source confirms the absence of dairy (e.g., condensed milk) in the base syrups or toppings, and menu items such as the mitarashi-dango kakigori use a glaze whose exact ingredients (potential mirin/dashi) are unconfirmed. places.chef: Tsuyoshi Kameyatani (亀谷剛) · Owner-chef: Tsuyoshi Kameyatani (亀谷剛), Co-owner: Keita Mera (目良慶太, IT-industry background) · French-trained chef who worked in Tokyo French kitchens (including Akebonobashi's Sucre Salé) and in Paris before becoming owner-chef of Bistro Rigole in Sangenjaya, where he earned the Michelin Bib Gourmand in 2018 and 2019. · Kameyatani breaks tempura down into five components — ingredient, batter, frying oil, seasoning and presentation — and reworks each one dish-by-dish, applying French technique (mousselines, reduction sauces, fermented batters) to the traditional tempura format, paired with a roughly 300-bottle list of mostly white and orange natural wines. · Signature shrimp tempura: a round parcel of shrimp wrapped in a shrimp mousseline (blended with coconut oil, sesame paste and fish sauce), coated in a tomato-tinted, beer-leavened batter, fried in sesame and grapeseed oil, and served over a concentrated Américaine sauce made from the shrimp heads and shells.
places.gfd: The kitchen's core tempura batter (used across most menu items, including the signature shrimp dish) is made with all-purpose wheat flour, cornstarch, rice flour, dry yeast and beer — gluten is built into the standard preparation. No gluten-free batter, substitution, or dedicated fryer has been reported by any source.
places.vgd: The menu is built around seafood tempura with fish-based mousses and sauces — e.g., the signature shrimp dish incorporates fish sauce and a shrimp-shell reduction — and no vegetable-only tasting course or vegan menu has been documented in any source, so it is not vegan-friendly.
places.hours: 17:00–24:00, irregular days off (不定休); reported closures vary slightly by listing

places.cu: そば・立ち食いそば
places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small standing-soba counter tucked on a backstreet between Jimbocho and Suidobashi stations, run day-to-day by its owner. The shop leans into its owner's personal interests — Kumamoto ("Higo") references in the name and decor, plus a visible fondness for the Hanshin Tigers base · 📍 Approx. map location — confirm the exact spot (auto-placed from address).
places.chef: owner-operator · Named for "Higo," the historical name for the Kumamoto region, reflecting the owner's Kumamoto ties · A small standing-soba counter tucked on a backstreet between Jimbocho and Suidobashi stations, run day-to-day by its owner. The shop leans into its owner's personal interests — Kumamoto ("Higo") references in the name and decor, plus a visible fondness for the Hanshin Tigers baseball team — giving an otherwise utilitarian tachigui-soba stand a distinct, homey character. · 豚天そば (pork tempura soba) — a bowl topped with an oversized slab of deep-fried pork
places.gfd: This is a standard tachigui-soba shop with no gluten-free accommodations found or claimed anywhere. Soba here is very likely a wheat-buckwheat blend typical of budget standing-soba counters, the tsuyu dipping/broth is soy-sauce (wheat) based, and the signature dish is wheat-battered deep-fried tempura (pork tempura) cooked in what is presumably a shared fryer. No dedicated gluten-free fryer, noodle, or sauce option was documented. Not recommended for celiac diners.
places.vgd: No vegan menu or accommodations were found. The shop's dashi/broth is presumed bonito(katsuo)-based like most standard soba-ya, and its signature dish is pork tempura soba, making it a meat-forward, non-vegan-friendly establishment with no documented plant-based options.

places.chef: Owner personally curates the natural-wine list · A small, narrow second-floor bar tucked up a stairway near Shinjuku Station's southeast exit, in the Shinjuku Sanchome dining area. It is an independently run wine bar (not part of a chain), seating roughly 20 across counter and table seats. · Built around natural wine paired with seasonal, Italian/Spanish-leaning small plates — the idea being that the food and the glass-poured natural wines are chosen to enhance each other. · Small-plate tapas-style dishes such as "Ebi no Taiyo" (shrimp), Iberico pork gyoza, oysters, and a vegetable appetizer platter, alongside 10+ natural wines available by the glass (many under ¥500/glass).
places.gfd: No gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or wheat-free soy sauce was mentioned in any source found. The menu includes wheat-containing items typical of an Italian/Spanish-style bar (e.g., gyoza dumplings, likely bread/pasta-style small plates), and it operates as a general shared kitchen. Celiac diners should not assume safety here — ask staff directly about ingredients and cross-contact before ordering.
places.vgd: No source confirmed a vegan menu or vegan labeling. The menu includes a vegetable appetizer platter (¥910) alongside oysters, shellfish, and Iberico pork gyoza, and Japanese-Italian fusion dishes here commonly rely on bonito/katsuo-based dashi and animal-based stocks that are not disclosed. A vegetable side dish could likely be assembled, but there is no confirmed dedicated vegan option — vegans …

places.chef: Operated as a branded tea salon of Fujii Chaen, a family-run Uji tea garden (est. Muromachi era) · Uji, Kyoto · The shop is run by Fujii Chaen, a tea-growing family business in Uji, Kyoto that has cultivated tea on its own roughly 1. 2-hectare plantation since the Tenbun era of the Muromachi period (mid-1500s) — about 480 years of continuous tea cultivation. This Shibuya location, opened December 5, 2019 on the 6th floor of Tokyu Plaza Shibuya (Shibuya Fukuras), was one of the garden's first branded retail/dining outposts outside Uji itself. · Bring the family tea garden's own Uji leaves — grown and processed under centuries-old practice — directly to Tokyo diners, using the tea itself (sencha, matcha, hojicha) as the centerpiece of both savory dishes and desserts rather than as a mere flavoring. · Matcha and hojicha brûlée-style parfaits, kamameshi (iron-pot) rice dishes, an obanzai-style kaiseki tea-meal set, and Uji-matcha soba, all built around the garden's own tea leaves
places.gfd: No gluten-free menu, wheat-free labeling, or dedicated-fryer/prep-area statement was found in any source reviewed. The menu includes 宇治抹茶そば (Uji-matcha soba) — most Japanese soba (not 十割/100%-buckwheat) contains wheat flour as a binder — and Kyoto-style obanzai dishes, which typically use shoyu (soy sauce, usually wheat-containing) and dashi. Treat as a higher-risk option for celiac diners and ask staff directly about wheat in the soba, soy sauce, and dashi before ordering.
places.vgd: No source confirms a vegan menu. The offering centers on Kyoto-style obanzai kaiseki sets, kamameshi rice dishes, matcha soba, and matcha/hojicha parfaits and other tea sweets. Traditional obanzai and dashi-based dishes in this style of Japanese cooking commonly use bonito (katsuobushi) stock, and the parfait/sweets menu likely contains dairy and egg. No statement found about plant-based dashi or…

places.chef: Hamano Kōichi (founder) · founder · Opened July 1 near Suidōbashi Station, this eel-rice-bowl shop (branded in Japanese simply as "うな重," pronounced "Unashige," and marketed as UNASHIGE) was created by restaurateur Hamano Kōichi (濱野浩一). Hamano previously spent years at the Global Dining restaurant group leading new-store openings, then headed its planning and development division from 2003 to 2010, before going independent to run cafés and small lodging businesses. He founded the eel-shop concept as a standalone company aiming to make unagi (normally an expensive, special-occasion dish in Japan) into an everyday, fast-food-priced meal. · The stated concept is a "unaju fast-food shop": by systematizing operations and streamlining eel sourcing, the shop hand-bastes and grills eel to order in the traditional style but sells it from about ¥1,210-1,320 — far below typical unagi-restaurant prices — to bring eel to a broader, younger, everyday clientele (office workers and students in their 20s) rather than treating it as a once-a-year luxury. · Unajū / unadon — eel fillets basted in a house tare sauce and charcoal/grilled to order in-house, plus shirayaki (unsauced grilled eel) and a hit…
places.gfd: This is a traditional-style unagi (eel) specialist: the eel is basted in a house tare sauce, which in Japanese kabayaki cooking is almost universally soy-sauce based and therefore contains wheat. No gluten-free menu, allergen chart, or ingredient labeling was found in any source consulted (Tabelog, press coverage, blog visit reports). No mention of a dedicated fryer or GF-specific handling was found — likely not applicable since the eel is grilled, not fried, but cross-contact with the shared t…
places.vgd: Every dish centers on grilled freshwater eel; no plant-based, vegetarian, or eel-free alternative was found in any menu description or press coverage. The shop's self-serve dashi broth station (used to turn the rice bowl into an ochazuke/hitsumabushi-style dish) is, per standard Japanese practice, very likely bonito/katsuo-based and not vegan. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

places.chef: Michio Tan (丹道夫) · Founder / Chairman of Daitan Group (parent company of Fuji Soba) · First shop "Soba-sei" opened in Shibuya, Tokyo in 1966; formally incorporated as Daitan Food Co. in 1972 · Fuji Soba traces back to a single standing-soba stall called "Soba-sei," opened in Shibuya in 1966 by Michio Tan, a former real-estate dealer who wanted a business with dependable daily cash flow. The stall's format spread to Nishi-Ogikubo, Shinjuku, and Ikebukuro, and in 1972 the operation was formally incorporated as Daitan Food Co. , rebranding as 名代 富士そば (Fuji Soba). It has since grown into one of Tokyo's largest standing-soba chains, with this Suidobashi branch being one of many locations across the city rather than an independent shop. · Tan built the group around independently-run sister companies: branches, even near the same station, are often operated as separate subsidiaries so that each store stays competitive rather than functioning as one centrally managed chain.

Because the back fat itself carries so much richness, the pork-bone broth is kept deliberately simple so extra seasoning doesn't fight the fat's own flavor. · Seabura ramen — a pork-bone shoyu broth finished by straining and ladling a generous pour of slow-simmered pork back fat over the noodles just before serving.

places.chef: Chain restaurant operated by Gift Holdings Inc. places.chef: Yoshida Kichizaemon (founder) · founder · Nihonbashi, Tokyo · Katsukichi opened in 1962 near Korakuen/Tokyo Dome and has kept its retro Showa-era interior almost unchanged ever since. The founder, Yoshida Kichizaemon, was the son of Iwatani Shohei, a well-known Meiji-era tobacco magnate. The dining room is filled with roughly 2,000 antiques — Imari porcelain tableware and reclaimed wood and water pipes salvaged from the old Tamagawa Canal — giving it the feel of a small private museum. · A craftsman's commitment to quality ingredients — branded pork, fresh breadcrumbs, and fresh oil — carried forward largely unchanged since the shop's founding over 60 years ago. · Tonkatsu made from select branded domestic pork fillet, hand-coated in fresh nama-panko breadcrumbs and slowly fried in fresh corn oil; also known for a steak served with a distinctive soy-sauce-based sauce rather than the usual demi-glace.

places.vgd: A meat-focused tonkatsu specialty restaurant; the menu centers on pork and shrimp cutlets, katsu-don, and seasonal Japanese dishes. places.chef: Koichi Murata (founder, 1973); now run by second-generation owner Shinsuke Murata · founder, chef · Founded in 1973 (Showa 48) in Kanda-Jimbocho by Koichi Murata, who had previously run an earlier curry shop called Indira in Takashimadaira, Tokyo. · In his twenties Murata traveled to France, ostensibly to study art, and ended up spending several years there. He worked in a friend's restaurant, where he became captivated by the depth and technique of classic French brown sauce (sauce espagnole/demi-glace). Bringing that sauce-making tradition back to Japan and folding it into curry produced what he named '欧風カレー' (European-style curry). · Murata summed up his curry as 'the aroma of India, the taste of Europe' — rather than a straightforward Indian-style curry, the sauce is built like a French brown sauce: butter-and-flour roux simmered for hours with beef or pork stock, wine, and fruit and vegetables cooked down slowly in butter, giving a rounder, less fiery, dairy-rich flavor with sweetness balancing the spice. · European-style beef or pork curry, served with a whole boiled potato and a pat of butter presented separately on its own plate before the curry arrives.

The name 'Oiwake' (追分) refers to the fork in old Naito-Shinjuku where the Koshu Kaido and Ome Kaido roads split, a busy travelers' crossroads. In the summer of 1947, just after the war, founder Fujii Toemon opened a small shop called 'Yanagiya' in Shinjuku Sanchome; having heard the old story of Oiwake dango from town elders, he set out to revive its taste on the very spot where the roads once met, and the business grew into today's Oiwake Dango Honpo. · Dough, red bean paste, and beans are all hand-prepared fresh in the shop's own kitchen every morning before the dango are made and sold the same day. · Otona no Mitarashi (大人のみたらし, "Adult's Mitarashi") — dango glazed in the shop's mitarashi sauce blended with sansho pepper and fresh shichimi spice, giving the classic sweet-salty soy glaze a warmer, spicier edge.

Diners choose from chicken, beef, shrimp, bean, or vegetable curry, and can dial the spice level up in steps (famously as high as 70x), which has made it a rite of passage for Tokyo spice enthusiasts as well as a lunchtime staple for office workers and students in the Jimbocho/Kanda area.

places.notes: Ramen Jiro traces its roots to a yatai (street stall) started around 1968 by Takami Yamada near Keio University in Mita, Minato-ku, which grew into the original honten (main shop) and, later, a network of independently run 'chokkei' (direct-lineage) branches trained in the founde
places.chef: owner · Mita, Minato-ku, Tokyo (birthplace of the original Ramen Jiro honten) · Ramen Jiro traces its roots to a yatai (street stall) started around 1968 by Takami Yamada near Keio University in Mita, Minato-ku, which grew into the original honten (main shop) and, later, a network of independently run 'chokkei' (direct-lineage) branches trained in the founder's method. The Kabukicho shop opened on 1997-08-11 as a company-operated ('foods-kei') branch, and was uniquely permitted to keep the 'Jiro' name after the trademark was formally registered in 2003 (when other non-lineage branches had to drop it). In October 2016 it relocated to its current Kabukicho 2-chome address under new management and converted to full chokkei (direct-lineage) status, with an owner-chef trained in the Jiro method. · Jiro-style tonkotsu-shoyu ramen: thick, chewy flat noodles in a pork-bone and soy-sauce broth, topped with two slices of fatty chashu pork, garlic, and a towering mound of cabbage and bean sprouts, customizable via the shop's 'call' system (amount of garlic, vegetables, fat, and sauce strength).
places.gfd: Ramen is built entirely around wheat noodles and a soy-sauce (shoyu) based tare; there is no gluten-free noodle substitute, no dedicated gluten-free prep area, and no indication the kitchen accommodates gluten-free requests. Not safe for celiac diners.
places.vgd: Broth is pork-bone (tonkotsu) based, finished with pork fatback/lard and topped with fatty chashu pork; there is no vegetable-broth or plant-based option. Only the vegetable toppings (cabbage, bean sprouts, garlic) are themselves plant-based, but the dish as served is not vegan or vegetarian.

places.chef: Hashimoto Ken (founder) · founder: Hashimoto Ken (橋本賢) · Shinjuku, Tokyo (founded 1954/opened as udon shop in 1965) · Sangokuichi traces back to 1954, when founder Hashimoto Ken went independent and opened a small (about 6-tsubo) shop near Shinjuku's east exit, first selling bags, then converting it into a ramen shop the following year. In 1965 the shop changed business again to become an udon restaurant. The name '三国一' ("best of the three kingdoms") comes from a trip: returning by shinkansen from a Sanuki-udon tasting tour in Shikoku, the founder saw Mt. Fuji through the train window — a peak visible from three provinces (Shizuoka, Kanagawa, Yamanashi) — and named the shop after it. The company now runs three shops around Shinjuku Station (east exit, west exit, and the Island Tower location), all still hand-making their own noodles. · Everything made in-house: noodles are hand-pressed twice daily at the company's own nearby noodle-making facility and delivered fresh, and the dressing, mayonnaise, and dashi used across the menu are all made from scratch on site. · Salad udon (サラダうどん) — cold udon topped with fresh vegetables, tuna or meat, and a house-made mayonnaise-based dressing
places.gfd: The restaurant's identity is built around hand-made wheat udon noodles, freshly pressed twice daily at their own nearby noodle factory — there is no gluten-free noodle substitute mentioned anywhere. Standard Japanese soy sauce (which typically contains wheat) and wheat-based dashi/seasonings are used throughout the menu. Not a safe option for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
places.vgd: A traditional udon specialist known for meat-topped and dashi-based bowls (pork, beef, miso-braised, salad udon with mayonnaise-based dressing). places.chef: Original flagship shop of the Tarekatsu chain (opened June 2007) · Niigata City, Japan — home of the tare-katsudon style · Tarekatsu's cooking style traces back to Niigata City, where in the early Showa era Michitaro Komatsu, founder of the original Niigata shop Tonkatsu Taro, began dipping thin, freshly-fried pork cutlets in a sweet-savory soy sauce tare instead of folding them into egg as in Tokyo-style katsudon. places.chef: eel specialist / kushiyaki grill counter · Shibuya, Tokyo · Founded in 1957 in Shibuya's Dogen-zaka district, the shop was built around a simple idea: eel (unagi), long considered a luxury food in Japan, should be something ordinary people could enjoy casually and affordably. Instead of the formal, pricier kabayaki-box style served at many unagi restaurants, the founders built the menu around charcoal-grilled eel skewers — served almost like yakitori — so diners could order a few at a time. · Keep unagi cuisine unpretentious and accessible — grill it simply over binchotan charcoal, sell it by the skewer rather than only as a formal set meal, and let regulars drop in without a reservation the way they would at a neighborhood yakitori counter. · Kushiyaki eel skewers grilling nearly every part of the fish over Kishu binchotan charcoal (roughly 400°C) — including kurikara (a coiled belly-meat skewer), hire (fin), tsumaki, tanshaku, kimo (liver), kabuto (head), baramimi, and rebaa. The kurikara skewer is said to have originated at this shop.

places.chef: small family-run izakaya / postwar food stall lineage · Shōchan started as one of the yatai (open-air food stalls) that lined Asakusa's postwar Hoppy Street, opening in 1951 (Shōwa 26). It became a fixed shopfront roughly four decades later but kept its stall-style, half-outdoor seating and its original simmering pot of beef stew, topped up continuously ever since (a "tsugitashi" nikomi sauce). · An old-school Asakusa drinking-stall spirit: cheap, simple, unpretentious dishes (many under ¥500) meant to be eaten quickly at the counter or an outdoor tent table while drinking Hoppy, with the same pot of sauce carried forward for decades rather than remade from scratch. · Gyu-nikomi — beef tendon, konnyaku (devil's tongue jelly) and tofu slow-simmered for hours in a sweet-savory, soy-based sauce that has been continuously replenished since the shop opened; also served over rice as gyu-meshi.
places.gfd: No gluten-free options, labeling, or accommodations are mentioned anywhere in the sourcing. The signature nikomi stew is simmered in a soy-based sauce (Japanese soy sauce/shoyu almost always contains wheat) that has reportedly been continuously topped up since 1951, meaning any wheat content is baked into the base and cannot be removed per-order. Not recommended for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
places.vgd: No vegan options are indicated in any sourcing. places.chef: Yasuda Shin'ichi (安田眞一) · Owner: Yasuda Shin'ichi (安田眞一), a certified senior sommelier · Opened in 2001 just outside Shinjuku Station's east/central-east exit as a hand-made soba specialty restaurant. The shop mills its own domestic (Hokkaido) buckwheat in-house with a stone mill, then hand-kneads, hand-rolls and hand-cuts the noodles fresh each day, keeping the wheat-flour binder to roughly 20% to preserve the buckwheat's natural aroma and flavor. · Minimal binder, all-manual noodle-making (hand-kneaded/hand-rolled/hand-cut daily) to let the stone-milled buckwheat's own flavor come through, paired with seasonal Japanese small dishes and a sommelier-selected list of wine and sake. · Hand-cut stone-milled soba (seiro / inaka seiro / tenpura seiro), served alongside dishes such as duck confit and binchotan-charcoal-grilled jidori chicken.
places.gfd: The soba here is nihachi-style: stone-milled domestic buckwheat hand-kneaded with roughly 20% wheat flour as binder — not 100% buckwheat (juwari), so the noodles themselves contain gluten. The dipping sauce (tsuyu) and the tempura batter used for tenpura seiro are standard preparations that typically rely on wheat-based ingredients. No gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or celiac-safe accommodations were found in any source, so this is not a safe choice for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
places.vgd: This is a traditional soba specialty restaurant, not a vegan or vegetarian-focused establishment. The menu features duck confit, binchotan-charcoal-grilled chicken, tamagoyaki (egg), and a sommelier-curated wine/sake list; traditional soba tsuyu is conventionally made with bonito (katsuo) dashi. places.chef: wagashi shop, confectioner · 徳太樓 (Tokutaro) was founded in 1903 (Meiji 36) in Asakusa. Per multiple secondary sources, the founder came from a lower-ranking samurai family of the Akimoto clan from Tatebayashi domain, and after the Meiji Restoration trained in confectionery-making at a shop called Utaro, which had ties to the well-known Eitaro Sohonten confectioner in Nihonbashi. The shop has continued in the same neighborhood, in what locals call "oku-Asakusa" (the quieter area behind Senso-ji), ever since. · A deliberately old-fashioned, hand-technique approach — most notably the spatula-applied (rather than dipped) batter coating — that the shop has kept as a point of difference from other Tokyo kintsuba makers since the Meiji era. · Kintsuba — a rectangular sweet of simmered Tokachi (Hokkaido) azuki beans, cooked down and skimmed to a lightly sweetened filling, then hand-coated with a wheat-flour batter applied with a spatula (rather than dipped, as most kintsuba makers do) and baked so all six sides brown evenly on a copper griddle. The technique gives Tokutaro's kintsuba an unusually thick, chewy skin compared to other shops' versions. The shop reportedly makes over 1,000 pie…
places.gfd: The signature and dominant product, kintsuba, is defined by a wheat-flour (komugiko) batter that is hand-applied with a spatula to the surface of the azuki filling and then baked — wheat is intrinsic to the recipe, not an optional ingredient. No source mentions any gluten-free item, dedicated gluten-free process, or cross-contamination protocol. This is not a safe or accommodating choice for celiac or gluten-free diners.
places.vgd: The signature kintsuba's filling is described by several sources as simply simmered azuki beans, sugar, and water, which reads as plant-based, but no source confirms the full batter/coating ingredients, and other items in the shop's range (dorayaki, monaka, manju, nerikiri, sekihan) were not detailed enough to confirm the absence of egg, honey, or other animal-derived ingredients. places.chef: Proprietress (女将) and family — currently run by a mother-daughter team with staff · Opened in 1947 (Shōwa 22), just after the end of World War II, in the Asakusa Kannon-ura district directly behind Sensō-ji Temple. places.chef: Founder: Kyuzo Shimura (1924) · Founded 1924 (Taisho 13) in Tsunohazu, Shinjuku by Kyuzo Shimura · Tsunahachi traces back to 1922, when founder Kyuzo Shimura opened a stand-and-eat tempura shop called "Amihachi" (網八). Customers habitually misread the character 網 (ami) as tsuna, and the mispronunciation stuck so firmly that in 1924 the shop was formally reopened under the name it kept the same location in Shinjuku's old Tsunohazu district as today's Sohonten. The original building was destroyed in the 1945 air raids and post-war land readjustment; the shop rebuilt and reopened on the same ground in 1948. Over nine decades the company grew into one of Japan's best-known tempura chains, with roughly 23 branches nationwide (Sapporo, Toyama, Nagoya, Kyoto, Osaka and more) as of early 2026. In 2026 the flagship Sohonten building closed for a full rebuild planned to run until summer 2028; during construction the original staff and craftsmen relocated a minute's walk away to a temporary location, 'Sohonten Bekkan' (総本店別館), inside the TRES SHINJUKU building, which opened June 23, 2026. · The house motto, carried since the founder's era, is to 'always serve the finest tempura at an accessib…

places.chef: 岩瀬健治 (Iwase Kenji) · Chef-owner · Kanagawa Prefecture · Iwase came to sushi relatively late, having started his culinary career at 21 after an earlier stint as a salaryman. He trained within the well-regarded "Sushi Sho" (すし匠) lineage of Edomae sushi restaurants, working at Sushi Sho Masa in Nishi-Azabu, Sushi Subaru in Aoyama, and Takumi Tatsuhiro in Shinjuku before striking out on his own in September 2012. The restaurant later relocated to its current Nishi-Shinjuku location near Tochomae Station in 2017. · Food writers describe the restaurant's approach as "呑ます鮨" (sushi that makes you want to drink) — richly seasoned tsumami dishes interspersed with delicate nigiri, built around the rhythm of pairing food with sake rather than nigiri alone. · An alternating omakase of nigiri and otsumami (small savory side dishes) in the "Sushi Sho style," running to roughly 33-35 courses in total. Fish is sourced directly from the Yanagibashi Rengo Ichiba market in Hakata, Fukuoka, with Iwase reportedly traveling there himself to select seasonal seafood before it is shipped to the restaurant.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · tsukemen] Owner Yaginuma Eiji worked in Japanese restaurants and ramen shops through his twenties. places.notes: [Mom & Pop · yōshoku since 1895] A Ginza Western-food house founded in 1895 by Kida Motojirō, at a time when Western cooking was eaten only in hotels and at court. He wanted ordinary people to be able to order a single Western dish. His great-grandson, Kida Kōichirō, runs it today as the fourth-generation owner, with long-serving staff. The house credits itself with much of Japanese yōshoku as we know it. Its pork cutlet adapted the veal côtelette with pork, because veal was scarce. Shredded cabbage beside the cutlet, it says, started when cooks were drafted in the Russo-Japanese War and there was no one to make warm vegetables. Rice on a flat plate and two omurice, both from around 1900, are also on its list. The original omurice began as a staff meal, with egg and rice mixed together. There are four floors, including a tatami room, and bricks from the old Ginza brick district hang on the ground-floor wall. Cash only.

Four generations on, the house keeps its 'casual yōshoku-ya' spirit, with long-serving staff working alongside the fourth-generation owner. · 気取らない「洋食屋」の精神 — the unpretentious spirit of a neighbourhood Western-food house. · Original pork cutlet; Meiji-born omurice and the original mixed-rice omurice; consommé jelly.

The Meiji-style omurice is seasoned with a little sugar-and-soy, and Japanese soy sauce contains wheat by default. No gluten-free dish is mentioned.

Its concept, 'Modern Shōjin', serves the bounty of Japan's land through cooking methods from around the world, guided by eating local and by 身土不二, the idea that body and land are one. The signature is a seasonal 'veggie meal stand': kombucha of the day, nine small dishes, black-rice multigrain rice and a clear soup. There are also soup curry, a fermented-food bibimbap, soy-meat taco rice, a kombu-mushroom-vegetable dashi vegan ramen, and vegan desserts and parfaits. The menu changes monthly and marks every dish VG and most GF.

places.notes: [Tonkatsu · since 1927] Ginza's first tonkatsu specialist. It opened in 1927 under founder Shibuya Nobukatsu, a former pharmacist who drew on that training to create a thick, sweet tonkatsu sauce from apple and onion, which the house calls the original chūnō sauce. He also cut fillet into bite-size pieces ('hitokuchi katsu'), put katsu between slices of bread, and created the 'special katsudon', a loin cutlet bound in egg with a second, unbroken egg on top. The family business, 有限会社梅林 under president Shibuya Masaya, is in its third generation. It has franchise counters at Haneda Airport, in Waikiki and in Seoul. The head shop is in the basement of its own building. It uses Kagoshima black pork, Yamagata Tsuyahime rice (free refills) and seasonal cabbage, and the fillet-katsu sandwich is packed in old-style wood-shaving boxes.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · Japanese omakase, Michelin ★★] Owner-chef Takemasa Shinohara trained at Kyoto restaurants including Sangencha and opened his own Shinohara in his hometown of Kōnan, Shiga, in his twenties. When it had become a destination, he left it behind and started again in Ginza in October 2016. A small lantern leads down to a calm room around an L-shaped counter of white wood, thirteen seats, with tableware down to old Baccarat. One omakase course (¥35,000 including tax in 2026, with seasonal extras such as crab or charcoal-grilled beef rice), changing monthly. Its signature is the hassun, a lavish platter of the season themed to the calendar, such as the Double Ninth in September. Michelin two stars, and The Tabelog Award Gold every year from 2017 to 2026. In October 2026 it marked ten years in Ginza and twenty since the first Shinohara, and many of his former cooks now run fully booked restaurants of their own. Book months ahead.

places.notes: [Stand-up soba · no sign] A one-person-wide stand-up soba counter in Yaesu 2-chōme, opposite Tokyo Square Garden, with no signboard: look for a noren and a retriever, the shop dog, by the door. Photography is strictly forbidden inside, and staff will stop you. A quiet owner takes orders. Prices are old-fashioned: kake soba ¥340, kakiage or kisu tempura ¥130 each, egg ¥70 (April 2026). places.cu: Tempura omakase — Michelin two stars since 2008 · vegetable tempura
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · tempura master] Kondō Fumio, born in 1947, joined the tempura kitchen of the Yama-no-ue Hotel in Ochanomizu after high school and became its head chef at 23. He opened his own counter in Ginza in 1991 and, more than 50 years into his career, still fries at the counter himself at lunch and dinner. His batter is cut as thin as possible so it doesn't soak up oil, and he treats tempura as a steamed dish too, timing the carry-over heat inside the batter. Above all he brought vegetables into high-end Edo-mae tempura, which had been seafood-only. His signature is a stump-thick sweet potato fried slowly for about 30 minutes. It has held two Michelin stars since 2008. He was named a 現代の名工 (Contemporary Master Craftsman) in 2019, and in 2023 became the first tempura chef to receive Michelin's Mentor Chef Award. Two counters of 12 and 8 seats, by reservation.

He went independent in Ginza in 1991. · 「天ぷらは、料理人がゲストをお招きする料理」 — tempura is the cook inviting the guest; and 「天ぷらの本質は蒸し料理」, tempura is at heart a steamed dish. · Thin-battered seasonal tempura; vegetables (sweet potato, carrot) as courses in their own right.

places.chef: 大塚せつ子 (Setsuko Otsuka) · Tokyo · Otsuka Setsuko is widely known in Japan as the "Mother of Rice Flour" (米粉の母), a leading figure in the domestic rice-flour movement who is regularly featured in media. She produced and launched RICE HACK Gluten-free Bakery, which opened on November 12, 2022 in Jingumae, Shibuya, operated through 株式会社ライステラス (Rice Terrace / Onden House). · That Japanese rice "can change the world" — her breads are not meant as mere wheat substitutes but as foods delicious enough that people with celiac disease or wheat allergy and people without can enjoy the exact same thing together. She emphasizes rice flour's own nutritional properties (rice bran, whole-grain character) rather than mimicking wheat. · Rice-flour bread and gluten-free baking — the shop's signature is a fully from-scratch baked curry pan (homemade curry filling and rice-flour breadcrumbs, crisped in the oven rather than deep-fried).
places.gfd: Fully dedicated 100% gluten-free bakery — there is NO wheat flour on the premises. Everything is baked from rice flour (specially grown Koshihikari, rice bran included), natural yeast, kibi sugar and rock salt. Findmeglutenfree lists it explicitly as a "Dedicated Gluten-Free Bakery," and a celiac reviewer (celiacchat.ca) reported no cross-contamination concerns and that the owner/staff understand celiac disease. Signature curry pan is baked, not deep-fried, so there is no shared-fryer risk. One…
places.vgd: Not a vegan-only shop, but it carries genuine vegan items among the gluten-free lineup: a chickpea vegan curry pan (¥360), a big vegan marinara/margherita-style rice-crust pizza, and several plain bread rolls/loaves and an "ichizen no pan" with a meat-free bolognese/stew. Many other items are NOT vegan — cheese curry pan, cheese-stuffed rolls, and a wafu pizza topped with cheese, mayo and shirasu…

places.chef: 山田英知郎 (Yamada Eichiro / Eishiro) · Tokyo · Owner-chef who founded MOMINOKI HOUSE in 1976, making it one of Japan's longest-running natural-food restaurants (40+ years). He trained/cooked in the United States and Britain and is regarded as one of Japan's leading macrobiotic figures, holding leadership roles in slow-life and natural-food organizations. He runs a YouTube channel ('もみの木チャンネル') and personally sources grains and vegetables from natural-cultivation (自然栽培) farms. · Cooking rooted in macrobiotics (玄米菜食) — whole brown rice, vegetables, fermented foods, additive-free ('無添加') seasonings and 'electronic ion water' — with gentle seasoning meant to be kind to the body. He verifies each farm's soil and water 'with his five senses' ('土、水など栽培環境のすべてを五感で確認') and has a stated ambition to help shift Japanese agriculture toward natural cultivation. · Macrobiotic / plant-forward natural food: vegemeat karaage, tofu steak, vegan sushi and brown-rice sets, alongside naturally-raised fish and game for non-vegetarian guests.
places.gfd: The official site advertises a new menu line explicitly labeled "グルテンフリー・五葷抜き" (gluten-free & no five-pungent-vegetables), so real GF dishes exist and the staff will engage with the request. However this is NOT a dedicated GF kitchen: it is an omnivore macrobiotic kitchen that also fries vegemeat karaage/tempura (wheat batter) and serves fish/game, so shared-fryer and shared-surface wheat cross-contact is likely. A celiac must specifically ask whether the GF items use wheat-free tamari — standa…
places.vgd: Clearly marked, abundant vegan menu ("ビーガンメニューあり") built on macrobiotic principles: vegemeat karaage, tofu steak, vegan sushi, vegetable curry, plus brown rice / miso soup / vegetable sets. Additive-free, naturally-cultivated ("自然栽培・無添加") ingredients. Because the same kitchen also cooks fish (e.g. Norwegian mackerel) and venison, it is not an exclusively vegan house — confirm your dish is the veg…

rm.bowl: 九州じゃんがら — the mild tonkotsu house bowl; regulars order it 全部入り (everything in).

places.notes: [Ramen · Tokyo chain] The Ginza branch of Kyushu Jangara, a Tokyo ramen company founded in Akihabara in 1984. It opened on Mihara-dōri in Ginza 7-chōme in 1991 and moved to this spot on 2010-07-07. Its 16 seats are all at tables. The house bowl is a mild pork-bone soup with chicken frames and vegetables. The rest of the line-up runs from the creamy Hakata/Kurume-style Bonshan to the Kumamoto-style Kobonshan with black-garlic oil. The 'zenbu-iri' (everything in) bowl, with braised pork belly, mentaiko and a seasoned egg, is a phrase the shop says was born at its own counter. Pickled mustard greens and red ginger are free at the table. There is also a plant-based shoyu ramen. Menus in English, Chinese, Korean and Thai are kept at every branch, and 2026 diners describe a queue of overseas visitors at peak times.
places.chef: ramen company (タスグループ — 九州じゃんがら) · Founded in Akihabara, Tokyo, in 1984; Kyushu-style tonkotsu · Kyushu Jangara is run by Tas Group (タスグループ), which began in 1979 as the ブルカン塾 cram school and opened its first ramen shop in Akihabara in 1984, in the company's words to shore up the school's finances. It now runs five Kyushu Jangara shops in Tokyo — Akihabara, Harajuku, Ginza, Akasaka and Shiba-Daimon — plus a vegan bistro in Harajuku, and in 1993 moved its prep into a central kitchen. · Mild tonkotsu (Kyushu Jangara), creamy Hakata/Kurume-rooted Bonshan, Kumamoto-style Kobonshan with house black-garlic oil; zenbu-iri toppings; a plant-based shoyu ramen.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The company describes its ramen noodles as a blend of several wheat flours bound with egg white, and lists no gluten-free noodle. Its FAQ publishes no allergen information. The vegan bowl is seasoned with dark soy sauce (濃い口醤油), which in Japan is brewed with wheat by default, and the seasoned egg is marinated in the house soy sauce. Not suitable for celiacs.

At the Akihabara branch the same bowl is documented with egg-free noodles and soy-meat chashu; ask at Ginza that it is made the same way. Every other bowl is built on …

places.n: 中華 銀座亭 (Chūka Ginza-tei)

rm.bowl: みそチャーシュー (miso chashu) — a gentle miso soup over wok-fried bean sprouts, cabbage and pork belly, with four thick slices of pork shoulder; ¥1,300 in 2023.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · machi-chūka] A 1975 neighbourhood Chinese counter on Hanatsubaki-dōri, run by the founder's family into its third generation. The grandfather left an office job, trained at the 1970s tsukemen chain つけ麺大王 (Tsukemen Daiō) and opened a franchise of it here; around 1977 he went independent as 銀座亭. Tsukemen is still the oldest dish on the menu. Set meals were added for the people who work Ginza's nights, and today orders run about six set meals to three noodle dishes to one drinking snack. Five or six cooks work the wok behind a U-shaped counter of 15 seats. Diners come for the miso chashu and the mapo harusame rice bowl. Tabelog named it one of Tokyo's 100 best Chinese restaurants (百名店) in 2024 and 2026. Expect a queue at peak times; staff hand over a picture menu on request.
places.chef: 北岡秋平 (Kitaoka Shūhei) · third-generation owner, runs the shop with his father (second generation) · Ginza 7-chōme, Tokyo — founded in 1975 by his grandfather · Kitaoka's grandfather left a salaried job, trained at つけ麺大王 and opened this counter in 1975 as one of its franchises, then went independent around 1977 under the name 銀座亭. Kitaoka worked at a yakitori restaurant before joining his father at the shop in 2020; they had expected the Tokyo Olympics to make the shop busy that year. · 「これからも『銀座亭』が提供してきた、食べて安心する味を守っていきたい」 — to keep serving the comforting food the shop has always served. · Miso chashu ramen (wok-fried vegetables, four thick slices of pork shoulder); mapo harusame rice bowl; tsukemen descended from the つけ麺大王 recipe.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. This is a neighbourhood Chinese counter (machi-chūka) built around ramen, tsukemen, gyoza and stir-fries. The ramen-type noodles are wheat by default, and no gluten-free noodle or dish is mentioned in any source. The house miso tare is made in-house, and its miso type is not published (miso can be barley). The gyoza come with a vinegar-and-soy dip. The rice dishes and stir-fries are not documented ingredient by ingredient. One tiny kitchen does all of it. Not suitable for celia…
places.vgd: Not vegan. The owner says one house soup, made from chicken feet (もみじ), pig's trotters and vegetables, is the base of every noodle dish. The signature dishes are pork-heavy: miso chashu, the minced-meat mapo harusame rice bowl and twice-cooked pork. No vegetarian or vegan dish is mentioned in any source.
