rm.bowl: たんめん — the only bowl, in regular or large; reviewers note a sesame-oil aroma in the salt soup.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · tanmen] A 9-seat counter near Kabuki-za that has served exactly one dish since it opened in January 2019. The owner taught themself to make it, trying to recreate a tanmen they used to eat as a student. The bowl is a clear, salted chicken-frame soup with thin straight noodles, buried under napa cabbage and a little pork. The cabbage is simmered with the soup in a frying pan, but only so far that it stays crunchy. The shop buys whatever napa cabbage is best that season and posts its origin, which in 2026 was Nagano's Nobeyama and Saku-Asama highlands. Toppings are butter, cilantro and nori. Homemade chili oil, white pepper and vinegar sit on the counter. A September 2026 diner found the owner running the shop alone. Lunch queues are common.
places.chef: owner-operator · Ginza 4-chōme, Tokyo; opened 16 January 2019 · The owner set out to recreate the tanmen they used to eat as a student and worked it out by self-study (独学で研究), opening this one-dish counter in 2019. No other branch was found. · Tanmen: salted chicken-frame soup, thin straight noodles, a mound of seasonal napa cabbage and pork.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The shop serves one dish, tanmen: thin, straight ramen-type noodles, which are wheat by default, in a salted chicken-frame soup. No gluten-free noodle is mentioned in any source. Not suitable for celiacs.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · ramen izakaya] A Ginza back-lane ramen shop open since 1996, until 4 a.m. on weekdays: lunch for office workers and shoppers, a last bowl after drinks, and early-morning ramen. Iwano Tsutomu trained in about three ramen shops, joined Matsutomi in 2000 and took it over from the founder in 2013. He keeps the founder's base soup of pork bones and Hidaka kombu, which goes into every bowl. The most popular is shoyu ramen. The quiet favourite is the clam ramen, limited to 20 a day, made with clams bought fresh each morning and served with butter, kombu and egg noodles. At night it becomes a ramen izakaya, with a cheap drink set and the 特許しうまい, a shumai made by a patented method. Cash only.
places.chef: 岩野努 (Iwano Tsutomu) · owner (second generation, since 2013) · Ginza 6-chōme; shop founded 1996 · Iwano had always wanted his own ramen shop. He worked in about three ramen shops to study how each made its soup, joined Matsutomi at around 25 in 2000, and took it over from the founder in 2013. Long-serving staff help him keep the founder's recipes. · 「先代が作った味をそのまま受け継いでます」 — keeping the founder's flavour, changing it little by little and adding new dishes, and carrying the shop on for another ten or twenty years. · Shoyu ramen and clam ramen on a pork-bone and Hidaka-kombu base; tantanmen; patented shumai and gyoza.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. Ramen, tantanmen, tsukemen, gyoza and shumai. There are three kinds of wheat noodle (egg noodles, thin straight, thick), soy sauce and grated garlic are on the counter, and every noodle soup shares one base stock. No gluten-free dish is mentioned in any source.
places.vgd: The shop's own Tabelog listing ticks 'vegetarian options', but no source says what they are. Every noodle dish (shoyu ramen, tantanmen, clam ramen) shares one base soup of pork bones (げん骨) and Hidaka kombu, so none of them is vegan. The side dishes include morokyu (cucumber with miso). Ask the staff what they mean by the vegetarian option.
places.hours: Mon–Fri 11:00–15:00 & 17:00–04:00; Sat 11:00–15:00 & 18:00–22:00; closed Sundays and holidays. Cash only; a service charge is added. Free large noodles at lunch.

places.notes: [Ramen · French-chef chuka soba] Matsumura Yasushi spent 36 years in French kitchens, including as executive chef of Kyoto's ANA hotel, then turned to ramen to serve 'a full course in a bowl'. After his 勝本 shops in Suidōbashi and Jimbōchō, he opened this 6-seat counter in December 2018. He spent months after fit-out perfecting the bowl. The soup uses no tare: a golden consommé of duck, whole Nagoya Cochin chicken, prosciutto and scallop with kombu, shiitake and dried tomato, seasoned only with a little Guérande salt. It is paired with a thin noodle made for this soup by Asakusa Kaikarō. Tabelog has named it a ramen 百名店 every year from 2019 to 2025, and the 2026 Michelin Guide gave it a seventh straight listing (Bib Gourmand). The name refers to the 8.5-tsubo room and to a mountaineering saying about the eighth station. Book on TableCheck or queue. The owner and staff speak English.
places.chef: 松村康史 (Matsumura Yasushi) · owner-chef, company: 株式会社Food Operation Japan (also runs the 勝本 shops) · French cuisine — 36 years, incl. executive chef at Kyoto ANA Hotel (now ANA Crowne Plaza Kyoto) · After 36 years as a French chef, Matsumura decided to recreate 'a full course in a bowl' and switched to ramen. He opened 中華そば勝本 in Suidōbashi (March 2015) and つけそば神田勝本 in Jimbōchō (February 2016), and the group now also has 豊洲勝本. Ginza Hachigō, opened in December 2018, is where he put everything he knew. Turning 66 in October 2025, he said he hopes to stay at the stove as long as he can, and has an eye on opening abroad. · 「誰でも気取らず美味しい料理を手軽に楽しんでいただきたい」 — anyone should be able to enjoy fine food casually. · Tare-free golden consommé chuka soba; ravioli of truffle, foie gras and prosciutto; Kaikarō thin noodles; pepper-caviar chashu.

rm.bowl: ワンタンメン (wonton-men) — ¥1,100 in October 2026 (¥1,000 in 2023).

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · since 1956] A three-generation Ginza chuka-soba shop. Founder Nakano Taichirō started with a street stall and set up in Ginza 2-chōme in 1956. His grandson Kazuhiko, who trained in Cantonese kitchens, now runs it with his parents Kikuo and Kiyoko. When the building was rebuilt, the shop closed from 2016 to 2019. Its noodle maker retired around then, so Kazuhiko learned the craft and now makes the noodles and wonton skins in-house; the noodles are made after closing, sometimes until 2 a.m. There is one shoyu soup, chicken and niboshi, under every bowl. The wonton-men is the favourite, and the menma is rehydrated over four days. The name 共楽 means a happy life shared by the house and its customers. Twelve seats, a queue at opening, cash only.
places.chef: 中野和彦 (Nakano Kazuhiko) · third-generation owner, with 二代目 中野喜久雄 (father) and 中野きよ子 (mother) · Ginza 2-chōme; founded 1956 by 中野太一郎, who began with a street stall · Kazuhiko helped in the shop from primary school, trained in Cantonese restaurants from 20, and joined at 26 when his father asked. During the 2016–2019 rebuild of the building he worked in other ramen shops to learn noodle-making, and on reopening in 2019 switched both the noodles and the wonton skins to house-made. · 「お客様が喜んでくれて、また来てくれるのが一番」. The founder chose the name 共楽 hoping the owners and customers would share a happy life. · Shoyu chuka soba (chicken and niboshi); wonton-men with house-made skins; chashu of pork thigh; four-day menma.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. One shoyu chuka soba is the base of every bowl. The noodles and the wonton skins are made in-house from wheat, and the menma and chashu are seasoned. No gluten-free option is mentioned.
places.vgd: Not vegan. The single soup is chicken and niboshi (dried sardine) finished with soy sauce, and the toppings are pork chashu and meat-filled wontons.

places.notes: [Gluten-free · brown-rice Italian] The basement restaurant of FANCL Ginza Square, the cosmetics and supplements company's ten-floor Ginza building, open since September 2019. It cooks Italian without wheat flour. The fresh pasta is made by hand every day from a blended brown-rice flour and still has an al dente bite. The bread is brown rice, the rice is FANCL's own germinated brown rice, and the dolci are gluten-free too. There are weekday lunch plates, weekend lunch courses and a build-your-own dinner. It has 36 seats, including a private room that looks onto a waterfall. It is a fixture of celiac travellers' Tokyo lists, with 130+ reviews on FindMeGlutenFree. The brown-rice bread is sold to take away.

places.notes: [Gluten-free · Mom & Pop · kushiage omakase] A six-seat, reservation-only counter where a single chef cooks and serves a seasonal omakase of gluten-free fried skewers: two starters, eleven skewers, soup, a palate cleanser and dessert. Everyone starts together at 7 p.m. There is no sign. You walk through the Ginza Park Building and buzz 201 at the side entrance. Celiac reviewers call it the best gluten-free meal they have had in Tokyo, with mentions of the chef's warmth and a gluten-free rice beer. The course is seafood-heavy and soy-seasoned, so it suits neither vegans nor guests with a soy allergy.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · since the 1920s] Manpuku began as a chuka-soba street stall in the Taishō era. In 1929 the founder opened a shop in old Kobikichō, close to Kabuki-za. He had trained in Western cooking, so it ran as a 'Western and Chinese' (西支料理) restaurant; the faded wooden sign by the door still says so. His grandson Kubo Hidetaka is the third owner and has turned the menu towards Chinese food. Pork rice is the one Western dish left: ketchup fried rice made with the house chashu instead of chicken. The chuka soba keeps the soup the earlier generations made: a soy soup of seafood and meat stocks with a hint of ginger and negi oil, thin curly noodles, and a triangle of thin omelette on top. The wooden building was rebuilt in 2003 but kept its old frontage, and some families have been coming for four generations. Cash only.

Kubo gave up a university-era dream after an injury, trained in other Chinese restaurants at his father's insistence, and took over from his father at about 25. Under him the Western dishes (omurice, cutlets) gave way to more Chinese ones, such as liver and chives and ebi-tama. · 「先代からスープの味を変えてない」 — the soup has not changed since the previous generations. · Chuka soba with a triangle omelette; pork rice (ketchup fried rice with chashu); set meals.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · Hakodate shio] A Hakodate ramen shop near Kabuki-za, open since 2001 under the banner 'early-Shōwa Hakodate ramen'. Its founder had been won over by ramen on a trip to Hakodate. The present owner, Kiribayashi Masahiko, once cooked at a well-known Chinese restaurant and worked here in 2010–12. He left to run his own shop, and when that site was cleared in 2014 he took this one over; regulars greeted him with 'welcome back'. The bowl to order is shio soba. It is a golden, clear soup of Hokkaido ma-kombu, dried scallop, chicken frames, pork bone and vegetables, seasoned with Bizen rock salt. The noodles are rebuilt from an early-Shōwa recipe with coarse wheat flour and coloured with gardenia, because the old recipe comes out grey. The chashu sits in a soy-and-mirin tare that has been topped up for years. The room is fitted out like a Hokkaido fishing-port shack, and it is open until 4 a.m.

The president chose the décor and the name; the manager, Satō Hikaru, says the name was probably picked because the characters look cool. The draw is 麻辛丸, read 'machine gun', a registered trademark. Extra-thick, chewy noodles that taste of wheat go into a red, sour-hot dip on a chicken-frame base, with shredded chashu and house menma. Pork-loin chashu is the top topping. There is also a very light Japanese-style ramen on ultra-thin noodles. Office workers come at lunch, hotel guests in the afternoon and drinkers late at night. There is an English and Korean menu. Cash only.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · Aomori ramen] A six-seat basement counter under a red lantern, 30 seconds from Ginza Station. Owner Hasegawa Ichirō, whose name is on the door, had run soba and Italian restaurants and lived in the US for about five years. He opened here in December 2016, choosing Ginza with an eye to opening abroad. Several people around the shop were from Aomori, so he built the ramen on Aomori produce: Shamorock chicken, and clams from Lake Jūsan, billed as 'Japan's best'. Every bowl shares one soup of Shamorock chicken, grilled flying fish and tomato, now cooked between clear and cloudy. The clam ramen's tare adds shottsuru fish sauce. Pork chashu comes in very large slices. In 2026 he still cooks almost single-handed, and the shop had not raised its prices since opening as of 2023.

places.notes: [Ramen · back-fat tonkotsu] The Ginza branch of らーめん元楽, a back-fat ramen company whose head shop opened in Kuramae in 1995 and which also has a shop in Shimbashi. The soup uses only pork knuckle bones (genkotsu), simmered for three days with vegetables and chicken frames, skimmed hard, until it turns mellow and jellies when cold. The back fat that covers the bowl is fried, blanched, washed and simmered in the soup for two hours, so it comes out sweet and fluffy rather than greasy. Order 元 for shoyu or 楽 for shio. The pork-belly chashu is braised two and a half hours until it cuts with chopsticks. Half buta-meshi (pork over rice) is the usual side. Garlic and doubanjiang are on the counter.

Itō Hiromu runs the Akabane shop and spread the name to Ginza and Kanda. He makes the noodles and soup in a central kitchen and leaves each shop to its manager. The style is famous for its plainness: a bitter-edged niboshi soup glittering with sardine powder, firm low-hydration noodles, and in the classic bowl nothing but green onion. The niku-soba piles on chashu. Ginza also serves the uncle's Hinai-jidori chicken soba, which a 2026 diner says the Ōji branch doesn't have, and a niboshi tsukemen whose noodles come soaked in a kombu-water-like broth. 12 seats.

places.notes: [Ramen · vegan & GF options] The flagship of Soranoiro, the ramen company that opened in Kōjimachi just after the 2011 earthquake. It became known for 'veggie soba' made with vegetables in the noodles, soup and toppings, and for its vegan ramen and gluten-free ramen. After 14 years the head shop moved to Ginza. The chuka soba here is built on the frames of Amakusa Daiō, one of Japan's largest native chickens, with niboshi, bonito and aromatic vegetables. Its noodles are made of domestic wheat at the company's Kōjimachi workshop, and the chashu is Seto mochi-buta pork from Fukuyama in three cuts. Celiac and vegan travellers on FindMeGlutenFree report a separate gluten-free menu and a vegan gluten-free ramen at this shop.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · dashi ramen] A dark, quiet shop in a back alley between Ginza and Shimbashi, opened in 2010 by Sasanuma Takahiro after 18 years as a Japanese-cuisine chef. He worked at a Ginza restaurant known for sea-bream chazuke, and built his shop around the same idea: eat the ramen, eat some sea-bream rice plain, then pour the soup over the rest to make chazuke. The soup is chicken and pork stock, chilled overnight and stripped of fat, then joined with kombu and niboshi dashi; it is not a sea-bream broth, as many first-timers assume. Choose salt or white soy sauce. The bowl, modelled on a kaiseki soup course, carries pink sea-bream fish balls and pork-belly chashu torched to order. The spouted bowls were made by his pottery teacher in Hannō-yaki, so the soup pours neatly onto the rice. Listed in the Tabelog Ramen TOKYO 100 every year from 2017 to 2025. Queues form at the 11:15 opening.

places.notes: [Ramen · Tokyo shoyu, late night] The Ginza shop of 株式会社創龍, the company behind the Nogata Hope ramen shops (its first Nogata Hope opened in 1988). Opened in October 2018 as a step-up, glass-fronted room with high ceilings, sofa seats and a counter facing the kitchen. The focus is Tokyo: Kikkogo soy sauce from Kondō Jōzō, which the shop calls Tokyo's only soy-sauce brewery, and Edo-na greens. The signature 大江戸焦がし醤油 burns the house shoyu tare in lard, and the burnt lard seals the clear soup so it stays hot. Other bowls: a mellow white shoyu with shiro-tamari, ishiru and Izu Ōshima salt; a black shoyu with flying-fish dashi; Nogata Hope's original tonkotsu shoyu 元; the richer 濃 with fish dashi, garlic oil and spicy miso; and a tomato ramen. Open until 3 a.m. six nights a week, it fills with after-drinks crowds.

places.notes: [Ramen · clear tonkotsu] A Ginza-only spin-off of the Hakata shop 豚そば月や, opened on the sixth floor of GINZA SIX in April 2023. It rebuilt its Hakata pork soba from the ingredients up into a clear tonkotsu, light enough that diners finish the broth, with thin noodles ordered by firmness, from firm to extra firm. The bowl comes with a suggested order of add-ins: green onion, nori, chashu, a squeeze of kabosu, then pickled ginger. The other draw is Hakata tarako rice with a special spicy sauce; the cod roe comes from Yamato Violets of the Fukuya group, under a supply contract renewed in April 2026. There are dishes brought in from Fukuoka restaurants too, and a ¥3,300 Tsukiya set adds shumai, fried horse mackerel and tomato. Queues, many of them overseas visitors, form at lunch.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · machi-chūka since 1971] A rare independent neighbourhood Chinese restaurant in Marunouchi, under the brick railway arches near Tokyo Station's south exit, where the yellow Hato buses line up. The owner's uncle opened it in 1971. Owner Hirata Kōichi worked here for about forty years and took over as the second generation around 2014. Chefs with twenty or thirty years in the kitchen still cook the founder's recipes, and the menu has barely changed. It runs to more than sixty dishes, more than twenty of them noodles. The owner's recommendations are the tanmen and the meat-and-vegetable stir-fry, the most popular dish, which becomes a set for ¥200 more. Regulars also come for liver with garlic chives, offal stamina ramen and miso ramen. Prices are low for Marunouchi: ramen was ¥800 in September 2026. You pay first for a coloured plastic meal ticket, and Marunouchi office workers queue even after lunch.

places.notes: [Ramen · the Haru-chan original] The first shop of はるちゃんラーメン: six counter seats on the ground floor of the old Shimbashi Ekimae Building, opened in August 2021 by a woman who goes by Haru-chan and had worked in ramen shops for about twenty years. In 2022 she ran it single-handed in a kitchen barely big enough to turn round in, styled like 'Haru-chan's kitchen at home' in warm wood. She calls it chuka soba, not ramen, because chuka soba sounds warmer. The soup is a light salt base: the pork stock from braising the chashu, with niboshi and aromatic vegetables. It is filled to the brim so it stays hot to the end. Flat Daruma Seimen noodles, two cuts of chashu (shoulder and belly) sliced only to order, and pastel fu on top for colour. 2026 diners describe it as a Michelin Bib Gourmand shop, with a queue around noon. The brand opened a second shop in Ginza 3-chōme in 2024.

places.notes: [Ramen · yuzu wafu shio] A seven-seat counter in the basement of the Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan by Yūrakuchō Station, on the narrow 'Yokotcho' passage. It opened in 2005 as the sister shop of the long-running sweets house 甘味おかめ in the same building, and the company that runs Okame, Ishizuka Kōsan, runs it too. The menu is four bowls: wafu ramen and wafu chashu-men, each also made with yuzu. The soup is a pale-gold clear stock of chicken bones with bonito and kombu, very light. The yuzu versions get freshly grated yuzu in the centre to stir in, with mitsuba, mizuna, menma and negi. Thin noodles, three large smoky slices of chashu on the chashu bowls, and Okame's chameshi (tea-flavoured rice) on the side. Bowls arrive in about three minutes, and the queue moves fast; buy your ticket from the machine before joining it. It was ¥780 for wafu ramen in May 2026.

places.notes: [Tsukemen · Rokurinsha group] A 16-seat counter under the railway arches near the Hato Bus terminal at Tokyo Station, opened in January 2020 by 松富士食品, the company behind Rokurinsha and Sharin. On weekdays it opens at 7 a.m. with a ¥600 morning ramen (to 10:30): thin straight noodles, lots of ginger, a lighter broth with gentle niboshi and chashu scraps, and extra noodles instead of a large size. From late morning it is tsukemen: thick, chewy noodles served cold, a dipping soup one 2026 diner found meat-led rather than seafood-led, grated garlic to add, and portions so big that a 'large' surprised two reviewers. Spicy and chilled mala tsukemen, cold sesame noodles, chicken-oil rice and egg on rice are on the menu. Buy a ticket inside, wait, and collect your bowl when your number is called.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · tantanmen and a bar] Takanashi Tomoyoshi grew up in Shimbashi, worked as a bartender in Ginza, and in 2021 opened this 'neo ramen' shop in his home neighbourhood, because he liked the idea of ramen with drinks. Eight counter seats downstairs and a Chinese dining bar upstairs, marked by a tantanmen lantern next to the Daiwa Roynet Hotel. He asked an old friend, the owner of the Kinshichō tantanmen shop noodle house 錦鯉, to produce a tantanmen that goes with alcohol. It is built on a house paste of freshly ground sesame and cashew, a soup of chicken, dried ingredients, shijimi clams, Hokkaidō kombu and shiitake, minced domestic pork, and a chilli oil of four chillies. Noodles were developed with Kanno Seimen, with whole wheat in them. There is also a dry tantanmen with hand-massaged medium-thick noodles, a tantan tsukemen with black vinegar, a shoyu chuka soba, and a night-only 'Tōgenkyō' tantanmen with a fried chicken cutlet. Spice and numbness levels are adjustable. Try the ¥300 jarichi, a ginger-soy pork cutlet, dropped into the soup like pāko-men.

places.notes: [Ramen + sushi · nearly 24 hours] The Shimbashi branch, opened August 2024, of a sushi-and-ramen chain whose head shop is in Yokohama's central wholesale market. Open from 10 a.m. to 3 a.m., it fills late at night, much of the crowd from overseas. Founder Usuda Noriyasu is a former Maritime Self-Defense Force sailor who became an izakaya-industry manager and trainer.

places.notes: [Ramen · iekei, Budōka line] Opened 10 June 2026 by Kōno Jōji, 'George' to regulars, who spent a decade as manager of the Kichijōji shop of Budōka, the Tokyo iekei shop people travel from other prefectures for. His soup is Budōka's dark, deep pork-bone stock, of which the press release says 300 kg of bones go into a pot boiled hard, rounded off with chicken oil. Order noodle firmness, richness and oil at the counter. Ramen is ¥900 and rice ¥100, cheap for Ginza; soak the nori in the soup and wrap the rice in it. He wants to build 'a Ginza ordinary people can use every day'. The shop opened under the 'trust' scheme of Mujaki Foods, a restaurant-support company that pays the opening costs, so it is company-backed rather than independently owned. Sixteen L-shaped counter seats; diners in 2026 were split on the strong, slightly smoky soup.

rm.bowl: 極紫龍 (Goku Shiryū, five toppings) — ¥1,100 (September 2026).

places.notes: [Ramen · build your own] A single-storey ramen house near Ginza 3-chōme that says its ramen took ten years to perfect. The soup is pork knuckle and chicken feet boiled over a fierce flame; the noodles are kneaded with wheat bran for flavour and bounce. You choose back fat, garlic, noodle width (thin or medium-thick) and firmness, chashu (pork belly or loin), and three of ten toppings: seasoned egg, menma, nori, wood ear, white onion, green onion, spinach, spicy miso, meat sauce or extra vegetables (five with the 極 bowl, ¥1,100 in 2026). Free rice with lunch, draft beer, and gyoza with house soy or miso sauces. Some diners find it close to Jirō-style when loaded with garlic and fat.

rm.bowl: 長浜ラーメン (Nagahama ramen); 博多盛 ¥1,400 (October 2026).

places.notes: [Ramen · Hakata Nagahama] The Tokyo outpost of やまちゃん, a Fukuoka business founded in 1986 as a street stall (yatai) and now shops in Tenjin and Nakasu plus this one in Ginza. The company says it moved from stall to shop without losing the yatai style. In Tokyo the menu stays centred on ramen: a milky pork-bone soup that the company describes as rich but clean and free of smell, thin noodles ordered by firmness (hard, extra hard or soft), and extra noodles. Under a red lantern and noren, it is a classic end to a Higashi-Ginza night, open until 4 a.m.; a 2026 diner remembers ending nights at Yamachan or Hashigo. Hakata-mori with toppings ¥1,400; negi bokkoshi, spicy noodles, vinegared offal, draft beer, and a free small rice at lunch.

places.notes: [Ramen · duck] A duck-ramen shop of the Keisuke brand, opened in August 2014 behind GINZA SIX. The brand belongs to Grand Cuisine, whose Keisuke shops date from 2005 and build 'ramen as cuisine' from Japanese and French technique, each brand on one theme (miso, shoyu, chicken paitan and more). Here the theme is duck: a deep duck broth, moist duck chashu, duck wontons, duck tsukemen, and 一番搾り duck-oil abura-soba (¥1,100, September 2026). Seasoned-egg kamo soba was ¥1,350 and all toppings ¥1,800 in 2026. About eight counter seats and two tables for four; diners describe a calm, Japanese-restaurant feel amid the ramen queues of the street.

places.n: the vegan marshmallooow 銀座三越店 (The Vegan Marshmallooow, Ginza Mitsukoshi)
places.hood: Ginza 4-chōme, Ginza Mitsukoshi main building B2 — direct from Ginza Stn
places.cu: Vegan cakes and baked sweets · rice-flour gluten-free cakes · takeaway counter
places.notes: [Fully vegan · some GF · takeaway] A permanent counter of THE VG MARSHMALLOOOW NEW YORK's vegan sweets brand on the B2 sweets floor of Ginza Mitsukoshi. It began as a pop-up in 2021, when medallists from the Tokyo Olympics came by, and went permanent in August 2022. More than thirty sweets are always on offer, the brand says the largest vegan range in Japan, made with no milk, butter or eggs, using soy-milk cream and rice oil. Many are also gluten-free: rice-and-soy-flour sponges for whole zuccotto cakes sold on the day, rice-flour tart cases for seasonal fruit tarts, and a Mont Blanc of Kumamoto chestnut. The cacao-mass Fort Chocolat uses no oil at all. Seasonal cakes for Christmas and Mother's Day are taken by reservation. Not every item is gluten-free, so read the labels.

It has also run an online shop with frozen delivery. · 「厳選した植物性素材の美味しさを引き出したヴィーガンスイーツ」 — vegan sweets that draw out the flavour of carefully chosen plant ingredients. · Vegan zuccotto and whole cakes; rice-flour gluten-free tarts and Mont Blanc; cacao-mass Fort Chocolat.

places.notes: [Some GF (diner-reported) · yakitori izakaya] A busy basement branch of the Fukumimi kushiyaki-bistro chain (a 2025 diner had been to its Shinjuku shop, and FUKUMIMI GINZA 6 is another), with counter, tables, sofa seats and sunken-kotatsu semi-private rooms for up to 56. Skewers are grilled at the counter; 2026 diners mention heart, bonjiri, horse sashimi, spicy stir-fried chicken and colourful side plates. It is popular with overseas visitors, and many of the staff are not Japanese. FindMeGlutenFree users list it with a gluten-free menu of skewers and salad, but the restaurant itself says nothing about gluten, so ask for salt-seasoned skewers. Cashless only, ¥660 seat charge, and reservations recommended.

places.n: 銀座とんかつ はし勝つ (Ginza Tonkatsu Hashikatsu)

places.cu: Tonkatsu and katsu curry · eel · ramen · bentō
places.notes: [GF — ask · tonkatsu] A narrow seven-seat counter facing the wall, opened in October 2023 in a former stamp shop near Higashi-Ginza. The walls are papered with menus in Japanese and English. Loin and fillet katsu sets run about ¥1,300–1,500, katsu curry about ¥1,650–1,700, and there is eel and ramen too. Diners give a ¥300 repeat coupon and cheerful service good marks, the batter and meat less so. On FindMeGlutenFree, one reviewer with a celiac card was told the kitchen can make a gluten-free tonkatsu. Nothing from the shop confirms how, so ask about the coating and the fryer before you order.

places.gfd: Ask, and expect a shared fryer. Also on the menu: katsu curry, which has a wheat-based roux, and ramen. Treat it as unconfirmed until the shop tells you how it makes a gluten-free cutlet.

places.n: KOMEDA is □ 東銀座店 (Komeda Is, Higashi-Ginza)

places.notes: [Fully vegan · Komeda's plant-based café] Komeda Coffee, which runs over 1,140 cafés nationwide, opened this one in July 2020 as its single plant-based outlet, under the slogan 「お肉を休む日を、つくろう。」 (make a day off from meat). The name puns on kome (rice) and daizu (soy), with the box □ for whatever the guest feels. The famous morning service is plant-based: toast with soy-milk spread, red-bean paste or sesame confit. In 2026 the coffee comes with oat, almond or soy milk, and the menu includes rice-and-wheat pancakes such as the salted one or fruit for ¥1,380, soy-meat burgers, soy-meat Bolognese, a soy-ham-katsu hot sandwich, an amazake smoothie and a coffee float. The bright, quiet room seats 68 and is popular for working. Expect a queue on weekends; you can take a number via LINE.

places.hood: Yūrakuchō 2-chōme, Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan B1F side alley — by Yūrakuchō Stn
places.cu: Butcher-run yōshoku set meals · ginger pork, hamburg and fries in any combination
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · butcher's set meals] A thirteen-seat counter in the basement food alley of the Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan (built 1963), run by a butcher's business and opened about forty years before 2017. Mynavi's 2017 feature met the owner, Takahashi Fusa, who serves the room herself. Tonkatsu came first; about 2007 the menu was reworked into combination sets: ginger pork cut from the same domestic loin as the tonkatsu, hamburg, menchi katsu, beef cutlet, scotch egg, sasami, aji fry and fried shrimp, any two together. Add-on fries cost a few hundred yen, and a ham cutlet was ¥100 in 2017. In 2026 sets run about ¥1,200–1,300, there are chairs outside for the queue, and staff take your order and cash in line, so food arrives as you sit. Lunch sells out of hamburg by mid-afternoon.

places.notes: [Yōshoku · family company since 1933] The Western-food restaurant of 株式会社カリオカ, a Ginza family business founded in 1933 by the grandfather of today's president, Hoshihara Takashi, as a café serving Brazilian coffee, hence 'Carioca'. In a 2015 interview he said Ginentei had marked 45 years; the company also runs bars in the same building and shops in Yokohama, five in all. It moved from Ginza 6-14-2 to the seventh floor of the Carioca Building, and the lift opens straight into a quiet room. The 'Nanban' in the name reflects the founders' aim of introducing foreign culture. Signatures: beef stew, beef cutlet, tongue stew, prawn gratin, hayashi rice, and an unusual demi-glace 'curry rice' with chunks of beef over rice tossed with red pepper. Beef-stew course about ¥6,800 (2026).

places.hood: Ginza 4-chōme, behind Kabuki-za — close to Higashi-Ginza Stn exit 3
places.cu: Stew and gratin only since 1955 · served in earthenware pots · converted storehouse
places.notes: [Yōshoku · stew and gratin since 1955] A stew house that opened in 1955 behind the Kabuki-za, long loved by actors, in an old storehouse-like building: sliding door, two tables and tatami to the right, polished stairs to more rooms. For seventy years the menu has been only stew and gratin. The stew comes in an earthenware pot, rich yet clean, which one diner calls Japanese cuisine. Sets include three small dishes (pickles, namasu, kinpira) and rice with free refills; the gratin is creamy white sauce browned with Parmesan, and the mini set pairs stew with a smaller gratin. Beef stew ¥3,300, beef and tongue ¥3,500 (October 2026, after a September price revision). Reserve the day before and you get a sorbet.

places.n: カフェ・ド・ランブル (Café de l'Ambre)
places.hood: Ginza 8-chōme, a back street near the 8-chōme crossing — 5 min from Shimbashi
places.cu: Coffee only since 1948 · aged "old coffee" · nel drip · Blanc et Noir (Queen of Amber)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · coffee only since 1948] A coffee-only shop that opened in Ginza in 1948, three years after the war, and for coffee people a place of pilgrimage. Founder Sekiguchi Ichirō, who pioneered 'old coffee' (green beans aged ten years or more before roasting), died in 2018 at 103. His nephew Hayashi Fujihiko, who was in and out of the shop as a child and working there before twenty, now runs it. The ice-box fridge and the balance scale with brass weights date from opening day and are still used to weigh every order. Hayashi pours from an enamel pot while moving the flannel dripper, into a small hammered-copper pan made by a regular. The signature is No. 7, Blanc et Noir, 'Queen of Amber': sweetened coffee chilled in a shaker, poured into a champagne glass and floated with evaporated milk (¥850 single in 2021); Café Noir blend ¥750. A cowbell rings as the door opens; in 2026 the small room fills with overseas visitors.
places.chef: 林不二彦 (Hayashi Fujihiko, owner) — founder 関口一郎 (Sekiguchi Ichirō, died 2018 aged 103) · owner (nephew of the founder) · Opened 1948 in Ginza; founder died 2018 aged 103 · Hayashi is the nephew of founder Sekiguchi Ichirō, about fifty years his junior. He spent childhood summers at the shop, began working there before twenty, and took it over "a long time ago" as a natural course rather than out of passion. · 「モタモタやっていたらおいしいものもおいしくないでしょう？ 同じ味でも手際良く出した方が、ね」 — be quick; slow service spoils good coffee. · Aged old coffee; Blanc et Noir (Queen of Amber); flannel-drip blends.

places.cu: Kissaten since 1979 · hand-drip coffee from a copper kettle · Indian-style curries · cheesecake
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the John & Yoko kissaten] Up a narrow, steep stair at the corner behind the Kabuki-za, Narusawa Hiroko opened Kinohana in 1979. She had always wanted work of her own, helped at a friend's restaurant once her children were older, and then studied coffee and café management. On 4 August 1979, its fourth day, Yoko Ono walked in, then John Lennon. Their handwritten note still hangs on the wall, and Beatles fans visit as a pilgrimage. The name comes from a book on her shelf; she loves mountain walking. Beans are delivered from the roaster every other day, ground to order and hand-dripped from a copper kettle (her teacher's habit; this is the third kettle), and she tastes every cup before it goes out. About twenty years in, a young Indian man she met through friends left a curry recipe, and the curries now fill the lunch hour: bean and vegetable curry ¥1,100 and eggplant keema, with salad and coffee for about ¥650 more (2026). Her friend has made the cheesecake since opening. There is also a John Lennon set (¥1,150).

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · nel-drip coffee since 1978] A grown-up coffee house near the Yūrakubashi crossing: a long single-plank counter, worn leather chairs, jazz, and no groups of four or more. It opened in 1978 in a basement on Yanagi-dōri and moved here about thirty years ago. Owner Hasegawa Yoshikazu began as a regular, went into coffee work, and took it over because he couldn't bear to see it disappear. He roasts everything on a classic 'buta-gama' roaster in the glass booth by the door, taking specialty beans deeper than most, and every cup is brewed through flannel; staff sew the filters themselves in quiet moments. Blends from ¥920 (2025), plus seasonal single origins, royal milk tea, chocolate cake and fruit-and-nut chiffon.

places.n: 銀座 みかわや (Ginza Mikawaya)
places.hood: Ginza 4-chōme, Ginza Mitsukoshi annex 1F — 2 min from Ginza Stn
places.cu: "French you eat with chopsticks" since the post-war years · original gratin · crab croquette · tongue stew
places.notes: [Yōshoku · Sally Weil's lineage] The shop's own history begins in September 1887, when Hosaka Yoshijirō, a descendant of a Mikawa family that served the Tokugawa, opened the Mikawaya grocery next to today's Wakō, drawn in Hiroshige IV's print of Ginza. His successor Hosaka Kōji led the Ginza street association. After the war the former president Tonaka Toyoichirō took over and reopened it as the French restaurant Mikawaya. He was one of a handful taught directly by Sally Weil, first head chef of Yokohama's Hotel New Grand. Its gratin descends from a dish Weil improvised for an unwell guest, butter rice under prawns in cream sauce, browned with cheese, the dish the rest of Japan came to call doria. The house still uses the opening recipes and serves 'French food eaten with chopsticks': pickles with rice dishes and green tea after the meal. Diners order crab cream croquettes, beef or tongue stew, hamburg, omurice, and courses from about ¥11,000; takeaway and mail order sell the croquettes and tongue stew.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · loaf-sized sandwiches] A New York-deli-looking kissaten in the alley beside the Kabuki-za, opened in 1983. When the theatre was rebuilt, the owner, Haraguchi Makoto, decided the shop needed a signature and made the sandwiches absurdly big: "one serving is a whole loaf." The bread is baked that day and very soft; the boiled-egg filling is fist-sized, and the 'special egg sandwich' uses about eight eggs. Nobody finishes, so wrapping the rest to take home is normal. In 2019 a sandwich set came with a heap of salad, soup and a drink (¥1,200). In 2026 a special egg sandwich with iced coffee was about ¥2,000, and an egg-and-potato takeaway set ¥1,000. The walls are covered in Saga Prefecture posters and signatures. Busy, shared tables, cash only, weekdays only, and it shuts when the bread runs out.

places.hood: Ginza 5-chōme, Nishi-gobankan B2F — 1 min from Ginza Stn
places.cu: Basement kissaten · aged-bean coffee · waffles and crêpes · Art Nouveau antiques
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · Art Nouveau basement] Down an unpromising staircase, or a lift, in a plain building a minute from Ginza Station is a surprisingly large, high-ceilinged, hushed room. It is filled with the Art Nouveau furniture, ceramics, antique clocks and stained glass collected by owner Ida Toshimitsu. "Customers change, but the shop doesn't," he told san-tatsu in 2019, when it had been open thirty-eight years. The coffee is mellow, made with aged beans; the Meissen Blend, Brazil-based, was ¥900 in 2019, poured into period cups, and the waffles cost ¥600. In 2026 diners came for banana crêpes topped with peaches and berries (about ¥800) and chocolate waffles, and likened the room to a Studio Ghibli set.

places.notes: [Kissaten · smoking allowed] A glass-fronted 35-seat coffee house on a back street behind GINZA SIX, opened February 2016, which calls itself a 'saten', old slang for kissaten, to keep the form alive. Manager Satō Yukie spent fifteen years at the Sapporo roaster Miyakoshiya's Ginza and Shimbashi shops; she opened it with an owner who had retired from a trading company in their forties, and her husband Ueno Ryūma, a former colleague, joined soon after. The couple now run everything. Beans are roasted in the corner almost every morning. Blend ¥900 with refills at half price (2021); Neapolitan set with a drink up to ¥1,100 (2026). One of very few cafés in Ginza where every seat allows smoking.

places.hood: Marunouchi 3-chōme, a lane between the JR tracks and the Shinkansen viaduct — 5 min from …
places.cu: Family kissaten (~1958) · big yōshoku plates · spaghetti, pork sauté, curry · smoking allowed
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · a family kissaten under the viaducts] The ground floor of a free-standing house (a mahjong parlour is upstairs) in the lane between the JR tracks and the Shinkansen viaduct, signposted 'Coffee & Lunch FUJI' with a blue Key Coffee sign. It was founded about 66 years before 2024, just nearby, by the father of the owner's husband, as a drinks-only café, and moved here in 1986. When her husband died, Fujita Keiko, then 45 and a full-time housewife, suddenly became the owner. She has run it for about forty years since, slowly building up the food. When the Tokyo Metropolitan Government was still in Marunouchi, bidders for city contracts used it as their office, and it had a row of public phones. The sasanqua outside was transplanted from the old city-hall streets. Plates are generous: pork sauté of about 250 g of loin with soup and rice (¥1,180), nine spaghetti dishes led by carbonara (¥1,250 with salad, soup and coffee), omelette curry, baked curry, chocolate parfait (¥950), coffee ¥500 (2024 prices). In 2026 two staff handle the lunch rush. Smoking is allowed.

places.hood: Yūrakuchō 2-chōme, Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan B1F, down the spiral stair — 1 min from Yūrakuchō S…
places.cu: Jun-kissa since 1965 · seasonal fruit parfait · custard pudding · red sofas and stained glass
places.notes: [Kissaten · since 1965] A glittering jun-kissa that opened with the Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan in 1965, at the foot of the spiral stair to the basement. Its first manager, a businessman who loved luxury, gave it bright red sofas, stained glass and artworks, such as a peacock made only of hearts, and most of that décor survives. The lamps on the dividing poles were once its only light; the room was brightened when older regulars said they couldn't read their newspapers. The floor is run by men in white shirts and ties, aged about fifty to seventy, under the friendly third-generation manager Noyama, and some waiters of twenty years know regulars' names, orders and seats. The seasonal fruit parfait (strawberries, cream and ice cream; melon ¥1,200 in 2026) has been on the menu since opening, alongside a firm kissaten custard pudding with sticky caramel. Blend coffee ¥800. Around 95–120 seats, quick turnover.

Staff are hired as men with kitchen and floor experience. Not tagged mom-and-pop: no owner or family is named. · Seasonal fruit parfait; kissaten pudding; blend coffee.

places.notes: [Izakaya · under the tracks since 1953] A red-lantern offal-yakitori bar inside the arched tunnel that runs under the tracks from the Hibiya side to the Ginza side, in the same spot since 1953; trains rumble overhead and the ceiling slopes like an attic. Skewers are threaded from 7:30 each morning for that day and grilled raw over charcoal at the street-side grill: kashira (here skirt, not temple), pork belly with salt, pepper and garlic miso, and tsukune in a tare topped up since opening. Order at least two of each. The beef-offal stew in a house miso (¥630 in 2024) and a Hoisu sour (¥500), the Shōwa-30s shōchū mixer, complete it. Manager Iwamoto Yūji, who has worked in izakaya since fifteen, took over during the tail of COVID. Overseas visitors photograph the place inside and out, and strangers end up talking.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · machi-chūka under the tracks] A neighbourhood Chinese restaurant under the JR viaduct by Yūrakuchō's Kyōbashi exit, ten seconds from the station. It opened here in 1967; before that it was a food stall in the 'sushiya yokochō' that stood where the Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan is now. Owner Uei Keiichi says there's no single best-seller, because regulars all have their own orders, but jokes the free house chilli oil (garlic and chilli, also sold in jars) might be it. Cooks of twenty years and more use different noodles for shōyu, miso and tsukemen, and there are monthly specials. Prices are station-cheap: shōyu ramen ¥650, or ¥750 with half fried rice; noodles ¥650–900, a dozen set meals ¥850–950 with rice, soup, pickles and seasoned nori; gyoza ¥550 with a Sichuan-pepper salt (2025). Open all day without a break.

Orders run from crisp butter toast and a banana milk float with vanilla soft-serve to omu-hayashi and a 'surprising omurice' with a shrimp-and-mushroom risotto inside (¥1,100, 2026). A good escape when the basement queues are long.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the sing-along izakaya] At the very back of the Kōtsū Kaikan basement, a neon sign and a noren mark a family izakaya where everyone sings. It began about sixty years before 2024, when the current master's father, a sandwich-board man, opened a snack-bar-cum-pub in the 'sushiya yokochō' that once stood here, hence the karaoke. It moved into the Kōtsū Kaikan around 1967 and kept the name 'Honjitsu Kaiten', 'opening today', the line those sandwich boards always carried: "so as not to forget where we started," master Abe Hisao suspects. He runs it with the mama. Regulars, mostly forty to sixty, sing Ōe Senri, YMO and Godiego and drift between tables. Most of them met here. The master, once a vocalist, will duet with you. The food is home-cooked: vegetable-heavy sauce yakisoba (¥780), black mapo tofu (¥620, or a bowl for ¥130 more), keema curry with chickpeas (¥750), karaage, curry croquettes, grilled stingray fin and oden (2024–2026). Songs cost ¥200 each. First-timers and solo drinkers are welcomed in.

places.notes: [Kissaten · since the Shōwa building opened] A basement coffee parlour that opened with the Shimbashi Ekimae Building itself. San-tatsu gives 1967, and some 2026 diners say 1966, the year the building was finished. A plastic-sample showcase marks the door, and regulars pick up a newspaper on the way to their seats; these days groups of young women come for the jun-kissa boom too. The draw is a classic pudding à la mode: a firm, eggy custard pudding with vanilla ice cream alongside (¥800 in 2022), or just pudding with whipped cream (¥530), or the 'Royal' without ice cream (¥720). There is also Napolitan with Tabasco and grated cheese (¥630) and cream soda (¥530). Shrimp pilaf comes as a set. It opens at 8 a.m. for commuters' morning coffee.

places.notes: [Yōshoku · Napolitan since the Shōwa boom] 'Pont Neuf', French for 'new bridge', so 'Shin-bashi'. It opened in 1967, a year after the Shimbashi Ekimae Building was finished, as an ordinary jun-kissa of coffee, pudding and sandwiches. Under the second manager, in Japan's boom years, it turned to hearty food for Shimbashi's salarymen: Napolitan first, then hamburg spaghetti, the 'Pont Neuf burg' and hamburg sandwiches. The third manager, Uekusa, began in 2007 helping the long-serving ladies wash dishes, and took over in 2018. He thickened the boiled-ahead spaghetti from 2.0 mm to 2.2 mm. The Napolitan is mellow rather than sharp and uses ham, not bacon. The hamburg, beef-and-pork with pepper and garlic, is finished in the oven. Both share an original sauce of minced meat and seasonings. A food critic's praise made the Napolitan famous. In 2026: Napolitan ¥1,100, hamburg spaghetti ¥1,400, and on Friday nights a bacon-and-cheese Napolitan for ¥2,000. Diners call it a 2026 Tabelog top-100 yōshoku shop.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the fish diner that never closes for a break] A popular fish house that Okada Masayuki, born 1935, opened in 1968 after training at Kanda Sanshūya. In 2020, past eighty, he was still going to the fish market every morning, Tsukiji and then Toyosu: "there's nowhere else, so what can you do." It long stood in an alley that shielded salarymen who didn't want to be seen drinking at lunchtime. When the old building came down, the shop reopened at Ginza 2-3-4, and it now stands in full view. It runs without a break from morning to night. City-hall staff came at five, newspaper reporters at odd hours. Sit at shared six-seat white-wood tables, the counter or the tatami upstairs, and order from the wall and the whiteboard: thick-cut sashimi sets (¥1,100 in 2020), a seafood bowl on warm rice, oyster-fry sets (¥1,350), and the regulars' favourite chicken-tofu pot with ponzu (¥480). Staff of twenty years and more keep it brisk rather than chatty. A 2021 Tabelog set-meal top-100 pick.

places.n: バー ルパン (Bar Lupin)
places.hood: Ginza 5-chōme, building basement — 3 min from Ginza Stn
places.cu: Bar since 1928 · Golden Fizz · Islay whisky · the literary bar of Dazai, Ango and Oda Sakunosuke
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the literary bar since 1928] A basement bar opened in 1928 by Takasaki Yukiko, a popular hostess at Café Tiger who struck out on her own with the backing of writers Kikuchi Kan, Satomi Ton, Izumi Kyōka and Kume Masao. It became a counter bar in 1935, and the slab of yachidamo ash on the counter has been in use ever since. Hayashi Tadahiko's photographs of Dazai Osamu, Sakaguchi Ango and Oda Sakunosuke sitting cross-legged here hang on the wall. It was bombed in January 1945, renamed 麺包亭 to avoid an 'enemy' word, closed, and reopened after the war as a café pouring black-market drink. When the building was rebuilt in 1972, every fixture was stored and the room rebuilt to the same layout. Yukiko worked the bar until about 1981. Her grandson Takasaki Naohiko now manages it, and bartender Hiraki Ikuo shakes Ango's Golden Fizz (egg yolk, lemon) and pours from shot glasses dating to 1928. In 2026 the room fills with fans of the anime Bungō Stray Dogs alongside old regulars. Try the Thunderclap: brandy, whisky and gin.

places.hood: Yūrakuchō 2-chōme, Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan B1F — 2–3 min from Yūrakuchō Stn
places.cu: Tonkatsu and katsudon since 1962 (from the old すしや横丁) · lard-fried domestic pork · niboshi miso soup
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · katsudon from the すしや横丁] Nakamura Bunzō's father opened a canteen in 1962 in the 'sushiya yokochō', the shanty strip of sushi bars, drinking dens and offal stalls facing Yūrakuchō Station's tracks. When the Kōtsū Kaikan replaced it, the shop came underground. In the city-hall days lunch was mobbed with civil servants and there was no day off. When the government moved out, the area's restaurants thinned and times were hard. "Customers kept coming to see my cheerful father and mother — I'm only copying them," Nakamura says. Domestic pork from his father's suppliers is trimmed, coated in coarse fresh crumbs and fried in hot lard, then simmered with tare and egg over pot-cooked domestic rice. The katsudon comes with niboshi miso soup and house pickles for ¥1,000 (2025; ¥1,100 in an October 2026 review), a remarkable price facing the station. There is also a mixed fry set of fillet cutlet, fried shrimp and fried horse mackerel. In October 2026 a dozen people were queuing before the 11:00 opening. Write your order on the mini whiteboard at the door. There are eleven counter seats. A small onigiri comes while you wait, and Nakamura serves bigger portions than his father did: 'I'm short-sighted,' he jokes.

places.cu: Kyūshū izakaya since 1978 · horse sashimi, gameni · the "high-school message notebooks" for 3,400+ schools
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the high-school reunion izakaya] A basement izakaya on Sotobori-dōri opened in 1978 by Fukuoka-born owner Matsunaga Tomokazu and run with his wife, okami Matsunaga Yōko. Ingredients are flown in from Kyūshū daily, but since the Isahaya Bay sea-gates cut off its Ariake Sea supply it no longer insists on Kyūshū alone and buys fresh fish from Kantō and Tōhoku too. The menu still leans Kyūshū: Kumamoto horse sashimi that has never been frozen, kibinago sashimi, gameni (chikuzen-ni, chicken and vegetables simmered in dashi, ¥1,050 in 2024) and black-pork belly skewers in a sweet soy tare (¥800), with sweet Kyūshū soy sauce and Fukuoka's 'Yūkun' daiginjō from Takahashi Shuzō. It is famous for something else, though: since opening, guests have filled 'high-school message notebooks', one per school, now more than 3,400 of Japan's 4,874 high schools (MEXT, 2020). The first, in 1987, was for Kurume University Fuzoku High School, started for a regular who came 300 days a year. Write your school on the memo the staff bring and they will fetch its notebook from the index. Alumni book it out nightly; courses such as the 'High School Freshman' (¥3,800 in 2026) keep a reunion simple.

places.cu: Standing sake bar of a family sake shop · ~40 seasonal and aged sakes by the 80 ml · ¥100–350 snacks, some hand-made by the okami
places.notes: [Standing sake bar · the Kurihara family's sake shop] A standing sake bar on the ground floor of the Shimbashi Ekimae Building, opened on 22 May 2012, the same day as Tokyo Skytree, by さかや栗原, a family sake shop based in Minami-Naruse, Machida. The eldest son now runs the shop, and the second son runs the sister 和酒Pub 庫裏 in the basement of the same building. The walls are lined with framed sake labels from all 47 prefectures, collected by okami Kurihara Itsuko since 1983, when she married into the shop, and sent unglued and unused by the breweries; some breweries and brands no longer exist. About 30 seasonal and 10 aged sakes are poured 80 ml at a time for ¥300–1,000, and the okami will pick one to suit a beginner. The three-glass omakase set is ¥1,000 (2024 and 2026). Snacks are mostly pickles and dressed dishes at ¥100–350. Those marked '伊', for Itsuko, are made by the okami every day: inari tinted pink with chopped red ginger (¥200), a potato salad with boiled egg whose dressing changes for the regulars (¥100), and seasoned eggs. Pay as you go: one 2024 evening came to exactly ¥1,000. In October 2026 diners praised the range for the price, including Ishikawa's Fukumasamune and Miyagi's Suminoe. It is one of a small group of 庫裏 sake bars in Shimbashi and Ginza: a 2012 reviewer called it the group's third shop, and Retty also lists a 和酒BAR 庫裏 in Ginza.

places.cu: Charcoal yakitori since 1931 · big skewers, duck, winter wild fowl · the signature "dry curry" finish
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the 1931 yakitori stall] In 1931 the founder 保立繁之助, a trained kappō cook, and his wife なか pulled a yakitori stall out from behind the Kabukiza every night and set it up in the Kōjunsha's fuel yard, where kabuki actors and Ginza's cultural crowd ate. The stall became a shop in 1939, passed to the second generation, and moved to its present site in 1958. It is now in the third generation; the Tabelog shop page describes three generations 'showcasing the strong family bonds'. The skewers are large and grilled over charcoal: duck, chicken wings, tsukune both in tare and with salt, liver, skin (¥600–850 each), and from 15 November to 15 February wild duck, teal and moorhen. The famous finish is the dry curry. The founder first made it as a staff meal, with curry powder a customer brought as a gift, before curry rice was common. Staff ask about it with your first order so they know how much rice to cook. Sake is warmed in a pure-silver kettle and poured from a height. Courses are ¥8,600 (90th-anniversary) and ¥9,500 (duck loin) from January 2025. Dry curry with chicken soup is ¥1,000 and can be taken home.

places.hood: Yūrakuchō 1-chōme, a back alley by the tracks — 1–2 min from Hibiya Stn A4/A5
places.cu: Teishoku canteen since 1920 · lard-fried katsudon on a bed of nori · daily set ¥800
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the 1920 canteen by the tracks] Opened in 1920 as a 24-hour oden stall under the Yūrakuchō tracks, it added a second shop in 1932 where The Peninsula Tokyo now stands, and settled in this alley in 1947, serving teishoku alongside oden, chameshi and even sushi. 岩崎博茂, born in 1942, became the third-generation owner in 1959, at 17, when the father collapsed: "I only do it because I had to." The wife, 君榮, already worked here and is two years older; they married at 20 and 22, and in practice 君榮 ran the shop. With their daughters, the four of them handle the lunch rush in 12–15 seats. The signature katsudon is pork in an egg-and-flour batter and breadcrumbs, fried in lard, simmered in a 'trade secret' warishita with onion and egg and served in a square box over a layer of nori. Regulars order it as a 'wakare', with the cutlet and rice served separately. In autumn 2026 the katsudon set is ¥1,000 and the daily set ¥800, with chicken katsu, tonkatsu and mackerel; popular sets sell out after 13:00.

places.n: もつ焼き ふじ (Motsuyaki Fuji)
places.hood: Yūrakuchō 2-chōme, inside the pedestrian tunnel under the JR tracks toward Shimbashi — 4–…
places.cu: Charcoal motsuyaki since the 1950s · never-frozen domestic pork offal · miso motsu-nikomi
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the tunnel motsuyaki] A half-open-air offal grill built into the wall of a tunnel under the JR tracks, with trains rumbling overhead and no front door. The previous owner told the story like this: around 1953 the space was a politician's election office, then the politician's mistress opened a rice-ball stand, and the second generation made it a motsuyaki shop. 五十嵐義幸 began helping in 1974, at 19, after a day job, kept two jobs for decades, and became the third owner in 1991. Around the change to Reiwa the business passed to the fourth generation, the son 貴洋, a former carpenter, but the father still mans the grill. Never-frozen domestic pork offal is prepped in-house from midday. The kashira uses pork skirt rather than cheek, the shiro is boiled long enough to be tender, and the tare is just soy sauce, sugar and sake, topped up as it is used. The motsu-nikomi is offal only, stewed in two misos (¥400 in 2024). Skewers were ¥180 each and draft beer ¥580 in 2024, poured by 貴洋, an Asahi-certified dispenser. In 2026 diners also praise the oden, potato salad and tsukune, and say it can sell out early. Orders are placed by phone, and on some nights the crowd is mostly overseas visitors.

places.n: 有楽町 天米 (Yūrakuchō Ten Yone)
places.hood: Yūrakuchō 2-chōme, under the JR tracks toward Shimbashi, across the tunnel from Motsuyaki…
places.cu: Edo-style tempura since 1952 · sauce-soaked "shittori" tendon · Toyosu fish at night
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the soft-batter tendon under the tracks] Opened in 1952 by a cook who had trained at the grand tempura house 天米 in Kanda Sudachō and was allowed to use its name. He died soon after, and the okami's cousin, 川口成一, was adopted into the family to become the second generation, and after more than fifty years still fries the tempura. 安子, a nurse until marrying in, has been okami for over fifty years and raised three sons. The third son, 敬紀, joined at 29 after ten years in Japanese restaurants and now leads as third generation. Seafood is fried in sesame oil. For the tendon, each piece is passed through a don-tsuyu that has been topped up since opening, so the batter turns soft and moist rather than crisp. Bowls come with a lid to keep them warm, and the rice is cooked a little firm in a two-shō pot. Lunch tendon was ¥1,200 in 2024 with a side dish, miso soup and pickles. In 2026 the limited tempura-and-sashimi set (Tue, Thu and Fri lunch) is ¥1,400, with sashimi from Toyosu, and at night tendon is ¥1,800 and kakiage-don ¥2,100. There is also omakase with sashimi and simmered fish. There are six counter seats, tables and a sunken kotatsu table for six, and a painting by Kumagai Morikazu on the wall.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the yakuzen kitchen behind the Kabukiza] A two-storey house in the alley behind the Kabukiza, named after Shennong, the Chinese god of farming and medicine. Owner-cook 三上康介 is from Iwate and the son of a cook. Working in a care home's kitchen, the owner heard residents on salt-restricted diets complain about bland food and wanted to serve 'food that keeps you from getting ill' instead. That led to yakuzen school in Tokyo, qualifications as a Chinese-medicine yakuzen practitioner and international yakuzen practitioner, two years of kitchen training, and the shop in 2020. A younger brother, 隼平, a yakuzen coordinator, looks after more than 30 house medicinal liqueurs, and their mother came from Iwate to help. Lunch is herbal curry over Iwate Hitomebore rice from a school friend's family farm, with salad, sides and unlimited herbal teas. The keema is mixed meat, onion and 20+ spices sweetened with liquorice root instead of sugar. In 2023 the cheese keema was ¥1,600, and in 2026 a two-curry plate is ¥1,800. Dinner brings samgyetang, bak kut teh, tandoori chicken and soups adjusted to a body-type check sheet, plus a mulberry-leaf tiramisu sweetened with monk fruit (¥770).

places.notes: [Yōshoku · where katsu curry was born] Founder 岡田進之助 had been head chef at Kōjimachi's 宝亭, one of the restaurants that laid the foundations of Western cooking in prewar Japan, and at the Prime Minister's residence. In 1947 the founder opened 'Grill Swiss' to make costly Western food affordable, naming it after neutral, green Switzerland out of a longing for peace. In 1948 the regular Chiba Shigeru, star second baseman of the Yomiuri Giants, wanted to eat a lot and eat fast, and asked for a cutlet on the curry rice. The result was katsu curry, still on the menu as 'Chiba-san's cutlet curry'. The curry sauce is minced meat with onion, carrot, apple and ginger, simmered for two weeks and made without wheat flour. Every meal comes with a clam-and-bacon potage, made with the same bacon supplier and evaporated-milk brand for decades. In 2022 the lunch-only original katsu-curry set was ¥1,430 and limited to 20 a day, the 'Shōwa gratin' ¥2,640 and yōshoku shumai ¥660. The shop moved to this second-floor room in February 2022, and 庄子あけみ, the third-generation mama counting from the founder, looks after the guests. In October 2026 there were queues at opening for the katsu curry, cream croquettes and hamburg-and-fried-prawn lunch sets. A branch in the Yaesu underground mall is marked closed on Tabelog (last reviews September 2025), leaving this as the only shop found.

places.notes: [Izakaya · Kagawa sake under the tracks] A two-floor izakaya under the Yūrakuchō viaduct, founded in 1976 by the father of today's okami, 武田理沙, who took over in 2022. The name comes from Kinryō, the sake of Kagawa's Nishino Kinryō brewery (founded 1789). When the brewery came to Tokyo, this was the first shop to stock it, and it still pours several Kinryō labels, unusual in the city: honjōzō from ¥500 a gō, and junmai ginjō 'Setouchi Olive' (¥500) and 濃藍 (¥880) by the glass (2024). The okami's pick is 'oyaji no genkotsu' (¥880), a boneless take on Kagawa's honetsuki-dori: mature-hen thigh from Kagawa, marinated in soy, garlic and mirin, crusted with black pepper and grilled. A veteran cook grills yakitori over charcoal (¥190 a skewer, salt or tare). There is also horse-mackerel namerō with house garlic miso (¥660), and grilled rice balls with bonito and soy (¥450 for two) to finish. The ground floor is packed elbow to elbow, with round stools and kabuki prints; upstairs is roomier, under an Itō Jakuchū rooster. The okami calls the staff the 'Kinryō Theatre' and holds a rakugo night on the first Saturday of even months. In 2026 a regular's order ran to motsu stew and cartilage karaage at ¥590 each and an eight-skewer platter for ¥1,430.

places.notes: [Izakaya · the old house by the tracks] A dark, timbered old house along the JR line that looks like a listed building among the offices. Inside are a former robatayaki counter, tables with sunken hearths that are no longer lit, and folk crafts, paintings and old tableware collected by the previous owner. 'It was founded in the early Taishō era, more than a century ago,' says manager モウさん, who came to Japan from Myanmar in 1992, has worked here since 2000, became manager in 2023 and now runs the shop as a couple. Lunch runs ¥900–1,100 (2026). The favourite is the original nikutama-meshi (¥950 in 2024, ¥1,000 in 2026): four pieces (in 2024) of pork belly braised in soy and Shaoxing wine with star anise around a whole boiled egg, with miso soup and salad. Ginger pork, tonkatsu and salt mackerel are also on the lunch menu. The big platters once lined up on the counter at night stopped with Covid. Now the menu runs to dishes such as duck with orange (¥1,100), pork belly with shishitō in tomato (¥980), yellowtail with daikon and creamy scallops (¥1,100 each). The upstairs has sunken-kotatsu seating.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · 400 years of wagashi] Founded in 1617 at Teramachi-Sanjō in Kyoto, the shop supplied sweets to the palace, the shogun's deputy, temples and shrines, and has a record of sweets made for Emperor Go-Mizunoo. It followed the capital to Yaesu in 1872 and later opened in Ginza. War destroyed both shops and only Ginza was rebuilt. After several moves within Ginza it came to this ground-floor shop in September 2022, which added a café. It is now in its thirteenth generation of the 樋口 family. いいだばし萬年堂 in Iidabashi was opened by a son of the eleventh generation and is a separate shop. The signature is 'Omedetō', a steamed sweet that looks like red rice. Take-away is the main trade, but the ten café seats serve sets with matcha. Awa-zenzai (¥1,650) uses the new Iwate millet 'Iwate Awakogane' under the house koshian, served in a wooden box with a tea snack and hōjicha. The made-to-order an-warabi with matcha (¥2,090) is bean paste kneaded with bracken starch, dusted with kinako and served with brown-sugar syrup (January 2026). Fu-manjū and the Yoshino-tsuyu kuzu sweet were on sale in 2026.

In 2013 the founder's grandson and third-generation head, 日比康造, a musician, opened 'Tsuki no Hanare' to bring that salon back. The walls change every two weeks with young artists' work, an 'oekaki set' lends you the shop's paints and a sketchbook to keep (¥1,000 in 2021), and musicians play every night for free. Tables used at Gekkōsō since the Taishō era sit among French rattan chairs. The food is Creole, which 日比 ate in New Orleans: gumbo, and pulled-pork rice in barbecue sauce (¥1,150 in 2021). There is also a whole-lemon cake (¥750) with hand-drip coffee (¥680), and the lavender 'Yosano Blue Moon' cocktail (¥1,200), after the 'pale purple sake' of Yosano's verse. A store manager runs the room day to day; in 2026 the site advertised for a successor as the current manager prepares to go independent.

places.hood: Ginza 7-chōme, fourth floor of the Ishii Kishūya Bldg — 5 min from Ginza Stn B3
places.cu: Classic Edomae sushi in the 鶴八 lineage · red-vinegar rice · 8-seat counter run by a woman taishō
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the taishō who trained at Shimizu] An eight-seat white-wood counter on a Ginza 7-chōme fourth floor, run by owner-chef 三好史恵 with one young assistant. Born in Aichi, she studied interior design, worked at a design office, spent a year in Britain and cooked in a Japanese izakaya. At 28 she apprenticed at the Edomae master shop 新ばし しみづ, of the 鶴八 lineage, and opened Sushi Take in 2014 after eight years. 'It was a completely male world,' she says. She once thought of smashing every plate and running, but all she would have heard was 'Of course she quit, she's a woman.' In the first year she opened 365 days, on almost no capital, carried by a tuna wholesaler who let her pay later, a Ginza bartender who lent cash and senior apprentices who told her never to quit. Some guests still ask whether the 'taishō' will make their sushi, mistaking the assistant for the boss. The rice is brown with red vinegar. Diners describe an omakase of appetizers and five small dishes, then twelve or so nigiri such as kasugo, kohada, shako, marinated tuna, simmered clam, sea urchin and anago, finished with tamagoyaki. There is also a sushi-only course and, unusually now, à la carte. In 2026 diners put it at ¥20,000–40,000 a head.

places.hood: Ginza 2-chōme, ground floor of the Ginza Aruka Bldg, unsigned wooden door — 7 min from Hi…

places.notes: [Mom & Pop · the couple's nine-seat counter] 'A small shop with a nine-seat counter, where the two of us, a married couple, quietly hung our noren in a corner of Ginza,' writes owner-chef 小川武士 of the shop, opened in early summer 2017. There is no sign, just a closed wooden door. The kitchen uses modern techniques, including an in-house tank, ice-temperature ageing and low-temperature cooking, alongside the inherited craft of Edomae sushi. The only menu is an omakase of 5–7 small dishes and 10–12 nigiri, about 18 courses with soup, tamagoyaki and a roll, for ¥28,600 (official site; one June 2026 diner paid ¥25,300). Rice and portion size can be adjusted. In 2026 diners describe hairy crab with crab miso, a flight of three sea urchins, miso-marinated salmon roe, smoked tuna, yuzu-scented chawanmushi, abalone, torigai and a herring served for only two weeks of the year. Sake is chosen to match the food from ¥1,800. Dinner runs in two seatings, bookings are online only, and very casual clothes and outside drinks are declined.

places.hood: Ginza 4-chōme back alley, Hatori Bldg B1F — about 1 min from Ginza Stn
places.cu: Couple-run basement kappō-izakaya · sashimi, dobin-mushi and seasonal small plates · regulars of ten years and more
places.notes: [Izakaya · the couple in the basement] A small basement eatery down a Ginza 4-chōme back alley with a six-seat counter and two tables, run, reviewers say, by a married couple, and full of regulars. One has been coming for more than ten years, another, from Noto, has eaten in Ginza for fifty years and calls it a rare find. Neither is named in any source. The cooking is careful kappō in an izakaya setting. Appetizers come intricately presented, a corn-wrapped shinjo has kernels laid as if carved off the cob, and the dobin-mushi is steamed in a teapot, with matsutake in autumn. There are sashimi platters of fine fish, heshiko and pickles, grilled crab shell, shrimp shumai, an omakase of pike conger, clear soup and sashimi, and Inaniwa udon to finish. Drinks lean to shochu, with sudachi or kabosu. Diners spend about ¥8,000–15,000.

places.hood: Ginza 6-chōme, Ginza Stn C2 exit 5 min
places.cu: Edomae sushi since 1963 · "Maguro no Kiyota" · nine-seat counter
places.notes: [Sushi · Maguro no Kiyota] A plain nine-seat counter in Ginza 6-chōme, founded in 1963 by Shigezo Fujimoto, according to a 2026 diner. It is known as 'Maguro no Kiyota' for its tuna and has passed from chef to chef. The fourth, Norihiko Yoshizawa, was born in Kyoto in 1976 and trained at Kiyota for more than fifteen years under Mr Kimura, from choosing fish to making sushi (Tabelog). In 2026 diners describe an omakase of sashimi then nigiri: Ōma tuna in akami, chūtoro and seared kama-toro, kohada from Kumamoto, kelp-cured flounder, cuttlefish, Hagi red sea urchin, anago, sea-urchin rolls and abalone rice porridge. The counter is lively, with regulars and overseas guests. It is among Ginza's priciest: ¥40,000–80,000 a head in reviews, with lunch from about ¥30,000.

places.notes: [Soba · Yamagata in a Ginza basement] A pink sign behind Matsuya leads down to a cosy, slightly worn basement room hung with celebrity autographs, serving the food of Yamagata. The owner, a woman from Yamagata, chats with guests, according to an October 2026 diner. The soba is thick, chewy country-style soba. The signature is Zaō chilled jidori soba, cold soba in rich chicken broth topped with firm, crunchy local chicken: ¥1,000, or ¥1,100 in one review, with ¥200 extra for a large. Wild-vegetable soba comes heaped with sansai sent from Yamagata, and tempura or kakiage cost just ¥200, a Ginza rarity. In the evening it serves Yamagata sake, simmered herring (¥820) and beer (¥780 a medium bottle). Lunch queues form at noon.

The owner, a woman soba-maker, makes the soba by hand each day and pours her recommended sake for regulars. Lunch runs from seiro soba with wasabi rice to a tamagoyaki set with a small soba, and a ramen limited to 20 a day (¥1,200 in 2026). The soba-yu comes in a Nambu iron pot. Saturday mornings bring a dashimaki-tamago breakfast, and dogs are welcome. At night it is a salaryman soba-izakaya: duck soba, duck hot pot, steak and a long sake list. Smoking is allowed at the tables, a sore point for non-smokers in 2026 reviews. Dinner runs about ¥8,000–10,000 with a ¥600 appetiser charge. Lunch is about ¥1,000–2,000.

At lunch office workers come for two daily set meals, usually one of them fried. The namesake 'Ariake' tempura set has shrimp, whiting and shishitō with rice, and you choose soba, udon or miso soup (¥1,200 in 2026). There is also a menchi-katsu set, a tendon set with miso soup (¥1,050) and kitsune udon (¥650). Arrive before noon to avoid a wait. From 17:00 it turns into a cheap solo-drinker's counter: okara as the appetiser, octopus and tuna sashimi, shishamo, chive omelette, yakitori and niku-dōfu, with soba to finish if you get that far. Cash only.

places.notes: [Soba · soba kappō meets Wakiya's Chinese] An eight-seat counter, with a four-person private room, on the third floor of the Wakiya building in Ginza 5-chōme, easy to miss. Reviewers say the Iron Chef of Chinese cuisine, Wakiya, opened it out of a love for soba and greets guests at the start, while Chef Mori does the cooking and a manager-sommelier pours sake. Courses mix the two kitchens. A ¥15,000 soba-kappō course in 2026 ran to appetizers, fried soba dumplings, karasumi soba, shark-fin omelette, tonpōrō, tempura, seiro soba, warm soba and a Dattan-tea pudding. Other diners mention sukiyaki in a sauce built on soba kaeshi, abalone with soba grains, soba dumplings with uni and caviar, and shark-fin soba. Special events include a summer new-soba gathering and a one-day Daidai × Wakiya collaboration menu. Expect ¥15,000–40,000 a head plus 10% service.

At a simpler lunch, sudachi soba, zaru soba and duck nanban are cooked in an open kitchen. One July 2026 diner found the tempura soggy and the prices high for the location.

A July 2026 diner says the owner trained at Ginza Yabe, the same school as Onozawa and Taiichi. The soba is short, thin, stone-ground and 100% buckwheat, served as seiro (¥1,200) with grated daikon and green onion. There is also a duck soba in a yuzu-scented broth (¥2,500). With sake (about ¥1,000 a gō) come smoked duck with white miso, two kinds of nama-fu dengaku, and light-battered tempura of wild greens, myoga, lotus root, sweet potato, pumpkin and conger eel (assortment ¥1,800). Some 2026 diners found it pricey, with doors opening a minute or two late and slow service from a small team.

places.notes: [Sushi · omakase a minute from Ginza crossing] A fourth-floor sushi restaurant in an old Ginza 5-chōme building with a clean, pleasant room inside: a counter and private rooms for 2–8, 20 seats in all. At the counter, sushi alternates with appetizers. They come with light-roast single-origin coffees like Kenyan Tim Factory and Geisha. There are also hōjicha financiers and an organic afternoon tea from ¥15,000. The chef comes from pastry, and the salon now serves lunch and dinner courses with wine, about ¥10,000–30,000. A 10% service charge applies after 18:00.

places.hood: Ginza 3-chōme behind the Kabukiza, ground floor — 5 min from Higashi-Ginza Stn
places.cu: Casual Parisian French at a 10-seat counter · game and pâté · ¥5,000 weekday lunch course
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · Paris behind the Kabukiza] A bright, playful ten-seat counter behind the Kabukiza, opened in September 2021 by owner-chef Makoto Aoki. In the chef's own words on Tabelog, Aoki was born in Tokyo in 1969 and learned the trade at the family restaurant, Ginza Sushi Aoki, and at the French restaurant L'Oiseau, moved to France in 1995 and ran Restaurant Makoto Aoki in Paris for thirteen years from 2006. The menu brought back is casual, authentic French: cucumber-yogurt soup, Parisian pâté de volaille, cod fritters with Portuguese sauce, beef-tongue brick with cochonnaille, chanterelle risotto, Amami fish with squid-ink coulis, Tokachi venison (game is the chef's reputation), foie-gras and fennel mille-feuille, and hot apple chausson with cassis sorbet. The weekday lunch petit course is ¥5,000, with half glasses of wine from ¥1,250. Wines change monthly to match the course. Regulars come back again and again (one has made 21 visits). One October 2026 diner found the room too loud to hear the chef.

Reviewers say a married couple runs it: the husband cooks, having once been head chef at a Chinese restaurant, and the wife is the sommelier. Neither is named in any source. Dishes are Japanese-French and eaten with chopsticks, with luxury ingredients used generously. It opens with beef rice noodles topped with caviar, then simmered abalone with Tosa vinegar, bonito tartare with anchovy and garlic, sweetfish with wild asparagus and karasumi, fried scallop and zucchini, a crab and eggplant soup, tenderloin steak and a pudding. Wines are chosen to match, including by the glass. Expect ¥15,000–35,000 a head. Bookings can take a month, though last-minute seats sometimes open.

Some courses add caviar and snow crab, with A5 black Wagyu as the main. Diners praise the non-alcoholic drinks list. Book about a week ahead; it was full on a weekday at 8 p.m. in October 2026.

The chef, from Kyūshū according to a long-time regular, runs it single-handed and still sends dishes out smoothly. The hors-d'oeuvres course changes each visit: prosciutto and pear, red-pepper mousse with snow crab and consommé jelly, foie-gras terrine, grilled whelk with mushrooms, sweetbreads, then a meat main. Portions are generous, and you can ask for smaller ones. In 2026 five à la carte dishes with two drinks came to ¥6,600, finished with bottarga pasta. Solo diners are welcome at the counter for a glass of wine or champagne. There is a ¥900 charge, and lunch is only for groups of four or more booking the ¥11,000 course.

The house asks guests not to come with strong perfume, scented fabric softener or tobacco smell on their clothes, to protect the aromas. A regular of more than a hundred visits calls the owner its highlight, with deep and opinionated knowledge of French wine. Glasses lean to young vintages and new producers, while bottles run deep in 1990s Burgundy, plus Alsace and the Rhône. A June 2026 diner was served at the counter by a French-speaking Mr Haba. The food is French-Italian, with trippa, pasta and risotto, which the kitchen once made off-menu with shaved white truffle. Book ahead. About ¥15,000–30,000 a head.

In Tabelog's chef text Sakata describes more than forty years in French cooking and a 'Culinary Masters' award from the agriculture ministry, work as a cultural ambassador for Iwate and Miyagi, and a commitment to domestic ingredients, which reviewers say the chef sources personally around Japan. 2026 diners describe a vegetable-forward course that does not feel heavy. It includes white asparagus and shirasu salad, truffle-topped pâté, foie gras with crunchy truffle, and bread with a fluffy six-herb whipped butter. The chef's omakase was ¥33,880 including tax in April 2026.

Regulars of ten years and more come back for the starter they always request, a cauliflower mousse. Then come venison with no gaminess, risotto heaped with truffle, rich crab miso, angel-hair cream pasta with sea urchin and caviar, and braised beef. The course was ¥12,000 in January 2026, and drinks are reasonably priced. Weekday nights fill up, while Saturday nights can be quiet enough to feel like a private booking. Lunch is a single hour, 12:00–13:00, Tuesday to Friday. ¥500 table charge.

Fugu comes first, then tempura of autumn eggplant, sanma wrapped in shiso and corn, then hanpen from Nihonbashi Kamimo (as a reviewer spells it), fresh abalone, and black-haired Wagyu fillet and strip loin. A clear soup, whiskies such as Akkeshi, Bowmore and Ardbeg, and Chablis round it out. Special fugu dinners are also offered, and one party took home a beef bento. Expect ¥20,000–40,000 a head; it suits client dinners.

There is terrace seating by the door on the ground floor and a standing-bar-like room upstairs. The 'LAZUR classic course' (¥4,800) brings couscous with chicken and vegetables, tuna brik, salad and dessert. Drinks include Tunisian Celtia beer, Casablanca, the herbal liqueur Cedratine and fig brandy with soda. The owner explains how each dish is eaten in Tunisia and sometimes pours a complimentary Tunisian drink. About ¥4,000–6,000 a head.

places.cu: Lyonnaise bistro, moved from Toranomon · quenelles, boudin noir, praline tart · à la carte made into a course
places.notes: [French · Lyon's home cooking in a basement] A 20-seat Lyonnaise bistro in a Ginza 7-chōme basement, named after chef Hisashi Wakisaka, which moved here from Toranomon. Tabelog describes authentic regional cooking from classic recipes, the food that fills ordinary Lyonnais, made without additives. The signature tarte praliné takes hours: every raw almond is peeled and coated in red sugar. Regulars order soupe de poisson, salade lyonnaise, boudin noir, quenelles, sole or flounder Dugléré, domestic beef bavette and seasonal tarts.
