places.notes: [French · Ginza's grand maison] Shiseido's French restaurant, open on this site since 1973. A doorman opens the doors onto a spiral staircase and a room by the designer Pierre-Yves Rochon. Olivier Chaignon has been executive chef since 2013. An October 2026 private-room dinner ran hairy crab with caviar and turnip mousse, shellfish and grilled mirugai, sweetfish grilled with its scales, roast pigeon with buckwheat and confit thigh, cheese, a flambéed persimmon crêpe and the tea-sweets wagon. Diners praise the fish sauces, the dessert and chocolate carts, a champagne list of seven or eight to choose from, and Grand Cru Burgundy by the glass. Service is attentive and remembers regulars' dislikes, though two October 2026 reviewers singled out a cold staff member and one long-time regular found the menu too heavy on cold dishes. One diner booked lunch three months ahead; 15% service; private rooms ¥11,000–55,000; parking for 10 cars.

One October 2026 first-timer found it nostalgic rather than memorable. 23 wines include Sicilian reds and whites.

People queue before the 5 p.m. opening and it fills within half an hour, so groups of three or more should book early. Many guests are from overseas. You order à la carte from the grand menu and a chalkboard of specials. The popular carrot rémoulade comes first, then mushroom and watercress salad, sakura-meat tartare, bouillabaisse, sautéed Spanish mackerel, cassoulet (a full order serves four), rabbit with mustard sauce, Ezo venison en croûte, bear in season and an Okukuji-egg herb omurice. Portions are generous, so don't over-order. A thick wine list; 10% service charge. One reviewer notes it has held a Michelin Bib Gourmand.

places.cu: Gucci and Massimo Bottura’s contemporary Italian · head chef Rafaela De Vita · lunch about ¥12,000, dinner tasting · non-alcoholic pairing
places.notes: [Italian · Gucci's osteria inside Gucci Namiki] The third Gucci Osteria da Massimo Bottura, after Florence and Beverly Hills: 40 seats plus an 8-seat private room, up a green elevator inside Gucci Namiki, surrounded by emerald floral prints. Rafaela De Vita became head chef in 2025, and a returning diner noticed dish names turning more classic, around dashi and charcoal grilling. The menu changes about every three months. A September 2026 lunch ran caprese 'macarons' with basil cream, a prosciutto and cheese cannolo, grissini, truffled cauliflower gratin, Hokkaido-wheat bread and a squid-ink cacciucco. Others mention tricolour ravioli and beef cheek in red wine. A non-alcoholic pairing includes a hōjicha cocktail. Lunch was about ¥12,000 (October 2026), plus a 12% service charge; private room ¥25,000 extra.

The kitchen uses luxury ingredients such as caviar, foie gras and Wagyu, and a sommelier picks the wines. In October 2026 diners had the popular course of colourful appetizers, homemade pasta and a roasted meat main, the chef's omakase with beef steak or lobster, and a prix-fixe lunch with a choice of pasta, main and dessert. About ¥3,000–4,000 at lunch and ¥8,000–15,000 at dinner, plus a ¥550 charge in the evening.

places.cu: Brewery taproom · 11 taps from its own Itabashi brewery · 100%-beef burgers, roast beef · tasting flights
places.notes: [Craft beer · under the Yūrakuchō tracks] The station taproom of Tokyo Aleworks, a brewery based in Itabashi, open since 2020 under the elevated JR tracks a minute from Yūrakuchō Station. Forty places: a short counter, tables and a standing area. Eleven taps rotate daily, and a three-beer flight is the easy way in, though it can sell out. A September 2026 flight was Tasty IPA, Downtown Tokyo Brown and Yoyogi Lazy Hazy. Food is 100%-beef burgers, roast beef (the staff recommendation) and Japanese-style potato salad. Many customers are visitors from abroad, and it works as a quick stop after an event at the Forum. One regular finds the beers less refined than they'd like. Tabelog notes allergy information is available.

The house style is kama-age spaghetti boiled to order, often in a loose, soupy sauce. October 2026 diners had a garlicky spear-squid and spinach peperoncino with lemon, a seasonal chicken, mushroom and sanshō cream pasta, and a garlic tomato soup pasta, in large sizes. Reviews are split: fans call it consistently decent, while one diner waited 40 minutes for dry, oily pasta. About ¥1,000–2,000; no table charge.

places.cu: Sicilian trattoria · homemade busiate with red-shrimp sauce, Trapani seafood couscous · lunch sets ¥2,000–3,000
places.notes: [Sicilian · behind the Kabuki-za] A 48-seat Sicilian restaurant over two floors of a small pink house behind the Kabuki-za, open since 2013. It is a branch: Tabelog notes the main shop has been listed as a Michelin Bib Gourmand. The specialty is homemade busiate (twisted pasta) in a rich red-shrimp sauce, alongside Trapani-style seafood couscous. Weekday lunch sets come with focaccia and a big salad: a traditional Sicilian tomato pasta with orange cake, or a lean bistecca with plenty of potatoes. Free-flow party plans with Peroni on draft fill the third floor. One October 2026 diner found the tables cramped and noisy, the service slow and the one-drink rule costly at about ¥800 for a soft drink. ¥400 cover at dinner.

places.notes: [Italian bar · parties a minute from Ginza Station] A 48-seat basement Italian bar with café-style sofa seating, built for welcome, farewell and birthday parties, with projector and microphone. The whole place can be booked for ¥40,000. Courses with two-hour free-flow cost about ¥5,000, with grilled black Wagyu, a seafood paella diners rate, chewy-crust pizza such as quattro formaggi, and a Camembert and mentaiko ajillo. Free-flow drinks are basic: one diner found only Asahi Super Dry and a weak highball. There is a single restroom, and large groups can make it hot and loud. ¥600 appetizer and 10% service.

places.cu: Spanish · competition-winning paellas (seafood, Valencia) and fideuà · tapas · weekend paella sets
places.notes: [Spanish · paella on the Mitsukoshi restaurant floor] The Ginza Mitsukoshi branch of VIDRIO (びいどろ), a Spanish restaurant whose paellas have won a Tokyo paella competition and an international Valencia-paella prize, and whose fideuà won in Gandia. The 48-seat room is modelled on the port town of Gandia, with comfortable spacing and semi-private areas. Paella comes in individual pans, so two people can share different ones, such as seafood and squid ink. The weekend set adds a tapas platter, ajillo, dessert and coffee. À la carte, 2026 diners liked marinated sardines with gari, Galician-style scallops, a sea-urchin and ikura gratin, a mushroom ajillo, a truffle potato galette and fried squid. Mitsukoshi points can't be used.

places.notes: [Italian · top floor with a Ginza night view] The Ginza sister of Omotesando's Casita, on the 14th floor of Hotel The Celestine Ginza, open since 2017. It has 50 seats (14 at the counter) and views over the Ginza night skyline; one diner even spotted Tokyo Tower. Staff are attentive without being stiff, and will warn you if you've over-ordered. You can order à la carte and have it served like a course. 2026 diners praise the caviar capellini, sea-urchin pasta, a white-fish main, sirloin steak and the Basque cheesecake. The lunch course lets two people share different pastas and mains. Also open for breakfast. About ¥8,000–10,000 at lunch and ¥15,000–30,000 at dinner; 10% service, plus ¥1,000 a head after 9 p.m.

places.notes: [French café · Tokyo Kaikan at Hibiya] A bright, big-windowed 52-seat café-brasserie (12 at the counter) run by Tokyo Kaikan, open since 2023 and all day from 11:00. Many come for Tokyo Kaikan's famous Marron Chantilly, fluffy chestnut under rich whipped cream, or the daily cake (chestnut in October 2026) with tea. A weekend lunch course runs salad-style hors d'oeuvres with herring, pork fillet in Marsala sauce and an assorted dessert plate. The drinks list is long, with plenty of non-alcoholic choices and a pretty house soda. Service carries Tokyo Kaikan's standards. Two-hour limit when busy.

places.notes: [Spanish · back-street bar near Higashi-Ginza] A red-themed, 54-seat Spanish bar down a back alley between Ginza Mitsukoshi and the Kabuki-za. It has cushioned sofa nooks and loft-style private rooms for two to eight, though the ceiling is low. Lunch courses (five dishes, about ¥1,000–3,000) are reservation-heavy and fully booked at peak. The draw is the seafood paella, heaped with large shrimp, crab and mussels and finished with lemon, plus a hot shrimp ajillo with baguette and a balsamic salad. Dinner adds a sparkling-wine free-flow course, and there are plenty of non-alcoholic drinks. Staff are quick and kind.

places.notes: [Italian · a Venetian back-street osteria] A 56-seat osteria recreating a Venetian back-street wine bistro, with Italian staff and the Italian government's Ospitalità Italiana mark. It has been open since 2010 on a ninth floor in the same building as Unzen. The weekend prix-fixe lunch (about ¥3,000–5,000) opens with a plate of eight appetizers, then a choice of pasta, main (diners loved the pork) and dessert. There's a queue before opening, even for those with reservations. In the evening the standing-bar corner serves small snacks with beer and wine; two people spent about ¥5,000. Some October 2026 diners found the staff brusque and one found the pasta dry.

The ¥1,200 lunch is the daily pasta (sakura shrimp in August 2026) with a generous salad, a small appetizer and a drink or coffee. It's calm after the lunch rush, and the staff are friendly. Smoking is permitted throughout at dinner, and one diner noticed a cigarette smell even at lunch. Flavours are mild.

Open since 2018. Choose beef, pork or basil-chicken meatballs, or one of each, over pasta, rice or bread with fries or mash. Pasta sauces are tomato, chili, mushroom cream or spicy mala tomato. In 2026 the meatball pasta cost ¥1,000, a meatball burger ¥1,050 and the cheese version ¥1,100, with Carlsberg at ¥650. Diners rate the pork meatballs fluffiest. Good before or between films.

places.notes: [Spanish bar · Ginza 7-chōme, smoking allowed] A 60-seat Spanish bar near Shimbashi, open since 2012, for parties, day drinking and late Fridays (to 4 a.m.). The signature is angel-shrimp paella, or you can choose your own ingredients for a custom paella, served about 20 minutes after ordering. Also pinchos, prosciutto, ajillo, sangria by the decanter and fresh cider, plus a paella and salad lunch set. Staff are friendly; a tip-based table magician appeared one October night. Note that smoking is allowed at every seat, and one diner found prices high, likely due to the location. About ¥5,000–8,000 at dinner.

places.notes: [Italian · standing bar and dining room] A lively fourth-floor osteria that opens straight off the lift into a standing bar, with a calmer 16-seat dining room at the back, open since 2019. The standing counter takes no bookings and is lunch's only option. Wine is cheap for Ginza: glasses from ¥300 to ¥900, generously poured. Counter appetizers are ¥300–450 each, and pastas about ¥1,500. 2026 diners rate the bonito and sweet-shrimp carpaccio, the seafood platter, clams in white wine, prosciutto, a colourful vegetable appetizer, lemon pasta and tiramisu. It's full by 7 p.m. on Saturdays. About ¥4,000–8,000 a head.

You order by QR code. Lunch sets with pizza or pasta (such as squid ink) include free soft-drink refills. À la carte, diners had burrata and prosciutto salad, grilled vegetables, Bolognese, Margherita pizza and a chocolate terrine, served one at a time like a course. Friendly service, but reviewers call the flavours ordinary and à la carte pricey. 10% service after 5 p.m.

places.n: ラ・セヌ (La Scene)
places.hood: Uchisaiwaichō, Mercure Tokyo Hibiya B1F — underground from Shimbashi Stn exit 7, 5 min

places.notes: [French · hotel lounge at Mercure Tokyo Hibiya] The all-day restaurant, café and bar of the Mercure Tokyo Hibiya, open since December 2023. Its 77 seats are spread over sofas, tables, a private room and a semi-private room in a basement that still gets natural light, and you can reach it underground from Shimbashi without getting rained on. Surprisingly quiet for Shimbashi. The weekend lunch set includes a drink, a choice of four appetizers and a fish, meat or pasta main, with unlimited bread. Tea-time regulars come for the seasonal fruit tart, with a crisp crust, and flavoured teas such as mango-strawberry. Truffle fries are on the bar menu. Staff were kind even to a diner in sweatpants. Tabelog lists allergy information and vegetarian options.

Lunch sets pair a paella, such as seafood, squid ink with mayonnaise sauce, or duck breast and truffle mushroom, with an assorted tapas plate and a drink. A ¥3,850 lunch course adds steak. Paella takes time, so book or expect a short wait. Dinner courses of eight dishes with two-hour free-flow start at ¥6,600; ¥550 dinner charge otherwise.

Others had the seafood doria, a summer cold pasta with espuma, lasagna, chicken fritto, an Italian omelette and eggplant and stracciatella tomato spaghetti.

Every booking gets a private or semi-private room, 72 seats in all, including a basement room good for loud groups, though tall diners found it low and warm. The menu features tender Wakahime beef, angel shrimp and hearty grilled dishes, mostly as courses with free-flow drinks (¥12,100 for three hours in October 2026) and customisable drinks. Portions are generous, and staff warn you if the next dish will take a while. Dinner only, open late.

The 26-seat terrace looks straight at Mitsukoshi and the Ginza clock tower, best from autumn into winter. Two private rooms and an 8-seat counter too. Seasonal courses lean on lightly seasoned white fish: an October 2026 dinner's favourite was a hot, crisp anago tempura, alongside grilled fish and a juicy meat main, all beautifully plated. The ¥5,500 lunch course is good value for the view, but service can drag on busy days, so leave extra time. A birthday cake for two is available.

Pork dishes stood out, and the 'shortcake' dessert looked more like panna cotta. Portions are bigger than expected. Many hotel guests are tourists. Tabelog lists allergy information. Open from breakfast.

places.notes: [Soba kaiseki · nine ways with hand-made soba] A 14-seat soba restaurant near Higashi-Ginza with table and counter seats around a big kneading bowl, open since 2013. Buckwheat from across Japan is stone-ground and made into soba by hand, then served in seasonal courses. Lunch from ¥2,000 brings appetizers (two sashimi, figs, eggplant with sesame, maitake tempura) and mori soba. The ¥7,700–9,900 'Wan' courses parade many soba: sujiko and quail-egg soba, karasumi soba, matsutake soba, and mori soba in two styles, eaten with salt or kombu water. Dinner is course-only (about ¥7,000), with 10–15 sakes by the glass. Portions are small; some order extra soba.

The ¥11,000 omakase is built around tuna, from lean through medium and fatty, with the signature negitoro piled into an 'Everest'. Sea urchin and sweet shrimp also feature, on red-vinegar rice. Pieces keep coming until time is up, in four timed sittings each evening. The chef is cheerful and full of puns; most customers are visitors from abroad, and it's often full. The lift is tricky to find.

The style is relaxed: start with appetizers and drinks, then have as much or as little nigiri as you like, in the order you like. The rice is firm and sharp with vinegar. The chef is funny and happy to drink along with guests, even boisterous groups. The omakase was about ¥40,000 in 2026 (¥46,000 including the booking fee on TABLEALL), and drinks push bills to ¥50,000+. Same price at lunch; 10% service.

The premium loin set (¥1,980 in October 2026) has a thin, very crunchy coat and meat cooked pink. Shiny rice and a counter full of condiments (rock salt, wasabi, soy sauce, chili) let you vary it; rock salt is recommended for the tenderloin. The counter chef is cheerful. One diner felt rushed to order in the queue.

It buys fish from the same wholesalers as top sushi bars. Chef Katsunari Isogai, who trained in Japan and Italy, learned fish handling at Sushi Yoshitake. À la carte from an open kitchen: the day's carpaccio, horse-meat carpaccio, burrata, tripe, mussels in white wine, cold spaghetti with Hokkaidō sea urchin and seaweed, seafood ragù with abalone (ask for the tomato version), carbonara risotto, kinmedai or nodoguro acqua pazza and roast beef. A 2026 diner describes it as run by a couple, so order everything at once. Allow 2–2.5 hours.

Seafood from the Shōnai coast is seasoned with more than 50 oils and 100 salts from around the world. Vegetables from the Yamagata main shop come as bagna cauda. A January 2026 lunch (¥7,700 with a sparkling toast) ran torched seaweed rolls, fish matched to oils and salts, the signature bagna cauda, soup, Yamagata strawberries and Japanese black tea. Dinner courses add Ezo murasaki sea urchin and Yonezawa beef, and the chef may lecture on olive oil. Opinions split: some love it, one found it 'sushi carpaccio' with oil overpowering the fish. Late-afternoon lunch seating suits theatre-goers.

Highlights included sea urchin wrapped in shiso, bonito sashimi, a fruit-tomato jelly and even a Wagyu steak. places.cu: Chef Tohru Wachi’s meat-focused French bistro since 2001 · grilled lamb, duck, foie gras · coriander "herb bomb" salad, lagman · deep wine list
places.notes: [French bistro · Tohru Wachi's meat temple, since 2001] A 22-seat basement bistro that chef Tohru Wachi (和知徹) opened in 2001 as the chef’s own restaurant and still runs; 2026 marked its 25th anniversary. Wachi is known in Japan as a master of meat, and the cooking keeps it simple: grill or simmer the best ingredients and subtract the unnecessary. Signatures include a big joint of lamb grilled rosy and carved at the table, duck, pan-seared foie gras on toast (paired with aged Yquem for the anniversary), ham, and the coriander 'herb bomb' salad. Others are fried Brussels sprouts and the popular lagman lamb noodles. À la carte, casual and bookable a day ahead; solo diners welcome. Lunch only on dates posted on Instagram.

places.cu: Small meat-forward Italian trattoria · juicy sausages, crisp roast chicken, thick sawara carpaccio · hamburg-only weekday lunch
places.notes: [Italian · a little meat-loving trattoria in Kyōbashi] A 24-seat second-floor trattoria (6 at the counter) on a quiet Kyōbashi street, open since 2011, above an abura-soba shop. Weekday lunch is a single braised hamburg plate, hearty for the price. Evenings bring an assortment of five appetizers, juicy sausages, crisp-skinned chicken, roasted onion, tripe, potato and anchovy gratin, a thick sawara carpaccio and pasta. Wine is poured generously, the staff are friendly and the crowd is calm. Book, as it fills up. The restroom is outside, a floor up, and there's no bag storage under the wall seats.

places.notes: [Teppanyaki · Kōjun Building counter since 2004] A 23-seat teppanyaki (13 at the counter plus a private room for up to ten) on the fourth floor of the Kōjun Building, open since 2004. The day's fish, meat and vegetables are shown before cooking. The August 2026 'Kobushi' lunch course (¥7,650) ran appetizers, sashimi, seafood with a stylish sauce, top sirloin butt, grilled vegetables with nama-fu, garlic rice and dessert. Staff are calm and attentive, and the chef is friendly, which suits birthdays. The garlic rice gets the strongest praise; one diner found the strip loin too fatty.

The okonomiyaki is fluffy inside and crisp outside, light rather than heavy. The ¥7,000 omakase course with free-flow ran appetizers, tonpei-yaki, grilled beef tendon, cheese tofu, octopus, chicken with zucchini, okonomiyaki and coffee jelly; higher courses add Wagyu. The weekend-only lunch is six small savoury dishes, including Daisen chicken, grilled sesame tofu, a half okonomiyaki and a half yakisoba with thick noodles. Staff are kind.

places.cu: Casual sister of a members-only steakhouse (50 years) · licensed Wagyu sashimi, crisp sirloin, strip loin and filet · rice and miso soup · curry
places.notes: [Steak · the casual 'hanare' of a members-only steakhouse] The 23-seat annex of PENTHOUSE, a members-only Ginza steakhouse celebrating 50 years. It serves traditional steak casually and holds a licence to serve raw beef. Courses start with very tender beef sashimi and a carpaccio with myōga, red onion and house ponzu. Mains are a choice of two steaks, such as strip loin and filet, or the signature sirloin with a crisp crust, eaten with rice and miso soup. Grilled leeks come with sauce, and a spicy plain curry is also served. Monaka to finish. Quiet on weeknights. One diner found the sides and abalone uneven. Several restaurants share the building, so check the floor. About ¥20,000–30,000.

places.cu: Kikkoman-run teppanyaki (since 1987, renewed 2024) · Wagyu with a Colza-only soy sauce · signature course with lobster · ¥10,000–40,000
places.notes: [Teppanyaki · the soy-sauce maker's own counter] A teppanyaki restaurant run by the Kikkoman group, opened in 1987 and moved to the Toraya Ginza Building in late 2024 as Colza. Interior wood comes from old soy-sauce barrels and the tableware is custom-made. Counter seating plus a private room. The day's ingredients are shown first. Steaks such as sirloin cap or a melt-in-the-mouth strip loin come with a Kikkoman soy sauce made only for Colza, plus onions and fried garlic. The chef's signature course in October 2026 opened with Hokkaidō-soy tofu, autumn truffle and butternut purée, then grilled lobster with persimmon and celery. Suited to business dinners and celebrations.

places.hood: Ginza 4-chōme, Ginza Izakaten Bldg 2F — near Ginza Stn
places.cu: Charcoal skewers and French bistro plates with fine wine · Burgundy and monthly by-the-glass fairs · duck, lamb, venison · counter-centred
places.notes: [French bistro · charcoal skewers and fine wine] A counter-centred 24-seat wine bistro off Ginza 4-chōme, part of the group behind auxamis.com. One regular first came 20 years ago and finds the quality unchanged. Charcoal-grilled skewers of meat and vegetables, grilled Camembert, shiitake and venison go with a five-appetizer assortment. Mains are duck or lamb, and a rice porridge makes a good finish. The sommelier keeps the wine flowing with short, witty notes, and runs monthly by-the-glass fairs (Alsace in October 2026) plus Burgundy specials. About ¥6,000–10,000 a head.

places.cu: Homely Italian and Mediterranean for 36 years · signature Gorgonzola and bread gratin · baked oysters, squid-ink risotto
places.notes: [Italian · a 36-year Ginza 1-chōme favourite] A cosy, lively 25-seat Italian on a seventh floor that is easy to miss, serving creative Italian and wider Mediterranean dishes for 36 years. Per Precious, the menu was shaped by Ichinohe (一戸) with chef Ishikawa (石川) to avoid trend-chasing. Everyone orders the Gorgonzola and French-bread gratin (a small size exists), even people who don't like blue cheese. Also popular: baked oysters, Yoshida Farm caciocavallo baked with tomato, squid-ink risotto, sautéed squid and mushrooms, avocado and vegetable plates, and good pasta. A good wine list. Hard to book at times. ¥500 cover includes garlic toast and water. One diner had heard it might be closing, so check.

Prix-fixe menus let each guest choose fish or meat. October 2026 lunches ran Tosa bonito with mustard, chestnut and truffle soup, sea bream and beef in fine sauces. Earlier French Restaurant Week menus (¥6,000) included shrimp and basil beignets, swordfish, chicken and mushroom pie, and pear tart. French staff and a French sommelier choose and explain wines. Popular for celebrations, and closed through August.

places.notes: [Seafood · fish grilled like yakiniku] A 24-seat restaurant on the 12th floor of the Ginza Mitsukoshi annex (13 at the counter, 9 in a private counter room), opened in 2025. It serves 'yaki-uo', a fish version of yakiniku developed over eight years by the founder of Tsukiji Aozora. Premium cuts are grilled in front of you, such as fatty tuna billed as 'special kalbi', with house condiments and sauces. 2026 diners started with the brain, then had fresh mehikari, a yukhoe-like dish and a sukiyaki-style course (just under ¥4,000 plus ¥400 service). The ladies' lunch adds rice with refills, cold noodles and dessert. The grill staff are chatty. Many guests are visitors from Hong Kong and Singapore. A touch salty, and slow at times.

places.notes: [Burgers · fish, not beef] A 26-seat fish-burger specialist on a ground floor between Ginza-itchōme and Kyōbashi, open since 2022, with sofa, counter and terrace seats. Rather than battered and fried, the signature mackerel burger (¥1,000) uses a grilled patty of minced fish, with a free dip such as wasabi tartar. Others include a soft-shell crab burger with nuggets (¥1,750), an eel special, shrimp and salmon burgers, mackerel spring rolls and a seafood hot dog. Diners find them light, and the nuggets surprisingly good. Open until midnight.

The draw is a free-pour tasting of about 30 wines for ¥1,200 for 60 minutes, extendable by ¥600 per 30 minutes. Dishes run ¥380–1,880. The chicken and vegetable cream stew is the hit; one diner found the ¥1,800 lasagna plain and unlike its menu photo. Course plans with free-flow wine and champagne suit company events, and there's a fully private room for ten. The building's signage is poor, so look for it beside Menya Takeichi.

places.notes: [Soba kaiseki · buckwheat in every course] A 26-seat basement restaurant near Takarachō, open since 2019, serving 'sobako kaiseki'. Courses use buckwheat from Aomori's Shirakami mountains and mix Japanese and Western styles. Dishes have included soba dumplings with an oden-like simmered dish, soba folded with egg, simmered clams, soft-shelled turtle, a squid salad, soba served in a wine glass and a signature duck soba with bright-green matcha soba. Courses from ¥6,000. Private rooms for two to eight suit business dinners, and there's a counter and lunch. Drinks are ordered by smartphone, and one diner missed having dishes explained. 10% service.

Kantō-style soba with a rich tsuyu and soba-yu at the end. Regulars order the hearty pork seiro with green onion, or half-and-half sets with a rice bowl: a mini chicken-don of freshly fried kara-age in sweet-savoury sauce (¥1,200), a new braised-pork-and-fried-egg bowl (half set ¥1,300) and katsudon (¥1,200 on a ¥50-off day). Cash only; tables are shared when busy.

places.notes: [Tonkatsu · Ginza's first tonkatsu specialist] The flagship of Bairin, called the first tonkatsu specialist in Ginza and reaching its 100th anniversary in February 2027 (per a 2026 review). A freshly renovated 28-seat basement room has a 12-seat counter with five cooks behind it. Expect a short queue at noon and many overseas visitors. Katsudon is the order: the special tenderloin katsudon with an 80 g cutlet and soft egg is admired for its balance, and the black-pork loin katsudon is ¥3,200. Finely shredded sweet cabbage and a tangy sauce come with the cutlets. Generous for Ginza.

places.notes: [Yōshoku · a Ginza original since 1924] A calm 28-seat Western-style restaurant founded in 1924, now run by its third-generation owner-chef, who trained in French cooking at a hotel (per Hot Pepper). Lunch is a quiet, quick daily special: a demi-glace simmered hamburg, menchi katsu with fried white fish, or hamburg with salad, soup and rice, plus homemade potato salad. Dinner à la carte (Hot Pepper prices) includes omurice ¥1,750, scallops in grain mustard ¥1,600, fried soft-shell crab ¥1,500, pork sauté ¥2,300, beef stew with vegetables ¥2,500 and chicken cutlet ¥2,000. The B course centred on beef stew is ¥5,800. One diner found the staff curt.

places.notes: [Soba · ultra-thin ju-wari in a Ginza alley] The main shop of Sasuga, a calm, polished soba restaurant up a quiet Ginza 2-chōme alley. It has a 6-seat wooden counter, tables, a private room and a semi-private room. The soba is made by hand from buckwheat alone (ju-wari), cut very thin, with a smooth, springy texture; one 2026 reviewer says it has held a Michelin star. Some days lunch is course-only, such as the ¥3,500 Sasuga lunch or a ¥4,600 course, served warm and cold. Courses bring soba dumplings, buckwheat with grated yam, tamagoyaki and a sobagaki with sweet red-bean soup to finish. The owner chats about the neighbourhood. It suits a stop after the Kabuki-za.

places.notes: [Steak · open until morning in Ginza 8-chōme] A 28-seat basement steakhouse opposite Don Quijote, open since 2023 and running from lunch until 6 a.m. on weekdays. It's known on social media for a 1-pound (450 g) steak lunch at ¥2,200, served as three medium-rare pieces with onion sauce. A 400 g hamburg with rice is also ¥2,200. Ribeye, chicken and toppings are on the lunch menu, and dinner adds tender Wagyu. Diners call it great value, though the vegetables are minimal and the large rice small. The omakase course (¥9,800 in 2026) opens with a clean liver pâté, then about eight well-grilled skewers, including clean-tasting liver and tsukune with egg-yolk sauce, with salad and tofu between. Staff keep an eye on each guest's pace, and English-speaking staff draw many overseas visitors. A wide drinks list, with beer at ¥1,080; a 10% service charge is added. Two reviewers found it pricey for what it is.

Staff bow you in at the lift. The chef's omakase runs seasonal appetizers, tender black Wagyu and seafood teppan such as black abalone and Ise lobster. A Saturday-lunch hamburg steak (over ¥3,000) won over a sceptic. Attentive, accommodating service suits anniversaries and business dinners; one diner found the seating less suited to client meetings.

It serves 'new yet nostalgic' Western dishes with traditional technique. Lunch regulars come for the hamburg-and-fry set (¥1,600: a thick hamburg in slightly bitter demi-glace with fried shrimp and croquette) and the mixed fry (shrimp, squid, tenderloin cutlet, croquette, with optional fried oysters), served with mushroom potage and rice. The ¥5,500 evening course with free-flow runs appetizers, fried scallops, a hamburg main and curry rice to finish. One private room (up to 4).

Cakes include a pink domestic-strawberry Melusine shortcake and a rich cheesecake; drinks include a sweet-tart raspberry soda. Weekday lunch brings dishes like thick-cut bacon and pumpkin doria with crisp bread. Attentive staff.

Unlike the main shop, it takes reservations; walk-ins sometimes get a counter seat. Choose omakase, where you say stop when you've had enough, or order à la carte. Regulars rate the chicken neck and chōchin (the egg-bearing oviduct), which sell out, and the grilled deep-fried tofu and bell peppers. Skewers take time, and one sixth-time visitor in October 2026 got an uneven night. Seating fee ¥1,000; dinner runs about ¥10,000–15,000 a head.

Grilled rare over charcoal, it comes sizzling on an iron plate; you press it with a hot lid to the doneness you want, or staff cut it at the table. Three sauces come with it: onion, balsamic and a standout whole-grain mustard. A 200 g hamburg was ¥2,300 in 2026 (brown rice is an option), and the ¥3,000 lunch course adds appetizers, consommé and curry rice. Dinner turns to steaks, seasonal grills and a wine list (cover ¥500), with many overseas visitors. Private rooms for 6–20.

Every plate pairs two yōshoku classics at half size, such as Napolitan with an egg sandwich (¥1,200), Ginza miso curry with katsu toast, or a hamburg with crab-cream croquette (¥1,900), so you can try several. Two à la carte dishes are labelled vegan: falafel steak and maitake hummus. Desserts include pudding à la mode (¥800) and a chocolate parfait; the wine list leans natural. Some find the portions small for the price. Cashless only.

places.notes: [Soba · Hakone's Akatsuki An on the Mitsukoshi restaurant floor] The Ginza Mitsukoshi branch, since 2010, of the Hakone soba house. Buckwheat is stone-milled in-house every day and the noodles are made by hand in view; the head chef, Ozaki, learned directly from soba master Kunihiro Takahashi. The dipping sauce blends several Makurazaki katsuobushi, with different broths for hot and cold soba. The striking dish is a smooth, firm, jet-black charcoal soba. Tororo zaru (¥1,800 in 2026) and tender duck tsukesoba are regulars' picks. Open straight through the afternoon, it is handy for a 4 pm lunch, and families and overseas visitors fill the 34 seats (six counter, six semi-private). Kind, attentive staff.

Tea comes by the pot, from white teas to flavoured blends and about four seasonal autumn teas, and staff help you choose, including a tea that holds up with milk. Cakes, some made with tea, were ¥1,980 in October 2026; the iced tea is famously huge. Afternoon queues can run 45 minutes on busy days, though a weekday 1:30 pm visit walked straight in. Air-conditioning runs cold, and staff will adjust it.

Shoes come off at the door (slippers if you're barefoot), and there are tatami and private rooms for two or four. The Hana course runs appetizers and sashimi before sukiyaki of melt-in-the-mouth Wagyu; a premium sukiyaki set brings 120 g of beef with rice, though one diner found the dipping sauce salty. Service is warm and polished, with many overseas guests. Families get kids' bento; one family's allergy details were confirmed by email ahead, and a child got a birthday gift. 12% service charge all day.

Its signatures are bouillabaisse and seasonal seafood such as lobster; one diner loved a lighter Thai-style bouillabaisse. Lunch is great value: ¥1,800–2,000 sets with a shared salad platter (with couscous) and a choice of pasta (such as liver bolognese), gratin or curry. There are 38 seats at the entrance bar, counter, tables and a terrace over Hibiya Park, handy before the Hibiya theatres. Walk-ins sometimes get in at Saturday noon.

places.notes: [Yōshoku · Tsubame Grill's Ginza main shop] The flagship of the Tsubame Grill yōshoku chain, at its current site in Ginza 1-chōme since September 2025, with 40 seats and a calm room. The signature is the Tsubame-style hamburg baked in aluminium foil; there are also Japanese-style and seasonal-vegetable hamburgs, steak and a seafood cream croquette. Nearly everyone remarks on the tomato farci salad, a whole chilled tomato with a filling and dressing. Most dishes are over ¥2,000, and lunch orders go through your phone. Children and strollers are welcome, though there are no high chairs.

The house signature is pil-pil, salt cod slow-cooked in olive oil with garlic and chilli until cod and oil meld into one; reviewers add Iberian ham, tortilla, Galician octopus, crab gratin, wine-braised beef and squid-ink rice. Txakoli is poured from height in the Basque way, alongside 50+ Spanish wines (mostly by the bottle). Staff with Dalí moustaches set the mood. Open to 2 am on weekdays; charge ¥400; smoking only at the entrance terrace.

places.notes: [Yōshoku izakaya · Shimbashi's after-hours salaryman classic] A spacious basement Western-style izakaya on the Shimbashi edge of Ginza, serving since 1964 (per a regular) and open until 5 am on weeknights. The menu is nostalgic bar yōshoku, with the starred picks marked ☆: a much-loved potato salad, red octopus-shaped sausages, a plump hamburg in demi-glace, thick ginger pork or pork steak, an addictive curry pizza, Napolitan and a fluffy egg sandwich to finish. It's busy with regulars, groups and after-party crowds, and the staff are cheerful. 40 seats with a semi-private back area; table charge; weekends only for groups of 15 or more.

places.notes: [Teppanyaki · top-floor hotel teppan with a view] A 40-seat teppanyaki on the 21st floor of the Dai-ichi Hotel Tokyo, with counters and a private room for eight; one celebration party was moved to seats with a view of Tokyo Tower. The listing promotes Kobe beef; one September 2026 lunch featured Miyazaki Wagyu. The chef slowly fries Aomori garlic into chips and keeps the oil to grill the meat. Courses add a simmered-beef starter, scallops or abalone, and vegetables, ending with white or garlic rice (the garlic rice costs extra and comes after the meat). Sorbet runs ¥1,400. Lunch is about ¥6,000–10,000; service charge is included.

places.notes: [Soba · ju-wari soba high above Ginza 5-chōme] Opened in 2019, the Ginza sister shop of Komatsu An, a soba house dating from 1922: 40 seats on the 14th floor by exit A2, mostly tables, a short counter and eight private rooms in a calm, gallery-like space. Artisans make ju-wari soba from only buckwheat flour and natural water, and the courses feature tasting comparisons of soba and seasonings. Look for the Tokyo Soba tasting course (nine dishes, ¥13,000) and the lunch course (six, ¥8,000). With sake there are soba appetisers: coarse-ground soba dumplings, cream cheese cured in soba miso, dashimaki. It's quiet, with no music; one guest wished for more non-soba dishes.

places.notes: [Café · Minamoto Kitchoan's fruit kitchen above its Ginza shop] Opened 2019 over the wagashi maker Minamoto Kitchoan's Ginza head-office shop, a 36-seat café blending old and new Japanese design, with three private rooms. Every dish works in fruit, under the motto "more fruit-like than the fruit itself": beef Stroganoff in sour cream heaped with melon, pineapple, kiwi, Shine Muscat and figs, with an orange soup; pan-seared sea bream on watermelon and tomato salad or with muscat. Finish with a crisp fruit mille-feuille or banana pound cake, or seasonal fruit sodas. There can be a wait; browse the wagashi downstairs meanwhile. A bit pricey; English menu; dinner service charge 10%.

places.notes: [Sushi · Ginza's Edomae house since 1885] Founded in 1885 and now run by the fourth-generation owner 杉山衛 (Sugiyama), president since 1992, who is known for pioneering sushi with wine. Sugiyama's line is that the Ginza sushi counter is "a place for courtship". There are 40 seats: a white-wood counter of 24 (some upstairs) and three tatami rooms. The site highlights tuna, hoshi-garei (spotted flounder), shinko, kohada and sweet shrimp; reviewers single out an unusual shima-aji and shiitake nigiri and gentle classic rice. The owner chats warmly at the counter, easing the formality, and the wine pairing wins converts. It's also a stop for fans of the writer Ikenami Shōtarō. Dinner runs about ¥20,000–40,000. The group also has Marunouchi Building and Kōjun Building shops.

places.notes: [Soba · chicken tsukesoba by day, soba izakaya by night] A 40-seat second-floor shop in Ginza Inz 2 that began as a tsukesoba specialist and now doubles as an izakaya. At lunch, the draw is a labour-intensive rich chicken dipping soba (ramen-like but lighter), plus curry soba with shrimp tempura. At night there's crispy Ōyama chicken, good fatty tuna sashimi (about ¥1,500) and fried kisu with ume and shiso, finished with fragrant stone-milled seiro soba (¥680). Drinks include picked sake and an Ichiro's Malt highball. Friendly, quick staff; an otōshi charge applies in the evening; a few find it slightly pricey.

Daily fish are shown on a big platter to choose from, and staff prepare natural bluefin, botan shrimp, sea urchin and big nodoguro in front of you; one table had its nodoguro served half simmered, half grilled. Courses at about ¥11,000–12,000 might run sashimi, homemade satsuma-age, salt-grilled nodoguro, a seafood or tuna negima hot pot with Inaniwa udon, and clay-pot rice, with Nakamata shochu sent direct from the distillery. A 16-visit regular loves it; one diner found the fried shrimp heads greasy. Card only; 5% service charge.

The signature is funajo-meshi, a rice bowl heaped high with salmon roe at the table while staff beat a drum. Charcoal-grilled thick shiitake, sashimi and simmered eggplant also win praise. Staff are friendly and loud with the kanpai, and large groups make it noisy. Open to 3 am on weekdays. Smoking is allowed inside, so it's not one for smoke-sensitive diners.

places.notes: [Health food · the protein canteen on Corridor-gai] A 44-seat branch of the Kinniku Shokudō ("Muscle Canteen") chain, open since 2018 up a flight of stairs on Ginza Corridor-gai. Every item lists calories and protein-fat-carb numbers, and meals start with a small cup of protein shake. The signatures are a lean-beef hamburg and a surprisingly moist 200 g chicken-breast steak, plus skinless grilled chicken, domestic beef steaks, salmon and limited red-meat platters, with craft beer or wine. One dieting regular credits it with a 10 kg loss; another diner called the value merely average for Ginza. Seat-only bookings are capped at 90 minutes when busy; no cover charge.

Dinner courses feature wagyu; one diner rated a Shinshū beef rib-roast steak the highlight but found the course thin for the price. Staff are warm, and there are six private rooms (2–8; +10–20%). The shop asks you to mention allergies when booking.

places.notes: [Breakfast · hotel buffet with live sukiyaki] A 46-seat breakfast-only buffet on the second floor of Hotel Musse Ginza Meitetsu, open to non-guests since 2021 (enter from the hotel's second floor, which confuses some). It's a 50-minute all-you-can-eat (¥2,700 in September 2026) of small bowls made with homemade dashi, arranged prettily in a wooden masu box. Staff cook live sukiyaki and pork shabu-shabu in front of you, and there's salad, bread, curry and desserts; the grape juice gets praise. Calm and bright with attentive staff. The common gripe is that 50 minutes feels short; hotel guests take priority when busy.

The house beef is Arita wagyu, which the listing says won gold at the 2025 World Steak Challenge. The famous dish is a limited green-onion-wrapped tongue, bundled like an inari pouch and served with dashi; there's also offal and cold noodles, and à la carte diners pick their meat from packed portions. A gentle charcoal fire means no rushing. Courses with all-you-can-drink keep it reasonable, and ask about rare sake off the menu. The booking form asks about allergies.

places.notes: [Japanese · Akiyama's "super kappō" a minute from Ginza crossing] Open since 2004, a Japanese restaurant over two floors (46 seats), reached along a stone-paved passage scented with incense. The 9-seat counter faces an open kitchen where chef Yoshihisa Akiyama cooks what the listing calls "new Edomae Tokyo style". The seasonal omakase might run sesame tofu, conger eel, somen with sea urchin and junsai, charcoal-grilled ayu, beef shabu wrapped round a thick yuba roll, and mushroom or corn rice with red miso soup. It ends with the famous shaved ice (pumpkin in autumn). The signature vegetable dish is a nikogori terrine of ten vegetables. A sake sommelier pairs drinks; service is attentive without hovering. Tabelog Award Bronze 2017 and 2018; dinner ¥20,000–40,000; no under-12s.

A demi-glace hamburg set is also popular. Weekday lunch fills fast, so book the 11:00 entry (the only bookable slot). Reviews range from "zero guilt, full stomach" to one diner unimpressed by the vegetables and the dim lighting.

places.notes: [Yōshoku · bottomless bread above the anpan bakery] The third floor of the Ginza Kimuraya bakery building at Ginza crossing: 48 table seats serving classic yōshoku, with unlimited house bread with every dish. Regulars rave about the wheaty baguette, the soft, slightly sweet round rolls and the raisin bread. The beef stew (¥2,900 in 2026) is packed with beef and balanced sweet-sour; there's also a shrimp gratin (¥2,480), chicken and prosciutto salad (¥1,900), overflowing crab cream croquettes and hamburg curry gratin. No reservations: about 10 groups were waiting at 1 pm on one October day, but seating came within 30 minutes, some by the window. Kids' menu, strollers welcome; English menu; allergy information available.

places.notes: [Teppanyaki · Okinawa on the Mitsukoshi top floors] The Ginza branch, since 2010, of a steakhouse from Okinawa, on the 12th floor of Ginza Mitsukoshi, with 40 seats (5 at the counter) and blue tableware. Many staff are from Okinawa too. Chefs grill Wagyu sirloin or fillet, Kumejima prawns, vegetables and tofu in front of you, with Okinawan touches: a green papaya starter, purple sweet potato, goya champuru, sanpin tea and a zenzai topped with shaved ice. Lunch starts at ¥4,200 (a thigh-steak set with salad, teppan vegetables, tofu, champuru, rice and dessert), with Orion beer at ¥900 and garlic rice extra. Service is attentive.

The prix-fixe lets you pick a starter, main and dessert; regulars rave about the duck, recommended mussels, a jelly and a chocolate dessert. It's good value for Ginza (lunch about ¥4,000–5,000, dinner ¥6,000–10,000), though one table waited long between courses and spent three hours. Walk-ins are sometimes possible at Saturday lunch.

The house signatures are a special wagyu roast beef served since opening and a lavish caramel pudding parfait created by the house pastry chef and finished in front of you (¥2,200), plus Spaghetti Vivalentino, about 150 cocktails and plenty of whisky. Weekday afternoons are café time (iced coffee ¥1,200); until 5 pm you may bring cake from the affiliated shop downstairs at no charge. Evenings carry a ¥1,650 cover and two orders each. From 1 November smoking is allowed all day and under-20s may not enter.

It won double honours at the International Fideuà Championship in Spain in 2014, and its paella is made by a chef who is a certified judge; the paella can sell out at lunch. The ¥1,600 lunch lets you mix options such as shrimp-and-mushroom pasta and a prosciutto-studded hamburg. At night, try tomato and anchovy salad, mushroom ajillo, stuffed squid with a standout sea-urchin sauce and squid-ink paella. Queues at weekday lunch; some find the salad and tortilla salty.

The beef curry is a standard and the pork curry a quiet favourite. Course A (¥8,500) runs an amuse, tuna confit and more; lobster comes with seasonal vegetables. Desserts include chocolate cake and parfaits. A 4 pm visit walked straight in; 10% service charge.

It stays open to 22:00, or 23:00 Wednesday to Saturday, so late evenings are quiet with little waiting, and window seats look toward Ginza Mitsukoshi. No reservations; there is a designated smoking area.

It serves court-style Russian dishes alongside Ukrainian, Georgian and Uzbek specialities, with wines from Georgia, Moldova, Romania and Bulgaria. Portions are big. Important for allergies: it says it cannot accommodate dairy, egg, wheat, pork, mushroom or green-onion allergies.

places.notes: [Soba · Tanakaya's Ginza main shop] The 80-seat main shop of the Edo-style soba house that has kept the tradition since 1956, on two floors of tables and private rooms near the Sony-dōri and Miyuki-dōri corner. The buckwheat is stone-ground, and seasonal fish and vegetable tempura is fried light in sesame oil. Adults come to drink first, ordering tempura, seasonal snacks such as returning bonito, ginkgo and ayu, and shochu cut with soba-yu, then finish with zaru soba. Warm soba in a well-made broth and a crisp ten-don suit solo lunches. The room is calm and the crowd mostly older; Ginza prices. The Matsuya Ginza 8F branch is listed separately.

It serves thin, smooth, chewy Inaniwa noodles. Seiro ni-aji (¥1,400 in October 2026) comes with two dips, soy and a rich sesame miso; there's also tempura seiro with plump shrimp, tempura udon, a sweet-glazed ten-don, chicken tempura seiro and butter chicken curry. Lunch queues form before opening: take a number on the tablet outside and wait for an SMS. Evenings are calmer, but a 10% service charge applies after 5 pm. Many overseas visitors; orders by QR code; prices are high for udon.

places.notes: [Sushi · Midori's queue-famous Ginza branch] The 82-seat Ginza branch of the Umegaoka-born Sushi no Midori chain, on the Corridor side of Ginza 7-chōme, known for generous toppings at moderate prices. Expect queues: one weekday lunch took two hours from 11:00, and evening tickets go out from 4 pm, with about ten people waiting before then. Premium and omakase nigiri come piece by piece; extras such as daimyō mackerel and off-menu grilled squid tentacles with onion and butter can be ordered. Around ¥3,000–6,000 a head. Many overseas guests. It's busy and brisk: a 45-minute limit applies, and one diner found some staff curt; another found the rice tightly packed.

Chefs cook Ukai-selected beef in front of you, along with abalone (one diner's best of the meal) and seasonal courses. Autumn brought sea bream en croûte, clam soup, chestnut soup and a chestnut Mont Blanc, with extra matsutake to order; earlier menus ran black-wagyu tartare and strip loin with black pepper sauce. Wine and sake pairings are offered. Tabelog Award Bronze 2017–2020. Lunch about ¥15,000–20,000. Strict cancellation fees; service charge rises from 13% to 15% on 1 December 2026.

In 2026 it moved a short walk toward Shimbashi into a bright, stylish space (Tabelog's opening date is 1 October; one reviewer says January), with 30-plus table seats, a big counter with power outlets and friendly staff. The signatures are the egg sandwich and a tuna-egg-cucumber mixed sandwich (¥1,300, takeaway too), plus omurice and Napolitan. Lunch brings limited sandwiches and sets with a drink, such as pork ginger at ¥1,500. Hot coffee is ¥800. It's open until 4 am on weeknights; staff ask about smoking when you enter.

places.notes: [Soba · ju-wari soba and sake on Sukiya-dōri] A soba-and-sake restaurant on the second floor along Sukiya-dōri in Ginza 6-chōme, with a white-wood counter, tables and private rooms; reviewers compare it to a fine ryōtei. The owner makes ju-wari soba from Hitachi Aki buckwheat (rooted in a native strain from the old Kanasagō village), stone-milled fine with the inner husk to keep its aroma and sweetness. Evenings run to Japanese courses and plentiful soba-house appetisers, such as nori, miso-cured cream cheese, salted fish, dried squid, karasumi, tamagoyaki and homemade satsuma-age. Finish with soba, perhaps under a jumbo prawn tempura, and soba-yu cut with Ashibi shochu. Reviewers praise the owner's hospitality. On weekdays 15:30–18:00 there's a lower-priced ten-don and ju-wari soba deal. Dinner ¥10,000–20,000.

places.notes: [Regional · Yamagata around an irori, seven floors up a Ginza back street] Step out of the lift in an ordinary back-street building and you're in what feels like an old hot-spring inn, with an irori hearth where vegetable and fish skewers are grilled in front of you. The cooking is Yamagata's: sweet peppers, konnyaku, taro, tsukune and hatahata over the coals, beef grilled in a magnolia leaf, sashimi, and the prefecture's itasoba to finish. Local sake comes in a bamboo tube and is poured from a height. Courses start with six small appetisers; dinner runs ¥8,000–15,000. Reviewers praise the owner's and staff's warmth, and it's a favourite for business entertaining and farewells. Moved here from the Eldor Building.

The katsu is cooked fresh and cooled quickly for takeaway, and goes out in smart black bags meant as late-night gifts. There's a pork mille-feuille katsu sandwich of 16 layers (¥1,300), a salt katsu of eight layers of domestic beef tenderloin with Sicilian rock salt and butter (¥1,800), and an "egg katsu" sandwich with a fried egg. Prices are steep, and one buyer found the pork katsu dry ten minutes after buying. English menu with photos.

places.cu: Stand-up soba chain with seats too · chilled tanuki soba ¥500 · pork soba · freshly fried anago tempura · ten-don and cold soba sets · unlimited spring onion · from 7 am
places.notes: [Soba · Komoro Soba by the Kabukiza] A Komoro Soba branch near the Kabukiza with both standing and seated areas: buy a ticket at the machine, hand it over and grab a spot. It's quick even when busy, and prices are fantastic for the location. Picks include chilled tanuki soba with crisp tempura bits (¥500 in August 2026), pork soba, freshly fried anago tempura, and a ten-don set with cold soba. Firm, well-cooked noodles; pile on the free spring onions. Open from 7 am on weekdays, 7:30 Saturday, 8 Sunday.

places.n: RISTASIX (Courtyard by Marriott Ginza Tobu)
places.hood: Courtyard by Marriott Ginza Tobu Hotel 1F, Ginza 6-chōme — 3 min from Higashi-Ginza Stn e…
places.cu: Hotel all-day dining and lounge · Western, Asian and ethnic menu (pho) · seasonal Shine Muscat afternoon tea (¥6,000) · holiday lunch buffets · breakfast from 6:30
places.notes: [All-day dining · the Courtyard Marriott Ginza's lounge] The chic, urban all-day restaurant and lounge on the ground floor of the Courtyard by Marriott Ginza Tobu Hotel, opened with the hotel's renovation, in black and grey with blue-green accents. It serves breakfast from 6:30, then a Western-Asian-ethnic menu to 22:00; one regular is delighted it has pho. Prices are reasonable for a hotel lounge. The seasonal draw is afternoon tea: the 2026 Shine Muscat set (weekdays from 1 August to 31 October, 11:30–15:30 entry, 3-hour stay, ¥6,000) ran from white-peach soup to Shine Muscat tart and cannoli. Lunch buffets appear in holiday seasons. Friendly staff; birthday plates on request; no extreme casual wear.
places.chef: Opened with the hotel’s renovation (October 2026 review) · Hotel restaurant (rista6.courtyardginza.com). · Afternoon tea; all-day dining.
places.gfd: Ask. Hotel all-day dining with pho, seasonal lunch buffets and a Shine Muscat afternoon tea (tarts, cannoli, mousse); no source mentions gluten-free handling.
places.vgd: Ask. The menu mixes Western, Asian and ethnic dishes (pho is offered); no vegan dish is named.
places.hours: Daily 6:30–10:00 (breakfast) and 11:30–22:00 (Tabelog; may change). Smart-casual dress (no extreme casual wear).

places.cu: Meat-heavy izakaya in the Shimbashi Yokochō alley · beef-bone ramen · yakisoba · "mugen piman" · noodles and rice bowls · late nights · smoking allowed
places.notes: [Izakaya · a meaty stop in Shimbashi Yokochō] An izakaya up a flight of stairs in the Shimbashi Yokochō food alley under the tracks, cramped and cheerfully cluttered in the classic tavern way. The menu balances meat, fish and vegetables, but the hearty meat dishes stand out, with noodles and rice bowls to keep a young crowd going. Recent orders include beef-bone ramen and yakisoba after midnight, and "mugen piman" peppers. Staff are energetic and quick. Smoking is allowed, and hours aren't published. Expect ¥2,000–5,000.

places.hood: Caretta Shiodome B2F, Shiodome Yokochō food hall — 1 min from Shiodome Stn, 6 min from Sh…
places.cu: Tonkotsu "Italian ramen" · signature tonkotsu carbonara ramen (egg yolk, cheese, black pepper, prosciutto) · tonkotsu Genovese · seasonal fruit cold noodles · lunch sets ¥1,350 · finish with rice as risotto · pizza bar at night

rm.bowl: 豚骨カルボナーララーメン (tonkotsu carbonara ramen) — ¥1,100 in May 2026; ¥1,350 as a lunch set in June 2026.

places.notes: [Ramen · tonkotsu carbonara ramen in the Shiodome Yokochō food hall] Originally an Italian restaurant in Narashino, Chiba, reinvented as a ramen shop in a TV revival project led by Shinobu Sakagami of Gindaco, it moved into Caretta Shiodome's Shiodome Yokochō food hall in February 2026. You sit anywhere in the hall and order by phone. The signature tonkotsu carbonara ramen is a creamy pork-bone broth thickened with egg yolk, cheese and black pepper, clinging to thin, slightly firm noodles like pasta. It's topped with prosciutto, and fans add rice to finish it risotto-style. There's also a basil-scented tonkotsu Genovese, a plain tonkotsu ramen, cold ramen, and seasonal fruit cold noodles made with Asakusa Kaikarō noodles (Shine Muscat, then Nagano Purple grapes). Lunch sets are ¥1,350; the special has three slices of chashu and triple cheese. At night it becomes "Ita Bar", serving pizza, meat and sake.

places.n: ビヤホールライオン 銀座七丁目店 (Beer Hall Lion Ginza 7-chome)
places.hood: Ginza Lion Bldg 1F, Ginza 7-chōme on Chūō-dōri — 3 min from Ginza Stn
places.cu: Japan’s oldest surviving beer hall (1934) · Art Deco hall with a barley-harvest glass mosaic · Sapporo Black Label in big mugs · Ginza roast beef (from 13:30 weekdays, 12:30 weekends) · currywurst, fish and chips
places.notes: [Beer hall · Japan's oldest beer hall, 1934] Opened in 1934, designed by Eizo Sugawara and spared in the war, this is Japan's oldest surviving beer hall and a registered tangible cultural property: a "drinkable" landmark. Inside the heavy arches and scratch-tile façade is an Art Deco hall with barley-shaped green mosaic columns and a great glass mosaic of the barley harvest over the counter. Drink Black Label by the mug (the mega mug equals three glasses) with the signature currywurst, fish and chips, fried oysters, or the infrared-roasted Ginza roast beef with gravy, carved from 13:30 on weekdays and 12:30 at weekends. Expect queues on Friday evenings and many overseas visitors; prices have risen. The 2F beer restaurant serves dishes such as omu-hayashi and takes course bookings.

places.n: 東京會舘 銀座スカイラウンジ (Tokyo Kaikan Ginza Sky Lounge)
places.hood: Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan 15F (lift to 14F, then stairs), facing Yūrakuchō Stn
places.cu: Tokyo Kaikan French with a city view · "Tokyo Kaikan and Me" course ¥6,600 · traditional double consommé · sole meunière · marron chantilly · former revolving lounge, every seat by the window
places.notes: [French · Tokyo Kaikan's lounge over Yūrakuchō Station] Tokyo Kaikan's 118-seat restaurant on the 15th floor of the Tokyo Kōtsū Kaikan, right in front of Yūrakuchō Station. It was once famous for revolving; it no longer turns, but every seat faces the windows over Ginza. Take the lift to 14F and the stairs up. It serves Tokyo Kaikan's traditional French in modern form: the "Tokyo Kaikan and Me" course (¥6,600) runs a quiche amuse, the house double consommé (much praised), and sole meunière, a classic since opening. Other dishes include a dab with white-wine butter sauce and the famous marron chantilly, with unlimited bread. Opinions split: some love it for celebrations; one diner felt you pay for the view. 15% service charge.

places.n: 日比谷松本楼 (Hibiya Matsumoto-ro)
places.hood: Inside Hibiya Park (Hibiya-kōen 1-2) — 2 min from Hibiya Stn exit A14
places.cu: Historic Hibiya Park yōshoku · 1F grill and garden terrace · Showa-style sweet European curry · omurice with your choice of sauce · shrimp and scallop omurice in tomato sauce ¥1,850 · cake sets · weekend queues
places.notes: [Yōshoku · the restaurant inside Hibiya Park] A long-established Western-food restaurant set in Hibiya Park; this record covers the ground-floor grill and the garden terrace (the third-floor French dining room, Bois de Boulogne, is listed separately). The signature curry is a sweet, fruity, European-style Showa curry. Omurice comes with a choice of sauce and a side such as hamburg, fried shrimp or crab cream croquette. A shrimp and scallop omurice in tomato sauce was ¥1,850; a poulet, cake and coffee set ¥2,800, with seasonal fruit cakes shown at the table. The outdoor terrace is the joy of a fine day (paid special seats exist), and staff seated a party of 12 together. Expect a 30-minute wait at weekends or during park events; only the terrace open-deck table can be booked. Party plans with free-flow are about ¥8,500.
